title: Idaho Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: Idaho treats any money a tenant deposits for a purpose other than rent as a security deposit. At the end of the tenancy it must be refunded, except amounts needed for the contingencies the deposit arrangement specifies; nothing may be kept for normal wear and tear. The refund is due within 21 days, or within the time the lease fixes, never later than 30 days after the tenant surrenders the property, with a signed, itemized statement and a detailed list of expenditures for anything kept. After first giving the landlord three days' written notice demanding its return, a tenant may sue over a deposit not returned as required; the court may award three times the actual damages, and the winning party recovers attorney fees unless treble damages are awarded.

title: No Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: Idaho sets no limit on the amount of a residential security deposit.

title: No Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: Idaho does not require a landlord to pay interest on a security deposit or to hold it in an interest-bearing account.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: If a rental property changes ownership during a tenancy, the new owner becomes liable for refunding the security deposits made for that property. A seller should transfer the deposits, and a buyer should account for them at closing. A buyer also takes over the seller's remedies against the tenant for rent and lease breaches.

title: Separate Deposit Account for Third-Party Managers
bodyText: When a residential rental is managed by a third-party manager for the landlord, the security deposits must be kept in a separate account at a federally insured financial institution, apart from the manager's operating account. The rule does not apply to the property owner itself, managers with common members or principals with the owning entity, real estate licensees, or nonprofit business organizations established under Idaho Code Title 30, Chapter 30.

title: Nonrefundable Fees and Deposits
bodyText: Idaho has no statute allowing a 'nonrefundable deposit'. Any amount a tenant deposits for a purpose other than rent is a security deposit and must be refunded except for the contingencies the deposit arrangement specifies. A separately stated fee, such as a cleaning or lease-initiation fee, is a fee rather than a deposit only if it is not a deposit in substance; it must be stated in the rental agreement and be reasonable. Calling a deposit 'nonrefundable' does not make it so.

title: Pet Deposits Are Security Deposits
bodyText: In Idaho a pet deposit is a security deposit. It is refundable at the end of the tenancy except for the contingencies the deposit arrangement specifies, on the same deadline and with the same itemized statement as any other deposit. Monthly pet rent should be stated in the lease; whether Idaho treats it as rent (which the fee statute does not limit) or as a fee that must be reasonable is unsettled. A landlord may not charge a pet deposit, pet rent or any extra charge for a service dog.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: Idaho's unclaimed property act has no specific rule for tenant security deposits. A refund a landlord owes but cannot deliver appears to fall under the act's catch-all: it is presumed abandoned five years after the tenant first had the right to demand it. What the landlord must then do as a holder under the act was not researched. A lease term letting the landlord keep an unclaimed refund has no support in Idaho law.

title: Late Fees Must Be Reasonable
bodyText: Idaho sets no fixed cap or grace period for late fees, but any fee charged to a residential tenant, including a late fee, must be reasonable. For rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, the landlord may not charge a late fee larger than the amount the rental agreement states. Under a written lease, a late fee the lease does not include may be charged only after the landlord gives the tenant 30 days' written notice of the change.

title: Fees Must Be in the Lease
bodyText: For rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, an owner may not charge a tenant a fee, fine, assessment, interest or other cost larger than the amount the rental agreement states. Under a written rental agreement, a charge the agreement does not include may be imposed only after the owner gives the tenant 30 days' written notice of the change. Every fee must also be reasonable. The rule does not limit the amount of rent.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: For any residential lease, an Idaho landlord must give the tenant written notice at least 30 days before a rent increase takes effect.

title: Nonrenewal Notice
bodyText: An Idaho landlord who does not intend to renew a residential lease must give the tenant written notice of that intention at least 30 days before the nonrenewal.

title: Changing Month-to-Month Terms
bodyText: For a month-to-month lease, an Idaho landlord may change the lease terms by written notice given at least 15 days before the end of a month. The change takes effect at the end of the month, and becomes part of the lease if the tenant stays on. Rent increases need 30 days' written notice instead, and a fee change under a written lease needs 30 days' written notice.

title: Three-Day Notice to Pay Rent
bodyText:
To evict for unpaid rent, an Idaho landlord must first serve a written three-day notice requiring payment of the amount due, stated in the notice, or possession of the property. The notice must also tell the tenant that if a court enters judgment against the tenant, a residential tenant will have 72 hours to remove belongings before the landlord may remove and dispose of them. It may be served any time within one year after the rent became due. For the landlord to recover attorney fees, the notice must also tell the tenant that attorney fees will be awarded to the prevailing party.

Notices are served by personal delivery; or, if the tenant is away from home and work, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion there and mailing a copy; or, failing that, by posting a copy on the property, delivering a copy to a resident if one can be found, and mailing a copy. A subtenant in actual occupation must be served too.

title: Notice for Other Lease Breaches
bodyText:
For a breach other than unpaid rent, an Idaho landlord must serve a written three-day notice requiring the tenant to perform the lease term or give up possession; the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the lease or another interested person can save the lease by performing within the three days. No notice is needed if the breached term cannot afterward be performed.

A tenant who assigns, sublets or commits waste contrary to the lease ends the lease by doing so, and the landlord may recover possession after a three-day notice to quit. Because the statute also lists covenants not to assign or sublet among those enforced by the three-day notice to perform, which notice fits an unapproved sublet is unsettled.

A lease can also reserve a right of reentry: Idaho Code § 55-210 allows reentry on three days' notice, and § 55-212 then allows an ordinary district-court action for possession, without notice, once the right has accrued.

The library does not offer a separate reentry clause. Its default clause already lets you end the lease and recover possession, but only after written notice and a chance to cure, and a clause making reentry accrue without notice would give up that standard to gain only a slower ordinary action; how § 55-212 fits with the three-day notices is case law. A landlord who wants it can add a custom clause, after taking advice.

title: Drug Activity Evictions
bodyText: A tenant is in unlawful detainer if anyone is or has been engaged in the unlawful delivery, production or use of a controlled substance on the leased premises during the lease term; the statute states no notice or cure period for this ground. In an action only for possession of a tract of five acres or less, a landlord with reasonable grounds to believe that someone is or has been engaged in that activity may use the fast possession track: the court sets trial within 12 days of filing, continuances are limited to two days without a rent bond, and the case is tried to the judge without a jury. Joining a damages claim gives up the early trial.

title: Idaho Eviction Process
bodyText: Idaho evictions are unlawful detainer actions in the district court of the county where the property is. In an action only for possession, for nonpayment of rent or drug activity, on a tract of five acres or less, the court sets trial within 12 days of filing (not if a damages claim is joined), the summons must be served at least five days before trial, continuances beyond two days need a rent bond, and the judge decides without a jury. Other evictions follow ordinary timing, and factual issues are tried to a jury unless waived. Complaints and answers must be verified. A judgment for the landlord after a breach, nonpayment or drug activity declares the lease forfeited, and the court assesses damages and any rent due; an appeal does not stop enforcement unless the court orders it, and a tenant who appeals must post an extra bond for the rental value.

title: Belongings After an Eviction Judgment
bodyText: After a court rules for the landlord, a residential tenant has 72 hours to remove belongings (commercial tenants and tenants of five acres or more have seven days). The landlord may deliver the writ of restitution or ask the sheriff to deliver it. After that time, and three days after the court's finding, the sheriff removes the tenant, and the landlord may remove and dispose of the tenant's remaining property, including a vehicle removable under Idaho towing law, without compensating the tenant, subject to any security interests under Idaho's secured-transactions law. The court may award the landlord reasonable costs of removal and restoration for good cause.

title: Eviction Record Shielding
bodyText: For unlawful detainer cases filed on or after January 1, 2025, all court records are automatically shielded from public view if the whole case was dismissed, no appeal is pending, and either three years have passed since filing or the parties have filed a stipulation to shield. The parties can still see the records, and any party may petition to seal eviction records under the Idaho Supreme Court's administrative rules. Shielded cases are removed from public court records, so landlords searching those records will not see them.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: An Idaho landlord may not remove a tenant by force, threats or intimidation, or by breaking in; that is a forcible entry or detainer, and the court may enter judgment for three times the tenant's actual damages. The landlord must use the court's unlawful detainer process. Idaho has no statute specifically addressing lockouts or utility shutoffs by a landlord; both carry the same risk.

title: Removing Squatters
bodyText: An owner may ask the county sheriff to remove people unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling who are not current or former tenants under a rental agreement the owner authorized, are not immediate family, entered property not open to the public, refused to leave when told, and are not in pending litigation with the owner. The owner submits a verified complaint in the statutory form; the sheriff serves a notice to vacate immediately and restores possession, and may stand by while the owner changes locks. A wrongful use of this remedy exposes the owner to actual damages, statutory damages of three times the fair market rent, costs and attorney fees. This remedy cannot be used against a current or former tenant; for those the landlord must use an eviction. A separate court track for forcible detainer by people who never had a lease with the owner sets trial within 72 hours, excluding weekends and holidays.

title: Lease Void for Lewd Use
bodyText: If a tenant or occupant uses the premises for lewdness, assignation or prostitution, Idaho law makes the lease void at the owner's option; possession reverts to the owner, who may re-enter without court process. Because re-entry without process carries forcible-entry risk if the facts are disputed, landlords should get legal advice before relying on it. The state, a prosecutor or a county resident can also sue to abate a moral nuisance, which can close the building for a year.

title: Holdover Damages
bodyText: A tenant who stays after the lease ends without the landlord's permission is in unlawful detainer. In the eviction case the court assesses the landlord's damages and may enter judgment for three times the actual damages. Idaho has no statute fixing holdover rent or a double-rent penalty. No Idaho statute bars a lease from setting a daily holdover rate either, but the library does not offer one: the statutory measure already reaches every holdover the landlord sues over, as the actual damages (normally the rental value for the time the tenant stays) that the court may treble, and a contract rate would sit inside that trebled figure. A landlord who wants a set holdover rate can add their own clause and should take legal advice first. For agricultural land, a tenant who holds over for more than 60 days without a demand for possession is treated as renewing for another year.

title: Attorney Fees in Landlord-Tenant Cases
bodyText: In any eviction or other action under Idaho's landlord-tenant chapter, the prevailing party, landlord or tenant, is entitled to attorney fees, except where treble damages are awarded. For a nonpayment eviction, the landlord gets fees only if the three-day notice told the tenant that fees would be awarded to the prevailing party. Outside that chapter, Idaho awards fees to the prevailing party where the amount pleaded is $35,000 or less; a plaintiff must have made a written demand at least 10 days before suit and gets no fees if the defendant tendered at least 95% of the award before suit. Fees may also be awarded against a party who sues or defends frivolously.

title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs
bodyText: An Idaho tenant's remedy for a landlord's failure to maintain the property is a lawsuit for damages and specific performance, not rent withholding or repair-and-deduct. Before suing, the tenant must give the landlord three days' written notice listing each failure and demanding cure, delivered personally, to an employee at the landlord's place of business, or by certified mail. If the landlord does not cure within three days, the tenant may sue; a suit only for specific performance gets a trial within 12 days, and the court may award three times the actual damages. The one statutory repair-and-deduct right is for missing smoke detectors.

title: Landlord Maintenance Duties
bodyText:
Idaho has no general habitability code for rentals, but a tenant may sue a landlord who:
- fails to provide reasonable waterproofing and weather protection
- fails to keep in good working order the electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling or sanitary facilities the landlord supplies
- maintains the premises in a way hazardous to the tenant's health or safety
- fails to return a security deposit as required
- breaches a lease term materially affecting health and safety
- fails to install approved smoke detectors.

The landlord must verify at the start of each rental agreement that the smoke detectors work; the tenant maintains them after that.

title: No General Retaliation Statute
bodyText: Idaho has no general statute barring a landlord from retaliating against a residential tenant for complaints or for exercising legal rights. Idaho's Human Rights Act does bar reprisals against anyone who opposes housing discrimination or files or helps with a discrimination charge (Idaho Code § 67-5911; the Act reaches rentals, Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)), and federal fair housing law separately prohibits retaliation for fair housing complaints.

title: No Landlord Entry Statute
bodyText: Idaho has no statute setting how much notice a landlord must give before entering a rental or limiting when a landlord may enter. Entry rights come from the lease, which is why the Idaho lease sets a 24-hour notice with an emergency exception.

title: No Local Rent Control
bodyText: Idaho cities and counties may not enact, keep or enforce ordinances that regulate the rent, fees or deposits charged for leasing private residential property, or that force owners to participate in an optional federal housing assistance program. Local governments keep control of housing they own. Other local rules, such as rental registration or short-term rental rules, are not preempted by this section.

title: Housing Vouchers and Source of Income
bodyText: Idaho law does not protect source of income, and a city or county may not require owners to participate in an optional federal housing assistance program such as Housing Choice Vouchers. An Idaho landlord may decline vouchers unless federal law or a program agreement the landlord signed requires otherwise.

title: Idaho Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Idaho's Human Rights Act makes it unlawful, in renting or leasing, to discriminate because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin or disability; to refuse to rent or negotiate; to set different terms; to misrepresent availability; or to advertise, use application forms or ask questions indicating a discriminatory preference. It also requires allowing reasonable disability modifications at the tenant's expense. The rental of a unit in an owner-occupied building for no more than two families, and of rooms in the lessor's own home, are exempt from these housing rules. Federal fair housing law adds familial status and has its own exemptions.

title: Service Dogs in Rental Housing
bodyText: In Idaho a person with a disability may not be denied housing for rent because they are accompanied by a service dog, and may not be charged anything extra for it, though the person is liable for damage the dog causes. Intentionally violating this is a misdemeanor, and the person harmed can sue for damages plus punitive damages equal to the other damages, at least $500. Idaho's definition of a service dog covers only dogs individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the disability; emotional support animals are not service dogs under Idaho law, but federal fair housing law may still require accommodating them.

title: Misrepresenting a Service Animal
bodyText: It is a misdemeanor in Idaho for a person who does not have a disability, and is not being trained to assist people with disabilities, to use an assistance animal or service dog in an attempt to gain treatment or benefits as a person with a disability. The statute is not limited to public accommodations, so it can reach a false claim made to get housing benefits such as waived pet fees.

title: Servicemember Lease Rights
bodyText: Idaho has no state statute letting servicemembers end an ordinary residential lease early. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act gives qualifying servicemembers a termination right and other protections regardless of the lease.

title: No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Statute
bodyText: Idaho has no statute letting a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking end a lease early, change the locks, or be protected from eviction for calling for help. Federal law (the Violence Against Women Act) protects tenants in covered federally assisted housing.

title: No Owner or Manager Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Idaho does not require a landlord to disclose in the lease the name and address of the owner or manager. It is still good practice, and the tenant needs an address for the three-day notice the tenant must serve before suing over repairs or a deposit.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Idaho requires no radon testing or disclosure for rentals.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Idaho has no statute requiring mold disclosure or remediation in rentals. A mold condition hazardous to the tenant's health can support a tenant's lawsuit under Idaho's repair statute.

title: No Bed Bug Rule
bodyText: Idaho has no statute on bed bug disclosure or treatment in rentals.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Idaho requires no flood-zone or flood-history disclosure to tenants.

title: Former Drug Labs
bodyText: Idaho has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose to tenants that a property was used as a clandestine drug lab. But once law enforcement notifies the owner that a drug lab was found, the owner must meet the state's cleanup standards (or demolish the building), and the property must stay vacant until the Department of Health and Welfare certifies the cleanup. An owner who completes the cleanup, even voluntarily, is immune from later tenants' and neighbors' health claims based on the drug lab.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Sex Offenders Nearby
bodyText: Idaho law says no cause of action arises against an owner for failing to disclose to a transferee that property is 'psychologically impacted': for example, that a prior occupant had a disease very unlikely to be transmitted through occupancy, that the property was the site of a suicide, homicide or felony that did not affect its physical condition, or that a registered sex offender lived there or lives nearby. The statute is written for sales; whether it protects a landlord's nondisclosure to a tenant is not settled. For a sex offender living in or near the property, a separate law says you have no duty to disclose and no liability for not disclosing (Idaho Code § 18-8325); see edu-sex-offender-disclosure-id. The doubt remains for the disease and crime-site cases.

title: HOA Rental Restrictions
bodyText: An Idaho homeowner's association may not add, amend or enforce a restriction that limits or prohibits renting property in its jurisdiction, for any length of time, unless the affected owner expressly agreed in writing when the restriction was added or amended. A restriction on transfers that already applied when the owner acquired the property can still be enforced. Landlords renting in an HOA should check when any rental restriction was adopted.

title: Where Idaho Landlord-Tenant Law Lives
bodyText: Idaho has no comprehensive landlord-tenant act. Its residential rules are spread across the forcible entry and unlawful detainer chapter (eviction, tenant repair suits, security deposits, attorney fees), the chapters on estates and owners' rights (ending tenancies at will, rent-increase and nonrenewal notice, fees, the local rent-control ban), and scattered statutes elsewhere. Manufactured home parks and floating home moorages have their own residency acts, and some repair rules do not apply to agricultural tracts of five acres or more. Short-term and vacation rentals are governed separately.

title: Leases Over One Year Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In Idaho, an agreement to lease real property for longer than one year is invalid unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party being held to it. If an agent signs, the agent's authority must also be in writing.

title: How Statutory Notices Are Served
bodyText:
Idaho eviction notices to a tenant must be served in person; or, if the tenant is away from home and work, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at either place and mailing a copy to the residence; or, if those fail, by posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property, delivering a copy to a person living there if one can be found, and mailing a copy to the property.

A tenant's three-day notice before suing over repairs or a deposit goes to the landlord or agent in person, to an employee at the usual place of business, or by certified mail. No statute authorizes email service of these notices; Idaho's electronic transactions act does not exclude leases but does not change these service rules.

title: No Sales Tax on Long-Term Rent
bodyText: Idaho sales tax applies to hotel, motel and similar lodging, but not where a residence is kept continuously under a lease or similar agreement for more than 30 days. Ordinary residential leases are not taxed; short-term rentals are.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Unless a written contract fixes a different rate, Idaho allows interest of 12% a year on money due under a contract and on money after it becomes due. Judgments bear interest at 5% plus a base rate set each July 1 by the state treasurer. For written rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, an owner may not charge interest the agreement does not include (unless added on 30 days' written notice), so a landlord who wants to charge interest on late amounts should state it in the lease.

title: Foreign Adversary Rentals in a Restricted Area
bodyText: Idaho bars a foreign principal from a foreign adversary country from buying, holding, renting or otherwise controlling property inside a defined area of southwestern Idaho (the coordinates in the statute). A landlord or other private person is not required to determine or ask whether someone is subject to the ban and bears no civil or criminal liability under it; enforcement is by the Attorney General.

title: Tenant Waste and Damage
bodyText: An Idaho tenant who commits waste on the property can be sued for it, and the court may award three times the damages. Waste contrary to the lease also ends the lease, and the landlord can recover possession after a three-day notice to quit. The tenant must also keep the smoke detectors in good working order.

title: Consumer Protection Act Reaches Leasing
bodyText: Idaho's Consumer Protection Act covers leasing and renting real property, so the Act's rules against unfair, deceptive and unconscionable practices apply to advertising rentals, renting and collecting rent. In judging unconscionability, a court considers whether the landlord took advantage of a tenant unable to protect their interests, charged a price grossly above similar rentals, or induced an excessively one-sided transaction. The Act's list of unlawful practices also includes getting a signature on a contract that has blank spaces to be filled in after signing, and failing to give the consumer a legible copy of the contract when they sign. Those two items are worded for buyers and sellers, and whether they reach a residential lease is unsettled, so the safe practice is to fill in every blank before the tenant signs and hand the tenant a legible copy at signing. A tenant who loses money or property because of a practice the Act forbids may treat the lease or other agreement as voidable, or sue for actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater; a tenant who wins is awarded reasonable attorney fees, and an elderly or disabled tenant may recover an enhanced penalty in the cases the Act lists (Idaho Code § 48-608(1), (2), (5)).

title: Tenants When the Landlord Is Foreclosed
bodyText: Under Idaho's trust deed law, the buyer at a trustee's sale is entitled to possession on the tenth day after the sale, and anyone still in possession under an interest that came after the deed of trust becomes a tenant at sufferance, who can be removed on the fast eviction track without a notice. If the buyer reasonably determines on or after that tenth day that the property is unoccupied, it may dispose of titled personal property left there as other law provides, and may store untitled personal property but dispose of it only after 90 days' written notice, mailed to the last known occupant and posted on the premises (Idaho Code § 45-1506(15)). Federal law (the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act) gives bona fide tenants at least 90 days' notice and lets many finish their lease.

title: No Rental Application Fee Rule
bodyText: Idaho has no statute limiting rental application or screening fees or requiring a refund of unused fees. Bills to limit application fees failed in 2025 and 2026.

title: No Tenant-Death Statute
bodyText: Idaho has no landlord-tenant statute on the death of a tenant: the lease does not end automatically by statute, and there is no special procedure for the tenant's belongings. What happens to the lease and the tenant's belongings is left to the lease, general contract law and Idaho's probate code.

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: A person in possession or control of property is permitted to have an unauthorized vehicle towed or booted if a clearly conspicuous, large-print sign on or near the property says unauthorized vehicles will be removed or booted at the owner's expense and names the towing company. An abandoned vehicle on non-commercial property may be towed without a sign if the person signs the tow company's release. No vehicle may be treated as unauthorized and towed or booted solely because its registration is expired or improper.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Requirement
bodyText: Idaho does not require a landlord to have cause to end a tenancy at the end of a lease term or to end a month-to-month tenancy, as long as the required notice is given: one month's written notice for a month-to-month or other tenancy at will, and 30 days' written notice of nonrenewal of a residential lease.

title: No Statutory Residential Landlord Lien
bodyText: Idaho gives residential landlords no statutory lien on a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. A landlord who takes or holds a tenant's property to force payment risks liability; unpaid rent is collected through a court judgment.

title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText: If a tenant, someone in the household or a guest damages the home, for example by a fire or frozen pipes, Idaho has no casualty or rent-abatement statute: rent keeps running under the lease unless the lease says otherwise, and the tenant has no statutory right to end the lease because of the damage. The landlord can recover the cost of repair as damages, and a tenant who commits waste can be sued for it and may owe three times the damages; waste contrary to the lease also ends the lease after a three-day notice to quit. Rent lost while the home is repaired, or after the lease ends because of the damage, is recovered as ordinary contract damages, and the optional tenant-caused-damage clause says so in the lease. The tenant can still sue under Idaho's repair statute if the landlord fails a repair duty the landlord owes.

title: Banned Lease Terms in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no residential landlord-tenant act and no statute listing lease terms that are banned in an ordinary house or apartment lease. The only lists of banned rental-agreement terms are for manufactured-home lots, floating-home moorages and rent-to-own agreements for goods, and none of them reaches an ordinary rental. A few general statutes still limit what your lease can do. A term that stops either party from enforcing the contract in Idaho courts, or shortens the time to sue, is void, although an agreement to arbitrate in Idaho is allowed (Idaho Code § 29-110(1)). You may not charge a fee, fine, interest or other cost in an amount greater than the lease states, or one the written lease does not include unless you first give 30 days' written notice of the change, and every fee must be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305). You may not keep any part of a deposit for normal wear and tear, whatever the lease says (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)). Leasing is covered by the Consumer Protection Act, which makes unconscionable practices unlawful (Idaho Code § 48-603C). Idaho's statutes have no general rule, found in some states, voiding any contract term that conflicts with the policy of a statute. Whether other one-sided terms are enforceable, such as penalties, waivers of the landlord's liability for its own negligence or waivers of a tenant's rights, is decided by case law. The library does not include such terms.

title: Waiving Repair Duties
bodyText: Start with the default rule. Idaho has no habitability statute. Its rental standard is the list in Idaho Code § 6-320(a): a tenant may sue for damages and specific performance if the landlord fails to provide reasonable waterproofing and weather protection, fails to keep in good working order the electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling or sanitary facilities the landlord supplies, keeps the premises in a way hazardous to the tenant's health or safety, fails to return a deposit as the law requires, breaches a lease term materially affecting health and safety, or fails to install smoke detectors. No Idaho statute says whether a lease can waive those duties or the tenant's lawsuit, and Idaho has no general rule against waivers in residential leases. Whether a court would enforce such a waiver is a question of case law, and a one-sided waiver also risks challenge as unconscionable under the Consumer Protection Act (Idaho Code § 48-603C). Idaho's statutes also have no provision letting a tenant accept stated defects for a lower rent. The cautious course, which the library follows, is to put no waiver of these duties in the lease. The tenant's lawsuit does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

title: Changing Repair Duties by Agreement
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not say whether a landlord and tenant may agree to move the landlord's repair duties to the tenant or to change them, and Idaho has no rule like the uniform act's provision allowing a written agreement for the tenant to do specified repairs. Two points come from the statute itself. The landlord's duty to keep facilities in good working order covers the electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling or sanitary facilities 'supplied by the landlord' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2)), so the lease may state which appliances and systems you supply. And the tenant must keep the smoke detectors in good working order after you confirm at the start of the rental that they work (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6)). Idaho's statutes have no special rule for premises without a well or utility water. The Idaho lease gives the tenant ordinary upkeep and leaves the duties in Idaho Code § 6-320(a) with you. Whether a clause making the tenant responsible for waterproofing, the systems you supply or hazardous conditions would be enforced is case law, so the cautious course is not to shift those duties.

title: Material Breach of Repair Duties
bodyText: Idaho uses a materiality test in one place. A tenant may sue over your breach of a lease term only if the term materially affects the tenant's health and safety, whether the term is written in the lease or implied (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5)). The other grounds in the same section have no materiality threshold of their own: failing to provide reasonable waterproofing and weather protection, failing to keep the facilities you supply in good working order, keeping the premises in a way hazardous to health or safety, failing to return a deposit as required, and failing to install smoke detectors (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)). Before suing on any of them, the tenant must give you three days' written notice listing each failure and demanding cure; if you cure within three days, the tenant has no suit on that item (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)). Idaho's statutes give the tenant no right to withhold rent or end the lease over a material breach. The tenant's lawsuit under this section does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). What counts as material, and as hazardous, is for the courts. Because a maintenance promise in your lease can become enforceable under this section, with possible triple damages (Idaho Code § 6-317), promise only what you will do.

title: No Presumption on Rental Condition
bodyText: Idaho's statutes create no presumption about a rental's condition. Nothing presumes that a unit meeting a building or housing code satisfies your duties, that a unit is unfit, or that a reported defect is yours to fix. A tenant who sues under Idaho Code § 6-320 must set out the facts and prove the failure in the ordinary way (Idaho Code § 6-320(b)).

title: No Required Fitness Statement
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require a residential lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit to live in. Required lease contents exist only for manufactured-home lots, self-storage units and rent-to-own agreements for goods. Your duties come from Idaho Code § 6-320(a) whether or not the lease mentions them. If the lease does make a promise about condition that materially affects the tenant's health and safety, the tenant can enforce it under the same section (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5)), except on tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). The Idaho lease states your maintenance promise in its landlord maintenance section; no separate fitness statement is needed.

title: Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Idaho has no general rule that a tenant cannot waive rights in a residential lease, and no list of rights that cannot be waived. The only such rule for rentals is in the manufactured-home lot act, which doesn't cover an ordinary house or apartment. A few general statutes make particular protections binding whatever the lease says. A term that stops either party from enforcing the lease in Idaho courts, or shortens the time to sue, is void (Idaho Code § 29-110(1)). In an arbitration, a party may not give up in advance the right to be represented by a lawyer (Idaho Code § 7-906). A charge above the amount the lease states can't be imposed, one the written lease does not include can't be imposed without 30 days' written notice of the change, and every fee must be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305). You may not keep any part of a deposit for normal wear and tear (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)). Whether a lease clause waiving other statutory rights, such as the tenant's repair lawsuit or the three-day and one-month notices, would be enforced is case law. The Idaho lease waives none of them.

title: Tenant's Remedies When the Landlord Breaches
bodyText: If you fail to meet your duties, an Idaho tenant's statutory remedy is a lawsuit for damages and specific performance. It covers six failures: reasonable waterproofing and weather protection; keeping in good working order the electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling or sanitary facilities you supply; keeping the premises in a way hazardous to health or safety; not returning a deposit as the law requires; breaching a lease term that materially affects health and safety; and not installing smoke detectors (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)). Before suing, the tenant must give you three days' written notice listing each failure and demanding cure (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)), delivered to you or your agent personally, left with an employee at your usual place of business if you or your agent are absent, or sent by certified mail, return receipt requested (Idaho Code § 6-323). A suit only for specific performance is set for trial within 12 days. The court may award three times the actual damages (Idaho Code § 6-317), and the winner of a case under this chapter recovers attorney fees except where triple damages are awarded (Idaho Code § 6-324). The only repair-and-deduct right is for smoke detectors: after certified-mail notice and 72 hours, the tenant may install them and deduct the cost from the next month's rent (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6)). Idaho's statutes give an ordinary residential tenant no right to withhold rent, pay rent into court, or end the lease because you breached; the termination rights in the code belong to manufactured-home lot residents. Whether a serious breach lets a tenant treat the lease as ended is case law. The tenant's lawsuit does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for farming.

title: Clauses Excusing Landlord Liability
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not say whether a residential lease may excuse you from liability for injury or property damage caused by your own negligence, or make the tenant indemnify you for it. The statute voiding agreements to indemnify a party against its sole negligence covers construction, repair and maintenance contracts, not leases (Idaho Code § 29-114). Whether a court would enforce an exculpatory or indemnity clause in a residential lease is case law. Such a clause could also be challenged as unconscionable under the Consumer Protection Act (Idaho Code § 48-603C), and whether a clause could take away the tenant's lawsuit over the repair and safety duties in Idaho Code § 6-320(a) is also case law. A release that a person signs within 15 days after a personal injury can be disavowed within a year (Idaho Code § 29-113). The library does not include a clause excusing your own negligence. Its clauses make the tenant answer for damage the tenant, household or guests cause and require renter's insurance; the cautious course is to carry your own liability insurance rather than rely on an exculpatory clause.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: Leasing a home is trade or commerce under Idaho's Consumer Protection Act, and any unconscionable method, act or practice in it is unlawful (Idaho Code § 48-602(2), Idaho Code § 48-603C(1)). In deciding whether something is unconscionable, a court considers whether you, knowingly or with reason to know, took advantage of a tenant reasonably unable to protect their interests because of physical infirmity, ignorance, illiteracy, inability to understand the language of the agreement or a similar factor; whether you knew or had reason to know the price grossly exceeded what similar rentals cost (price alone is not enough); whether you, knowingly or with reason to know, induced a transaction excessively one-sided in your favor; and whether the conduct would outrage or offend the public conscience (Idaho Code § 48-603C(2)). A tenant who suffers an ascertainable loss of money or property from an unlawful practice may treat the agreement as voidable, or sue for actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees if the tenant wins; punitive damages are possible for repeated or flagrant violations, and an elderly or disabled tenant can recover an enhanced penalty in listed cases (Idaho Code § 48-608). The Uniform Commercial Code's unconscionability sections cover sales and leases of goods, not of a home. Idaho's statutes have no provision letting a court rewrite or end a running lease because it has become excessively burdensome. How courts apply these rules to residential leases is case law; keep lease terms balanced and explained.

title: Eviction Fees in the Lease
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes neither ban nor set a fee that a lease charges a tenant for being evicted.

Two statutes govern what you recover. In any eviction case the winning party gets attorney fees, except where triple damages are awarded, and in a nonpayment case you get them only if the three-day notice told the tenant that fees go to the winning party (Idaho Code § 6-324).

After a judgment for possession, the court may, for good cause, award reasonable costs of removing the tenant's property and restoring the premises (Idaho Code § 6-316(2)).

Any other charge, such as a flat eviction or filing fee, is a fee under Idaho Code § 55-305: it must be stated in the written lease, or added on 30 days' written notice, and it must be reasonable. Idaho's general contract statutes have no rule, found in some states, voiding damages fixed in advance. Whether a flat charge untied to your actual cost is an unenforceable penalty is case law.

The cautious course is to add no flat eviction fee, recover attorney fees and costs through the court, and use the Idaho notice-service and collection fee clauses, which state the amount or the method in the lease.

title: Liquidated Damages and Penalties
bodyText: Idaho's statutes have no rule on liquidated damages in a lease of a home. The Uniform Commercial Code's liquidated-damages sections cover sales and leases of goods only (Idaho Code § 28-2-718, Idaho Code § 28-12-504), and Idaho's general contract statutes have no section voiding damages fixed in advance. Whether an amount the lease fixes for a breach, such as an early-termination fee, is an enforceable estimate of your loss or an unenforceable penalty is decided by case law. A charge you impose on a residential tenant is also a fee that must be reasonable and stated in the written lease, or added on 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305). The cautious course: state any agreed amount in the lease, base it on a reasonable estimate of the loss you expect, and rely on proving actual damages where you can. The Idaho early-termination clause is subject to these questions.

title: No Penalty for Using Unenforceable Terms
bodyText: Idaho's statutes impose no penalty on a landlord for knowingly using a lease that contains prohibited or unenforceable terms, and Idaho has no list of prohibited residential lease terms for such a penalty to attach to. The nearest rule is the Consumer Protection Act, which covers leasing and makes unlawful any misleading, false or deceptive practice that you know or with due care should know of, and any unconscionable practice (Idaho Code § 48-603(17), Idaho Code § 48-603C). A tenant who loses money or property through one may treat the agreement as voidable or recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, with attorney fees if the tenant wins (Idaho Code § 48-608). The Act's list of unlawful practices does not name any lease term, and whether putting an unenforceable term in a lease is itself a deceptive or unconscionable practice is case law. The cautious course is to use only the library's clauses and not add terms that misstate a tenant's rights.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not say whether accepting rent after you serve a notice, or after you learn of a breach, waives the notice or the breach, and no statute says that accepting rent after you file an eviction leaves the case intact. The answer rests on case law. What the statutes do say: a three-day notice to pay rent or give up possession may be served at any time within one year after the rent becomes due (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)); within three days after a notice to perform, the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the lease or another interested person may perform or pay and save the lease (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)). The cautious course: once you have served a notice to quit or filed an eviction, do not accept rent for any period after the notice unless you intend the tenancy to continue. If you take a payment, agree in writing at the time that it does not waive the notice or the case, or return it promptly with a written explanation. No Idaho statute bars a lease clause saying that accepting rent is not a waiver, but whether one would protect you is also case law; the library does not offer one, and a landlord who wants it can add their own after taking advice.

title: Waiving or Shortening Notices to Quit
bodyText: Start with the default rule. Idaho requires written notice before you can recover possession: three days to pay rent or give up possession (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)); three days to perform any other lease term or give up possession (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)); a three-day notice to quit after an assignment, sublease or waste contrary to the lease (Idaho Code § 6-303(4)); and at least one month to end a tenancy at will (Idaho Code § 55-208). A rent increase or nonrenewal of a residential lease needs 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)). The statutes themselves drop the notice only where a breached term cannot afterward be performed (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)), and the drug-activity ground states no notice (Idaho Code § 6-303(5)). A lease with a right of reentry allows an ordinary action for possession without notice once the right has accrued (Idaho Code § 55-212), but the library does not offer a reentry clause. No Idaho statute says whether a lease may shorten or waive these notices. Whether such a clause would work is case law, and a shortened notice could cost you the fast eviction track and attorney fees, which depend on proper notice (Idaho Code § 6-310(1)(d), Idaho Code § 6-324). The Idaho lease does not shorten any of them; serve the full statutory notice every time.

title: Tenant Leaving Early and Re-Renting
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes do not deal with a tenant who moves out before a fixed-term lease ends, and do not say whether you must try to re-rent the unit to reduce what the tenant owes. Both questions are decided by case law.

The statutes that do apply: a tenancy at will ends on the tenant's written notice of at least one month (Idaho Code § 55-208(2)); no Idaho statute lets an ordinary tenant under a fixed term leave early without liability, although federal law lets a servicemember end a residential lease early in listed cases (FEDERAL: 50 U.S.C. § 3955); and no statute says when a unit counts as abandoned or how you may retake it, so if the tenant may still claim possession, use a notice and the eviction process rather than changing the locks (edu-self-help-eviction-id).

Property left behind outside an eviction has no statute either; the Idaho lease sets a notice-and-wait procedure. The Idaho lease says you will use reasonable efforts to reduce your damages from a default to the extent the law requires.

The cautious course, whatever Idaho courts hold, is to make reasonable, documented efforts to re-rent at a fair rent and credit the rent you receive against what the tenant owes.

title: Waiving Casualty and Mitigation Rights
bodyText:
Start with the default rule. Idaho has no statute on what happens to a residential lease when fire or another casualty damages or destroys the unit: no statutory right for the tenant to move out and end the lease, and no statutory rent reduction. It also has no statute on reducing damages by re-renting. So there is no statutory casualty or mitigation right for a lease to waive or keep; the question is empty under Idaho statute, and the rules come from the lease and from case law.

Separate from casualty is the tenant's lawsuit over waterproofing, the facilities you supply and hazardous conditions (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)), outside farm tracts of five acres or more (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)); no statute says whether a lease may waive it, and that is case law.

The Idaho lease's casualty clause lets either party end the lease, and reduces rent for an unusable part, when the casualty was not caused by the tenant's household or guests; its tenant-caused damage clause covers casualties the tenant causes.

title: Homestead and Exemption Waivers
bodyText: First ask whether the tenant has a homestead to waive. Idaho's homestead is the dwelling house or mobile home in which the owner lives, with its land (Idaho Code § 55-1001(2)), so a tenant renting your house or apartment normally has no homestead in it, and a lease waiver would waive nothing. The exception is a tenant who owns a mobile home placed on land the tenant rents: the mobile home itself can be a homestead (Idaho Code § 55-1001(2)). Idaho's homestead chapter has no provision for waiving the exemption in a lease or other contract. A homestead can be reached only for the debts the statute lists, such as judgments that were liens before the homestead took effect and mortgages or other consensual liens on the premises (Idaho Code § 55-1005, Idaho Code § 55-1010). For personal property, the exemption chapter also has no waiver provision, and you do not need one to collect rent: a creditor may levy on exempt property to enforce a claim for rent for any kind of dwelling place, except for property the law exempts without limit, such as Social Security, veterans' and public-assistance benefits, health aids and medical benefits (Idaho Code § 11-607(1)(a), Idaho Code § 11-603). The same rule covers damages for malicious or intentional injury to property and for offenses punishable by imprisonment in the state penitentiary, but not ordinary damages, such as negligent damage or unpaid fees (Idaho Code § 11-607(1)(a)4). A waiver of the exemption for unemployment benefits is void (Idaho Code § 72-1375(3)). The library offers no homestead or exemption waiver.

title: No Plain-Language Rule
bodyText: Idaho has no plain-language law for residential leases or for consumer contracts generally. No statute sets a readability test, requires a lease to be divided and captioned by sections, sets a minimum type size, or has a dollar threshold for such rules. The plain-language requirements in the code cover other documents, such as continuing-care agreements. Plain wording still helps you: the Consumer Protection Act covers leasing and makes misleading and unconscionable practices unlawful, and a court weighing unconscionability considers whether a tenant could not understand the language of the agreement (Idaho Code § 48-603C(2)(a)). The library's Idaho lease is written in plain words and divided into captioned sections as a drafting choice, not because a statute requires it.

title: No Required Waiver Statement
bodyText: Idaho has no statute requiring a residential lease to carry a statement listing the terms that protect the landlord or the rights the tenant gives up, and no procedure for having a lease form pre-approved by the Attorney General. Required lease contents exist only for manufactured-home lots, self-storage units and rent-to-own agreements for goods. Nothing in Idaho's statutes calls for a front-page summary of waivers; the library does not add one.

title: Completing Blanks Before Signing
bodyText: Idaho's landlord-tenant statutes do not require every blank in a lease to be filled in. The Consumer Protection Act, which covers leasing, lists as an unlawful practice getting a person's signature on a contract that has blank spaces to be filled in after signing (Idaho Code § 48-603(12)). That item is worded for buyers, and whether it reaches a residential lease is unsettled. Two other rules make blanks matter. A fee, fine or other charge not stated in a written lease can't be charged without 30 days' written notice, so a blank fee line gives you no fee (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)). And where words written or typed into a form conflict with its printed text, the written-in words control (Idaho Code § 29-109). The cautious course: complete or strike out every blank before the tenant signs, and have both parties initial any change made after signing.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy
bodyText: No Idaho landlord-tenant statute requires you to give the tenant a copy of the lease. The Consumer Protection Act, which covers leasing, lists as an unlawful practice failing to give the consumer, when they sign, a legible copy of the contract and of any other document they were asked to sign (Idaho Code § 48-603(13)). That item is worded for sellers, lenders and buyers, and whether it reaches a residential lease is unsettled. Idaho's statutes do not make a missing copy a defense to enforcing the lease. The cautious course: give each tenant a legible copy of the lease, the rules and every addendum at signing, and a fully signed copy once everyone has signed. The optional receipt clause in the Idaho lease records that you did.

title: Deadlines for Lease Lawsuits
bodyText: Idaho's deadlines for suing are in Title 5. A claim on a written lease must be brought within five years (Idaho Code § 5-216), and on an oral lease within four (Idaho Code § 5-217). Claims on a liability created by statute, other than a penalty, and claims for trespass on real property or for taking or damaging personal property, have three years (Idaho Code § 5-218). Personal-injury claims, and suits for a statutory penalty given to an individual, have two years (Idaho Code § 5-219). Claims not otherwise covered have four years (Idaho Code § 5-224), and a judgment can be enforced by suit within eleven years (Idaho Code § 5-215). Any payment of principal or interest counts as a new written promise to pay the rest, so a partial payment restarts the period; any other acknowledgment must be in a writing the tenant signs (Idaho Code § 5-238). Separately, a three-day notice for unpaid rent may be served at any time within one year after the rent became due (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)). A lease clause that shortens the time to sue is void (Idaho Code § 29-110(1)). Which period applies to a particular claim, such as a deposit refund or triple damages, is case law; the cautious course is to act within the shortest period that might apply.

title: Informal Dispute Resolution
bodyText: Idaho's statutes neither require nor expressly allow a lease term making the parties try to settle a dispute informally before going to court. A contract term that restricts either party from enforcing the contract in Idaho courts, or limits the time to sue, is void, although an agreement to arbitrate in Idaho is allowed (Idaho Code § 29-110(1)). Whether a required pre-suit notice-and-meeting step is such a restriction is case law, so the library does not offer one for Idaho for now. For repair and deposit claims the statute already requires the tenant to give you three days' written notice listing each problem before suing (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)). You may always offer to meet or to mediate before suing, and doing so never delays an eviction notice. If you use a mediator, what is said in the mediation is privileged and generally can't be used later in court (Idaho Code § 9-804), and each side may bring a lawyer (Idaho Code § 9-810). A landlord who wants a required informal-resolution clause can add one after taking advice.

title: Binding Arbitration in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho's Uniform Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid, enforceable and irrevocable, except on the grounds that would let any contract be set aside (Idaho Code § 7-901). The Act excludes only employer-employee agreements; it has no exception for consumers, residential leases or injury claims.

Two limits matter for a lease. The arbitration must not be required to take place outside Idaho (Idaho Code § 29-110(1)), and a clause may not shorten the time to sue (Idaho Code § 29-110(1)). Each party keeps the right to a lawyer at any arbitration hearing, and a waiver signed before the hearing is ineffective (Idaho Code § 7-906). The parties may agree on how arbitrators are chosen and who pays the arbitration fees (Idaho Code § 7-903, Idaho Code § 7-910), and a court confirms the award and enters judgment on it (Idaho Code § 7-911, Idaho Code § 7-914).

An arbitration clause works best when it leaves possession cases in court, since Idaho's fast eviction track for actions only for possession of five acres or less, on grounds such as nonpayment or drug activity, sets trial within 12 days and is tried by a judge without a jury (Idaho Code § 6-310(1)-(2), Idaho Code § 6-311A), and leaves small claims, up to $15,000, in the small claims department (Idaho Code § 1-2301).

No Idaho statute penalizes putting an arbitration clause, or any other term, in a residential lease. Whether a particular clause is unconscionable is judged under the Consumer Protection Act and contract law (Idaho Code § 48-603C); a balanced clause with a tenant opt-out and landlord-paid fees is the cautious form.

The library's optional arbitration clause (arbitration-agreement), offered for Idaho, fits these limits: it is held in the county where the property is, shortens no deadline, keeps the right to a lawyer, leaves possession, small-claims and deposit cases in court, lets the tenant opt out within 30 days, and has you pay the arbitration fees above the court filing fee.

title: Jury-Trial Waivers in Idaho
bodyText: No Idaho statute bans or authorizes a jury-trial waiver in a residential lease, and the library does not offer one. The Idaho Constitution keeps the right of trial by jury 'inviolate' and lets the parties to a civil action waive it only 'by the consent of the parties, signified in such manner as may be prescribed by law' (Idaho Const. art. I, § 7). The Idaho Rules of Civil Procedure (court rules) prescribe that manner once a case is filed: a party who does not serve and file a jury demand on time gives up a jury (I.R.C.P. 38(d), court rule), and the parties can agree to a trial by the judge (I.R.C.P. 39(a)(1), court rule). Neither rule mentions a waiver signed before any dispute. You seldom need one for an eviction anyway. A case only for possession of property of five acres or less, for nonpayment of rent, drug activity on the premises or forcible detainer, 'shall be tried by the court without a jury' (Idaho Code § 6-311A). In other eviction cases, issues of fact go to a jury unless the jury is waived 'as in other cases' (Idaho Code § 6-313), which means under the court rules. Whether a court would enforce a jury waiver signed in the lease is decided by case law, and a lease term that keeps a party from enforcing the lease in Idaho courts is void (Idaho Code § 29-110(1)). The library's optional arbitration clause is the only term that takes disputes away from a jury, and it leaves possession cases in court.

title: Confession of Judgment in Idaho
bodyText: No Idaho statute authorizes or bans a confession-of-judgment (cognovit) clause in a residential lease, and the library does not offer one. Idaho's bans cover consumer credit, where an authorization to confess judgment is void (Idaho Code § 28-43-305), and rent-to-own agreements for goods (Idaho Code § 28-36-106); neither reaches a lease of a home. The Idaho Rules of Civil Procedure (court rules) have no procedure for entering a judgment on a confession without a lawsuit. A lease term that keeps a party from enforcing the lease in Idaho courts is void (Idaho Code § 29-110(1)); whether that reaches a pre-signed confession is case law. You don't need one. If a tenant who has been served does not appear in an eviction case, the court must enter a default judgment for you (Idaho Code § 6-312). Collect unpaid rent and recover possession through the ordinary eviction process.

title: Move-In and Move-Out Inspections in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes do not require a move-in or move-out inspection, a written condition report or inventory, or any notice to the tenant about one, and they have no rule that a tenant who signs a damage list gives up a claim.

A written record is still worth making. At move-out you may keep from the deposit only the amounts necessary to cover what the lease's deposit terms list, never anything for normal wear and tear, and a partial refund must come with a signed statement itemizing what you kept and a detailed list of what you spent (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)-(2)). A move-in report with dated photographs, signed by you and the tenant, is the best evidence of what changed during the tenancy; the optional Move-In Condition Report clause sets one up. For a housing-voucher tenancy, check the housing agency's program rules on inspections and damage claims.

title: Preset Deposit Deductions in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes say nothing about a schedule of preset deductions or cleaning charges in a lease.

The deposit statute still decides how such a schedule works. At the end of the tenancy you must refund the deposit 'except amounts necessary to cover the contingencies specified in the deposit arrangement' (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)); you may keep nothing for normal wear and tear; and a partial refund must come with a signed statement itemizing what you kept, why, and 'a detailed list of expenditures made from the deposit' (Idaho Code § 6-321(2)).

So a lease may list the contingencies the deposit covers, and may give typical prices as a guide, but what you keep should be what the work actually cost and what was actually needed. A flat charge kept whether or not the work was needed or done risks being more than the amount necessary, or a charge for normal wear and tear.

A separate cleaning or similar fee charged to the tenant, rather than taken from the deposit, is a fee: it must be stated in the rental agreement and be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(2)). Money a tenant deposits with you for any purpose other than rent is a refundable security deposit whatever it is called (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)); whether a charge labeled a nonrefundable fee is really a deposit is case law.

Cautious course: list the contingencies in the lease (the Use of Security Deposit clause does), deduct documented actual costs, and use the optional carpet-cleaning clause only on its own terms.

title: Paying the Deposit in Installments in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho's statutes give a tenant no right to pay a security deposit in installments and set no rule for it. You may require the whole deposit before move-in, or agree to take it in installments. If you agree, write the schedule into the lease. Every installment is part of the security deposit, refundable under Idaho Code § 6-321 like the rest, because money a tenant deposits 'for any purpose other than the payment of rent' is a security deposit (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)). An unpaid installment is not unpaid rent, so don't demand it in a three-day notice to pay rent. It is a breach of the lease, enforced by a three-day written notice requiring performance or possession (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)) or by a claim for the money. Offer the same terms to every tenant in the same situation.

title: Deposits and the Last Month's Rent in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute that bars or requires applying a security deposit to the last month's rent. What decides the question is what the money is. Money a tenant deposits 'for any purpose other than the payment of rent' is a security deposit (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)). Money paid in advance as the last month's rent is rent: you apply it to that month, and it is not refundable as a deposit, but you can't use it to pay for damage either. A security deposit stays a deposit. Under the library's Use of Security Deposit clause it does not relieve the tenant of paying rent, so the tenant may not skip the last month's rent and leave the deposit to cover it unless you agree in writing. If you collect both, list them separately in the lease (the Due at Signing clause does), and don't label prepaid rent a "deposit". Lot rentals in manufactured home communities follow their own act, under which prepaid rent collected on top of periodic rent is treated as a deposit (Idaho Code § 55-2013(1)).

title: When the Deposit Clock Starts in Idaho
bodyText:
Your deadline to refund the deposit runs from 'surrender of the premises by the tenant': 21 days if the lease fixes no other time, and in any event no more than 30 days (Idaho Code § 6-321(2)). Idaho's statutes do not define when a rental is surrendered, do not require the tenant to give a forwarding address or a notice of intent to vacate before the refund is due, and do not require you to send the tenant a notice about the deposit before move-out.

Cautious course: count the days from when the tenant moves out and gives up possession; keys returned or a written confirmation are good evidence of that day, but don't wait for them if you know the tenant has gone. Ask for a forwarding address in writing at move-out (the library's deposit-return clause does); a missing address does not extend the deadline. If you have no address, send the refund and the signed itemized statement to the best address you have and keep proof of mailing.

title: Waiving Deposit Rights in Idaho
bodyText: The rule first: at the end of the tenancy you must refund the deposit except amounts needed for the contingencies the deposit terms specify; you may keep nothing for normal wear and tear; and the refund is due within 21 days, or the time the lease fixes, but never later than 30 days after the tenant surrenders the property, with a signed, itemized statement for anything kept (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)-(2)). Idaho's statutes have no section saying a residential tenant cannot waive these rights in a lease, and no general rule voiding lease waivers for ordinary residential tenancies. But the deposit statute leaves only two things to the lease, the contingencies the deposit covers and the refund time inside the 30-day outer limit; the rest is stated as a rule. A tenant may sue over a deposit not returned as the law requires, after giving you three days' written notice, and the court may award three times the actual damages (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(4), (d); Idaho Code § 6-317); that suit does not apply to farm tracts of five acres or more (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). A lease term giving up the refund, allowing deductions for normal wear and tear, or setting a deadline longer than 30 days is unlikely to be enforced, and could be attacked as unconscionable or deceptive under the Consumer Protection Act (Idaho Code § 48-603C). Don't put one in the lease. Lot rentals in manufactured home communities have an express rule: their rental agreements may not contain a waiver of rights under that act (Idaho Code § 55-2007(2)(a)).

title: Deposit Standards in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to post or hand out the standards you use to set or calculate security deposits, however many units you have, and they set no limit on the amount (see edu-no-deposit-cap-id). Cities and counties may not regulate the deposits charged for leasing private residential property (Idaho Code § 55-306). What does limit you is fair housing law: you may not set different deposit terms because of a protected characteristic (see edu-fair-housing-id). Cautious course: if you use more than one deposit amount, write down the objective criteria (for example credit score bands or the number of pets), apply them the same way to every applicant, and keep the record.

title: Resolving Deposit Disputes in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no special fast-track procedure for security-deposit disputes, and no rule letting you settle the deposit early, for example when a tenant abandons the unit. The ordinary rule applies: refund within 21 days, or the time the lease fixes, never later than 30 days after the tenant surrenders the property, with a signed itemized statement for anything kept (Idaho Code § 6-321(2)). Before suing you over a deposit under Idaho's tenant-remedy statute, the tenant must give you three days' written notice listing the failure. A claim for damages then goes as an ordinary civil case; the statute's early trial (within 12 days) applies only to an action exclusively for specific performance (Idaho Code § 6-320(a), (d)). Either side may use the magistrate court's small claims department, where the district court has created one; it hears money claims of up to $15,000 and does not award punitive damages (Idaho Code § 1-2301). If a tenant appears to have abandoned the unit, confirm it in writing before treating the property as surrendered.

title: Fees Instead of a Deposit in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute on fees charged instead of a security deposit, such as deposit-alternative or deposit-waiver programs. Two general rules decide how such a charge is treated. If the money is paid up front and held against damage or default, it is a security deposit whatever it is called, and must be refunded under the deposit rules (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)). If it is truly a fee, a charge the tenant pays for a program that replaces the deposit and does not get back, Idaho's fee statute applies: you may charge it only if the rental agreement states it (or, under a written agreement, after 30 days' written notice of the change), in no greater amount than agreed, and it must be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(2)). Paying the fee does not end the tenant's liability for damage unless the program says so. Describe accurately what the fee buys and who may still pursue the tenant, because the Consumer Protection Act reaches leasing and bars misleading representations (Idaho Code § 48-603(5), (17)). A program sold by an insurer or surety may also be regulated by Idaho's insurance laws.

title: Holding Deposits in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute on holding deposits or other money taken to reserve a rental before the lease is signed: no cap, no refund deadline, and no rule doubling it if you back out. Whether that money is a security deposit under Idaho Code § 6-321 is unsettled: the section covers 'Amounts deposited by a tenant with a landlord', and its refund rules run from the end of a lease. Once a lease is signed, money credited to the deposit is a security deposit. Put the terms in writing before you take the money: the amount; how long you will hold the unit; that it becomes part of the first month's rent or the security deposit if the lease is signed; that it is refunded promptly and in full if you decline the applicant or don't offer the lease; and what part, if any, you may keep if the applicant backs out (keep it close to your real loss, such as rent lost while the unit was held). A non-refundable holding fee is a fee; whether Idaho's fee statute (Idaho Code § 55-305) reaches an applicant who never becomes a tenant is unsettled, so state it in writing in any case. If a real estate broker takes the money, the Real Estate License Law's trust-account rules may apply (Idaho Code § 54-2045). Use the same terms for every applicant (see edu-fair-housing-id).

title: Nonrefundable Deposits and Notice in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no rule requiring a separate written notice for a nonrefundable deposit or fee, because Idaho does not recognize a nonrefundable deposit at all: any amount a tenant deposits for a purpose other than rent is a refundable security deposit (Idaho Code § 6-321(1); see edu-nonrefundable-fees-id). A true fee, such as a cleaning or lease-initiation fee, needs no separate notice, but for rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023 it must be stated in the rental agreement (or, under a written agreement, added on 30 days' written notice; an oral agreement is excepted), may not exceed the amount stated, and must be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(3)). Cautious course: list each fee in the lease by name and dollar amount, separately from the deposit, and never call any deposit nonrefundable.

title: Fee Disclosure in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no all-in pricing, junk-fee or first-page fee disclosure law for rentals. Its fee statute does most of the work instead. For rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, you may not charge a tenant a fee, fine, assessment, interest or other cost that the rental agreement does not include, or in a greater amount than the agreement states; under a written agreement, a charge the agreement does not include needs 30 days' written notice to the tenant; and every fee must be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(3); see edu-fees-in-lease-id). The Consumer Protection Act covers advertising and leasing rentals and bars misleading or deceptive practices (Idaho Code § 48-602(2); Idaho Code § 48-603(17)), so don't advertise or quote a rent that hides mandatory monthly charges. Charging a fee a written lease doesn't include, without that 30-day notice, is barred by the fee statute itself; whether it is also an unfair practice under the Act is unsettled. Cautious course: list every fee in the lease by name and dollar amount, or by an objective method stated there, and show mandatory monthly charges next to the rent in your advertising. Lot rentals in manufactured home communities have their own rule: the rental agreement must describe any other charges the resident pays (Idaho Code § 55-2007(1)(a)).

title: Fees for Services Not Provided in Idaho
bodyText: For ordinary residential rentals, Idaho has no statute that specifically bars a fee for a service you don't provide. (Floating home marinas have one: 'No fees may be charged except for rent, services and utilities actually provided' (Idaho Code § 55-2708(5)).) Still, any fee must be stated in the rental agreement and be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(2)), and the Consumer Protection Act, which covers leasing, makes it unlawful to represent that services have benefits they don't have, or to engage in any misleading or deceptive act (Idaho Code § 48-603(5), (17)). A tenant who loses money that way can recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, and attorney's fees (Idaho Code § 48-608(1), (5)). Cautious course: charge a service or amenity fee only for a service the tenant actually receives, describe it in the lease, and stop or credit the fee for any period the service is not available.

title: Fees as Rent in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not define "rent" for an ordinary residential lease, and nothing says that fees a lease calls "additional rent" count as rent. The only definition is for manufactured home lots, where rent means periodic payments for occupying the lot and other charges are defined as not including rent (Idaho Code § 55-2003(11), (14)). The label matters in two places. First, Idaho's fee statute does not limit rent (Idaho Code § 55-305(4)), so whether a charge is rent or a fee decides whether the fee rules apply; calling a fee rent may not take it outside them. Second, the three-day eviction notice for nonpayment is a notice after default 'in the payment of rent' that requires payment and states 'the amount which is due' (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)). Whether a fee labelled additional rent can be demanded in that notice is unsettled. Cautious course: put only unpaid rent in a three-day notice to pay rent. Collect late fees and other charges separately, by written demand, by a three-day notice to perform the lease or leave (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)), or by a claim in court, and don't rely on an "additional rent" label.

title: Late Fee Limits in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho sets no dollar or percentage cap on late fees for residential tenants and no grace period, including for manufactured home lots. The limits come from Idaho's fee statute: a late fee must be reasonable; for rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023 it may not exceed the amount the rental agreement states; and under a written agreement a late fee the agreement does not include may be added only on 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(3); see edu-late-fee-reasonable-id). The only late-fee figure Idaho's statutes set for any rental is for self-service storage units, where $20 or 20% of the monthly rent, whichever is greater, is deemed reasonable if the rental agreement states it (Idaho Code § 55-2304(7)); it does not apply to housing. What is 'reasonable', and when a late fee becomes an unenforceable penalty, are questions for the courts. Cautious course: state a flat fee or a modest percentage of the monthly rent in the lease, with any grace period, and charge it once per late payment.

title: Statutory Caps on Charges in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes cap almost nothing a private residential landlord charges. There is no rent cap, and cities and counties may not regulate the rent, fees or deposits charged for leasing private residential property (Idaho Code § 55-306). There is no cap on the security deposit (see edu-no-deposit-cap-id) and no fixed cap on late, application, pet, cleaning or other fees.

The limits that do apply: every fee must be reasonable, and, for rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, no fee, fine, assessment, interest or other cost may exceed the amount the rental agreement states (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(3)). Interest on overdue money is 12% a year unless a written contract fixes a different rate (Idaho Code § 28-22-104(1); see unpaid-amounts-interest-id). For a dishonored check, a set collection fee agreed in writing may not exceed $20 (Idaho Code § 28-22-105; see returned-payments-id).
