You may not charge anything extra for a tenant's service dog, though the tenant is liable for damage the dog causes (Idaho Code § 18-5812A(1)).

A price that grossly exceeds what similar rentals cost is one factor a court weighs in deciding whether a practice is unconscionable under the Consumer Protection Act (Idaho Code § 48-603C(2)(b)). Manufactured home lots and floating home moorages have their own rules on rent increases and fees.

title: Alarm Tampering Fees in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute that sets or authorizes a fee for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm. The tenant must keep the smoke detectors in good working order during the tenancy (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6)), and the library's Smoke Detectors clause has the tenant promise not to disable, disconnect or remove one. A fixed fee for tampering would be a fee under Idaho's fee statute: allowed only if the rental agreement states it (or, under a written agreement, after 30 days' written notice), never above the stated amount, and only if reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(2)). The library does not offer a fixed tampering fee, because a flat charge unrelated to your loss could be attacked as an unreasonable fee or a penalty, and Idaho court decisions on that were not reviewed. No statute bars adding one if it is stated in the lease and reasonable; a landlord who wants it can add their own clause after taking advice. You can recover the actual cost of repairing or replacing a detector the tenant damages, from the deposit as the lease's deposit terms allow or as damages. No Idaho statute requires carbon monoxide alarms in ordinary rentals (see smoke-detectors-id).

title: Late Fees for Subsidized Tenants in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho's statutes set no special late-fee rule for subsidized tenants. The general fee rules apply to the tenant's own share: a late fee must be stated in the rental agreement, may not exceed the stated amount, and must be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(3)). In the Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) program, federal rules also apply. The family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing agency pays (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.451(b)(4)(iii)); the agency's failure to pay is not a lease violation, and during the lease term you may not end the tenancy for it (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310(b)). So charge a late fee only when the tenant's own share is late, figure it on that share, and never charge the tenant because the agency paid late. If the agency pays late, the housing assistance payments contract provides for late-payment penalties against the agency, but only where they follow local practice and law, you charge them to assisted and unassisted tenants alike, and you also charge the tenant for late payment of the family's rent (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.451(b)(5)(ii)(A)). You may not charge a voucher tenant extra for items customarily included in rent locally or provided at no extra cost to unsubsidized tenants (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.510(c)), and the HUD tenancy addendum, added word for word to your lease, prevails over any other lease term (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.308(f)(2)). Public housing and other federal programs have their own rules. Cities and counties may not force you to take part in an optional federal housing assistance program (Idaho Code § 55-306).

title: Rent Receipts in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho's landlord-tenant statutes do not require a receipt for rent, even for cash. A general contract rule applies, though: 'A debtor has a right to require from his creditor a written receipt for any property delivered in performance of his obligation' (Idaho Code § 29-111). The section does not mention rent, but its words cover a tenant paying rent, so give a written receipt whenever a tenant asks, for any payment. Giving one for every cash payment is the safe practice. Idaho's statutes set no presumption that earlier rent was paid because a receipt for later rent was given. Keep your own ledger of every payment.

title: Rent Collection and Repair Duties in Idaho
bodyText: Some states say that whoever collects the rent keeps the landlord's repair duties, whatever a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage says. Idaho's statutes have no such rule. Idaho's repair duties are enforced through the tenant's action against the landlord (Idaho Code § 6-320(a); see edu-tenant-remedies-id), and those duties follow the landlord's position when it changes hands: a tenant has the same remedies for breach of the lease against the landlord's assigns as against the original landlord, except on covenants about title or possession (Idaho Code § 55-303); a new owner is liable to refund deposits paid during the tenancy (Idaho Code § 6-321(3)); and a person who takes the property, or the right to its rent, gets the landlord's remedies for rent (Idaho Code § 55-301). Cautious course: if you assign the rents or sell the property, expect the repair duties to travel with the right to collect rent, and say so in any management or assignment agreement.

title: Lockouts for Unpaid Rent in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute that lets a landlord lock a tenant out for unpaid rent, with or without notice or a lease clause. To remove a tenant for nonpayment you must serve a written three-day notice to pay or leave and then use the court's eviction process (Idaho Code § 6-303(2); see edu-eviction-process-id). Breaking in, or turning out the person in possession by force, threats or menacing conduct, is a forcible entry (Idaho Code § 6-301), and the court may award three times the tenant's actual damages (Idaho Code § 6-317). Idaho's statutes do not expressly address changing the locks while the tenant is away; whether that is actionable is for the courts, whose decisions were not reviewed, so treat it as unlawful self-help (see edu-self-help-eviction-id). The one statutory lock change is for a person who was never a tenant: after the sheriff serves a notice to vacate on an unauthorized occupant, the owner may change the locks with the sheriff standing by (Idaho Code § 6-310A). Don't put a lockout clause in the lease.

title: Utility Deposits in Idaho
bodyText: Utility deposits are mostly the utility company's business, not yours. If the tenant opens the account in the tenant's own name, any deposit the utility takes, and its refund, are between the tenant and the utility. For gas, electric and water companies regulated by the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, the Commission's customer rules (IDAPA 31.21.01) allow a residential deposit only on listed grounds (for example an unpaid prior account, a past disconnection for nonpayment, or a new customer without 12 months of service history who fails an objective credit screen), cap it at one-sixth of a year's estimated bills, let the customer pay it in two installments, and require interest on it. When service ends, the utility credits the deposit with interest to the final bill and promptly returns the rest; a continuing customer gets it back once all undisputed bills are paid with no more than one late payment in 12 months. City-owned systems and cooperatives are not regulated by the Commission and set their own rules. A utility deposit that goes unclaimed is presumed abandoned one year after it becomes payable (Idaho Code § 14-5-201(1)(k)). If you collect your own deposit for utilities, for example where service stays in your name and the tenant reimburses you, that money is a security deposit: it must be refunded under Idaho Code § 6-321, less unpaid utility charges the deposit terms allow, within 21 days or the time the lease fixes, never later than 30 days after the tenant surrenders the property, with a signed itemized statement for anything kept.

title: Rent Concessions in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho has no statute on rent concessions such as a free month, reduced rent or a move-in credit. State each concession in the lease, with its amount and the months it covers (the optional Rent Concessions clause does), so that your advertising and the lease match; the Consumer Protection Act covers advertising and leasing rentals and bars misleading practices (Idaho Code § 48-603(17)).

When a concession ends, rent goes back to the amount the lease states. Idaho requires written notice at least 30 days before any increase in the rent charged (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)); whether the scheduled end of a concession counts is unsettled, so remind the tenant in writing at least 30 days before it ends.

Idaho's statutes don't bar a lease term making a concession repayable if the tenant breaks the lease early. The library's clause doesn't include one, because a court might treat it as a penalty; a landlord who wants one can add their own clause after taking advice.

title: Rent Increases During the Lease in Idaho
bodyText:
During a fixed term, rent stays at the amount the lease sets unless the lease itself provides for a change. Idaho has no statute on rent escalation clauses for ordinary residential leases and no rent cap, and cities and counties may not regulate rent (Idaho Code § 55-306).

For every residential lease you must give the tenant written notice of any rent increase at least 30 days before it takes effect (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)). Give that notice even for an increase the lease schedules; whether the statute requires it then is unsettled. The optional Scheduled Rent Changes clause sets a fixed schedule or an index-based adjustment with that notice.

No Idaho statute bars a lease term letting you raise rent by any amount during a fixed term, on the 30 days' written notice, if the lease says so, but the library doesn't offer one: an open-ended right invites disputes over whether the tenant really agreed to the rent. A landlord who wants one can add their own clause after taking advice. Idaho has no retaliation statute, so a scheduled increase raises no retaliation question under state law (see edu-no-retaliation-statute-id).

Manufactured home lots and floating home moorages have their own rules, including 90 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-2006; Idaho Code § 55-2708).

title: Passing Property Tax Increases to Tenants in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes don't say who bears property tax increases on an ordinary residential rental, and they neither require nor bar passing increases to the tenant. Unless the lease says otherwise, the tax is yours, and you may raise rent only as the lease and the 30-day notice rule allow (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)).

If the lease passes tax increases through, Idaho's fee statute treats the tenant's share as a charge that must be included in the rental agreement, may not exceed the amount agreed, and must be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(2)). The optional Property Tax Increases clause meets that by stating the tenant's percentage and a yearly dollar maximum, requiring the tax bill and 30 days' written notice, and refunding the tenant's share of any later reduction.

Manufactured home community and floating home marina leases are different: their acts expressly allow an escalation clause for a pro rata share of property tax increases (Idaho Code § 55-2006(5); Idaho Code § 55-2708(4)(b)).

title: Rent Reporting in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute on reporting tenants' rent payments to credit bureaus. No law requires you to offer positive rent reporting, bars requiring a tenant to join a reporting program, or sets a state notice rule before you report late rent. Federal credit reporting law (the Fair Credit Reporting Act) governs anyone who furnishes information to a credit bureau. If you charge the tenant for a reporting service, the charge must be in the rental agreement and be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(2)). Cautious course: say in the lease whether you report rent payments and to whom, report only accurate information, and fix errors promptly when a tenant disputes them.

title: No Hardship Delay of an Idaho Eviction
bodyText: Idaho has no statute letting a court postpone an eviction because the tenant is ill, elderly, out of work, has young children or cannot find another home, and no winter, holiday or weather moratorium. The delays that exist are short and fixed. In an action only for possession for unpaid rent or drug activity on five acres or less, 'no continuance shall be granted for a longer period than two (2) days unless the defendant applying therefor gives an undertaking to the adverse party with good and sufficient security' for rent that may accrue (Idaho Code § 6-311). After judgment, 'a residential tenant shall have seventy-two (72) hours to remove his belongings from the premises' (Idaho Code § 6-316(2)), and the sheriff restores possession after that time and three days after the court's finding (Idaho Code § 6-316(2)). An appeal 'does not stay proceedings upon the judgment unless the court so directs' (Idaho Code § 6-319), and a tenant who appeals must also post an undertaking for the rental value (Idaho Code § 6-311D). One narrow exception: a nonprofit that claims Idaho's property-tax exemption for low-income housing must not evict tenants for 'inability to pay for a period of three (3) months if such inability is due to a catastrophic event' (Idaho Code § 63-602GG(3)(b)), meaning a sudden, serious medical condition or injury certified by a physician, psychiatrist or psychologist that keeps the tenant from working. A lease term cannot give or take away a court's power to stay its own judgment, so the library has no clause on this. Federal law can still delay you: a tenant's bankruptcy filing, and the CARES Act's 30-day notice to vacate on covered properties (see edu-cares-act-notice).

title: Who Receives Eviction Papers in Idaho
bodyText: No Idaho statute lets a lease name a person or address to receive eviction notices or court papers for the tenant. The three-day notices are served as Idaho Code § 6-304 provides: personally; or, if the tenant is away from home and work, on a person of suitable age and discretion there plus mailing; or, only if the home and workplace can't be found or no such person can be found there, by posting on the property, delivery to a resident if one can be found, and mailing. A subtenant in actual occupation must be served too (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)-(3)). Only 'the tenant of the premises, and subtenant, if there be one, in the actual occupation of the premises when the notice herein provided for was served' need be named as defendants (Idaho Code § 6-308). The summons 'must be issued, served and returned as in other actions' (Idaho Code § 6-310(2)), which sends you to the Idaho Rules of Civil Procedure. Under those court rules a summons may be delivered to the tenant personally, left at the tenant's home with someone at least 18 who lives there, or delivered 'to an agent authorized by appointment or by law to receive service of process' (I.R.C.P. 4(d)(1)(C), court rule). The rule does not say whether a lease clause is enough to appoint an agent, so the library offers no such clause; serve the tenant directly. A tenant in Idaho's address confidentiality program has designated the Secretary of State 'as agent for purposes of service of process and for the purpose of receipt of mail' (Idaho Code § 19-5703(1)(b)). The statute does not say a landlord must serve through the Secretary of State or may not serve at the rental. If you know your tenant is a participant, the cautious course is to serve at the rental as Idaho Code § 6-304 provides and also send a copy to the program address, and to ask a lawyer whether the program designation makes the Secretary of State an agent 'authorized by appointment or by law' (I.R.C.P. 4(d)(1)(C), court rule). The library's notices clause defers to the statutory methods and offers no clause naming an agent for the tenant.

title: How an Idaho Lease Is Forfeited, and How a Tenant Saves It
bodyText: In Idaho a lease is forfeited by the court after notice, not by the lease itself. For a breach other than rent, the three-day notice to perform or quit gives the tenant, a subtenant in occupation, 'any mortgagee of the term, or other person interested in its continuance' the chance to perform 'or pay the stipulated rent, as the case may be, and thereby save the lease from forfeiture' (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)). Two grounds have no cure: a breached covenant that 'cannot afterward be performed' needs no notice to perform (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)), and assigning, subletting or committing waste contrary to the lease 'thereby terminates the lease', with only a three-day notice to quit (Idaho Code § 6-303(4)). If you win an eviction for breach, unpaid rent or drug activity, 'the judgment shall also declare the forfeiture of such lease or agreement' (Idaho Code § 6-316(1)), and the court also assesses your damages and the rent found due. Relief after judgment exists only for land larger than five acres: where the lease has not expired, a tenant evicted for nonpayment has five days to pay the rent with interest, damages and costs into court, and then 'the judgment shall be satisfied and the tenant be restored to his estate' (Idaho Code § 6-316(1)). For an ordinary home on five acres or less there is no statutory relief after judgment; 'In all other cases the judgment may be enforced immediately' (Idaho Code § 6-316(1)). Whether a court can give equitable relief from forfeiture beyond these rules is case law not reviewed. Two special routes: use for lewdness or prostitution makes the lease void at your option (Idaho Code § 52-414), and a lease reserving a right of reentry is covered in edu-cure-notice-id; the library offers no reentry clause.

title: Paying to Stop an Idaho Eviction
bodyText: For unpaid rent, the three-day notice demands payment of the stated amount 'or possession of the property' (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)); full payment within the three days ends that ground. During a three-day notice, the statute also lets a subtenant, a mortgagee of the term 'or other person interested in its continuance' pay the stipulated rent and save the lease (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)); whether that sentence reaches a nonpayment notice is unsettled. After the three days, Idaho gives a tenant on five acres or less no statutory right to stop the eviction by paying, before or after judgment, and no deadline measured back from the sheriff's removal. Post-judgment redemption exists only for land over five acres (Idaho Code § 6-316(1); see edu-forfeiture-redemption-id). Idaho has no statute on partial payments: none requires you to accept one, prescribes wording for accepting one, or says whether accepting one waives the notice. Courts may treat accepting rent after a notice as a waiver; that case law was not reviewed. Cautious course: either refuse partial or late payments once you have served a notice, or accept them only with a written statement, given at or before acceptance, that the payment is partial, applied to the amount due, and accepted without waiving the notice or the eviction. No Idaho statute requires you to accept a payment from a charity or government agency for the tenant, or bars you from limiting payment methods (see acceptable-payment-methods). Paying a money judgment does not by statute cancel a judgment for possession.

title: Bonds in an Idaho Eviction: Only the Tenant Posts Them
bodyText: Idaho has no landlord's possession bond: no statute lets you post a bond and take possession before trial, and none provides an end-of-term possession bond with a confessed judgment. Possession comes from the judgment and the sheriff (Idaho Code § 6-316). No statute authorizes a confession of judgment in a residential lease; Idaho bans them in consumer credit and lease-purchase agreements (Idaho Code § 28-43-305, Idaho Code § 28-36-106), which are not ordinary leases, and the library uses none. The bonds that exist are posted by the tenant. In a fast-track action only for possession for unpaid rent or drug activity, a continuance longer than two days needs the tenant's undertaking for the rent that may accrue (Idaho Code § 6-311). A tenant who appeals a judgment for possession must give, besides the usual appeal bond, an undertaking with two sureties for 'the rental value of the real property' from the start of the case until final judgment (Idaho Code § 6-311D), and the appeal does not stop enforcement unless the court so orders (Idaho Code § 6-319).

title: Rent Into Court and Counterclaims in an Idaho Eviction
bodyText: Idaho does not make a tenant pay rent into court before the tenant may defend an eviction or raise a counterclaim. The money requirements are narrower. In a fast-track action only for possession of five acres or less for unpaid rent or drug activity, the tenant must give an undertaking for accruing rent to get a continuance longer than two days (Idaho Code § 6-311), and a tenant who appeals must post an undertaking for the rental value (Idaho Code § 6-311D). No statute requires rent to be paid in because a trial is adjourned for a long time. Idaho has no rent-escrow or rent-withholding procedure for repairs; the tenant's remedy is a separate action after a three-day notice, not available for agricultural tracts of five acres or more (Idaho Code § 6-320(a), (d)-(e); see edu-tenant-remedies-id). No statute speaks to tenant counterclaims in an eviction. The complaint and answer 'must be verified' (Idaho Code § 6-318), and the ordinary civil rules apply 'so far as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of this chapter' (Idaho Code § 6-322); under those court rules a claim against the other side that arises out of the same transaction must be stated as a counterclaim (I.R.C.P. 13(a)(1), court rule). How that fits the fast eviction track, and whether a tenant's counterclaim ends the 12-day trial, is case law. On your side, joining a damages claim with the possession claim gives up the 12-day trial (Idaho Code § 6-311E), so a possession-only filing keeps the case fast.

title: An Idaho Landlord's Remedies: Possession, Rent and Damages
bodyText: One Idaho eviction case can give you possession, the rent found due and your damages from the unlawful detainer, and the judgment declares the lease forfeited where the case is for breach, unpaid rent or drug activity (Idaho Code § 6-316(1)). The court may enter judgment for three times the actual damages (Idaho Code § 6-317), and, except where treble damages are awarded, the prevailing party gets attorney fees, which in a nonpayment case requires that the three-day notice gave the required warning (Idaho Code § 6-324; see edu-attorney-fees-id). Choose the route on purpose. A possession-only case for unpaid rent or drug activity on five acres or less gets a trial within 12 days (Idaho Code § 6-310(1)-(2)); joining a damages claim gives that up (Idaho Code § 6-311E). Winning possession first does not cost you the money: 'No provision of this law shall be construed to prevent the bringing of an action for damages' (Idaho Code § 6-311A). For money alone, the small claims department handles claims up to $15,000 (Idaho Code § 1-2301); it cannot award possession. Eviction cases themselves may be assigned to magistrates (Idaho Code § 1-2208(1)(b)). A suit on a written lease must be brought within five years (Idaho Code § 5-216). A buyer of the property takes over your remedies for rent, breach and waste (Idaho Code § 55-301), and you have the same remedies against an assignee of the tenant (Idaho Code § 55-302). Idaho has no statute on accelerating future rent or on a landlord's duty to re-let after a tenant leaves early; both are case law not reviewed, so claim only rent and losses actually suffered and keep records of efforts to re-let.

title: Minors as Tenants and Eviction Defendants in Idaho
bodyText: In Idaho a person is a minor until 18, but 'any male or any female who has been married shall be competent to enter a contract' and to sue or be sued on it (Idaho Code § 32-101). People aged 18 to 20 are adults who can sign a lease. A lease signed by an unmarried minor 'may be disaffirmed by the minor himself, either before his majority or within a reasonable time afterwards' (Idaho Code § 32-103). The exceptions: a minor cannot disaffirm an obligation entered into under the express authority or direction of a statute (Idaho Code § 32-105), or a contract to pay the reasonable value of things necessary for support when not under the care of a parent or guardian able to provide them (Idaho Code § 32-104); whether housing counts, and for how much, is case law not reviewed. So if you rent to a minor, the cautious course is to have a parent, guardian or other adult sign as a co-tenant or guarantor. In an eviction, only the tenant and any subtenant in actual occupation when the notice was served need be named (Idaho Code § 6-308). No Idaho statute bars or requires naming a tenant's child; a child who is not a tenant or subtenant does not need to be named, and naming one adds nothing. Under the court rules a minor may defend through a general guardian, conservator or like fiduciary, and the court 'must appoint a guardian ad litem, or issue another appropriate order, to protect a minor or incompetent person who is unrepresented in an action' (I.R.C.P. 17(c)(2), court rule); a minor under 14 is served through a guardian or parent and, unless the court orders otherwise, personally too (I.R.C.P. 4(d)(2)(A), court rule).

title: A Late Benefit Payment Is No Defense in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho gives a tenant no defense, continuance or reinstatement right because a Social Security payment, housing voucher payment or other government benefit arrived late. Rent unpaid after a proper three-day notice supports an eviction whatever the reason (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)). In a fast-track possession case for five acres or less the tenant can get a continuance of more than two days only by giving an undertaking for accruing rent (Idaho Code § 6-311). Idaho does not protect source of income, and cities may not force owners into optional federal housing assistance programs (Idaho Code § 55-306; see edu-source-of-income-id). The one narrow exception is for nonprofit low-income housing that claims the property-tax exemption: it may not evict for three months' inability to pay caused by a certified catastrophic medical event (Idaho Code § 63-602GG(3)(b)). If you accepted a housing voucher, the program contract and federal rules may limit or delay an eviction for the housing agency's share of the rent. Waiting a few days for a payment you know is in transit usually costs less than an eviction, but Idaho law does not require it.

title: Tenant Calls for Police or Emergency Help in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute giving tenants a protected right to call the police or emergency services, voiding a lease term that penalizes those calls, or giving a tenant a defense to an eviction filed soon after a call. Idaho also has no statute on local nuisance ordinances that count police calls against a rental property; whether your city has one was not reviewed. Silence is not permission. A lease term or practice that punishes a tenant for calling for help, especially a victim of domestic violence, invites a sex-discrimination claim under fair housing law (see edu-fair-housing-id), and in federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act an incident of domestic violence cannot be treated as a serious or repeated lease violation by the victim (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(b)(2)). The library's Idaho lease has no term limiting calls for help, and you should not add one. If a call reveals a real lease breach by the tenant, such as drug activity or damage, act on that breach through the usual notice, not on the call itself.

title: Criminal Activity and Crime-Free Lease Terms in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no crime-free lease statute. No statute requires, authorizes, regulates or bans a crime-free lease term or addendum, none lets a city require one, and none writes a no-crime covenant into every lease. Three statutes do reach crime at a rental. Drug activity: a tenant is in unlawful detainer if anyone 'is, or has been, engaged in the unlawful delivery, production or use of a controlled substance on the premises' during the term (Idaho Code § 6-303(5)), with a fast track for an action only for possession of five acres or less (Idaho Code § 6-310(1)-(2)); this works without any lease term (see edu-expedited-drug-eviction-id). Lewd use: using the premises for lewdness, assignation or prostitution makes the lease void at your option (Idaho Code § 52-414; see edu-lewd-use-lease-void-id). And it is a crime for any person 'Knowingly to keep or maintain' a dwelling or other place resorted to by people using controlled substances or used for keeping or selling them (Idaho Code § 37-2733(a)(5)), a reason to act promptly once you know. Other crimes, such as violence, threats or property damage, are not eviction grounds by themselves. They reach eviction only as a breach of a lease covenant, through the three-day notice to perform or quit (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)), or as waste (Idaho Code § 6-303(4)). The Idaho lease already has that covenant: the tenant may not use or permit use of the property for any illegal purpose (residential-use-only), or allow conditions that threaten persons or property (no-disturbance), and default-by-tenant enforces both with the notice Idaho law requires. The library therefore does not offer a separate crime-free clause or addendum for Idaho. A typical crime-free addendum promises termination for a single violation with no chance to cure, and because a past crime cannot be undone, whether Idaho gives the tenant three days to perform, or no notice at all because the covenant 'cannot afterward be performed' (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)), is unsettled; such a promise may not hold. A crime-free covenant is lawful as far as Idaho's statutes go. If you want one, add your own after taking legal advice; it should use the notice Idaho law requires, exclude tenants who are crime victims and calls for help, and be applied the same way to everyone. Federally assisted housing has its own rules, and on a property with a federally backed mortgage the CARES Act's 30-day notice to vacate may also apply (see edu-cares-act-notice).

title: No Drug-Free Housing Addendum Needed in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute requiring, prescribing or regulating a drug-free housing addendum. It does not need one for drugs: drug activity on the premises is itself an eviction ground. A tenant is in unlawful detainer if anyone is or has been engaged in the unlawful delivery, production or use of a controlled substance on the leased premises during the term (Idaho Code § 6-303(5)), with no lease term needed. When you have reasonable grounds to believe it is happening or has happened during the term, an action only for possession of a tract of five acres or less gets a trial within 12 days of filing (Idaho Code § 6-310(1)-(2)), and the judgment declares the lease forfeited (Idaho Code § 6-316(1)). The Idaho lease also bars any illegal use of the property (residential-use-only). Marijuana remains a controlled substance in Idaho, so no cannabis carve-out or accommodation rule is needed for it. For these reasons the library offers no separate drug-free addendum for Idaho. An addendum is lawful as far as statute goes; if you want one, add your own after taking legal advice, and do not let it promise eviction with no notice where the statute might require one. Federally assisted housing has its own required drug terms; follow the program's rules.

title: Nothing in Idaho Law Stops You Demanding Rent
bodyText: No Idaho statute bars you from demanding, collecting or suing for rent because the home needs repairs, has code violations, is not registered or licensed, or because you have not given some disclosure. The tenant's remedy for your failures is a lawsuit for damages and specific performance after a three-day written notice, not withholding rent (Idaho Code § 6-320(a), (d)), except on agricultural tracts of five acres or more, which the section does not cover (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)); damages may be trebled (Idaho Code § 6-317). The one statutory deduction from rent is for smoke detectors you fail to install after notice (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6)). There are time limits. A three-day notice to pay or quit 'may be served at any time within one (1) year after the rent becomes due' (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)); after that you can still sue for the money, within five years on a written lease (Idaho Code § 5-216) or four on an oral one (Idaho Code § 5-217). Only rent is unlimited in amount (Idaho Code § 55-305(4)); fees, interest and other charges must be reasonable, may not exceed the amount the lease states, and one the lease does not include may be charged only under an oral lease or, for a written lease, after a written 30-day notice of the change (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(3); leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023). Federal law: the CARES Act's 120-day ban on nonpayment filings and late charges for covered properties ran from March 27, 2020 and has ended (FEDERAL: 15 U.S.C. § 9058(b)); its 30-day notice to vacate is covered in edu-cares-act-notice. A tenant's bankruptcy filing can stop collection under federal law; get advice before acting.

title: Rent After a Condemnation or Vacate Order in Idaho
bodyText: No Idaho statute bars you from collecting rent after a home is condemned, declared unfit, or ordered vacated by a city or county, and none sets a penalty for taking it. That is not permission to keep charging. Once a lawful order stops the tenant living there, rent for a home the tenant cannot occupy is hard to justify under the lease, and the tenant has a damages action if you maintain the premises 'in a manner hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)), after a three-day written notice and except on agricultural tracts of five acres or more (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)-(e)), which a court may treble (Idaho Code § 6-317). One statute does require vacancy: once police notify you that a clandestine drug lab was found, 'The residential property shall remain vacant' until the state certifies the cleanup (Idaho Code § 6-2606(1)); it says nothing about rent, so the same cautious course applies. If the cause is fire or another casualty not caused by the tenant, the optional casualty clause lets either of you end the lease, with rent prorated and prepaid rent refunded (casualty-termination-id). Cautious course: stop charging rent from the date the order requires the tenant to leave, refund rent paid for later days, return the deposit under the usual rules (Idaho Code § 6-321), and get advice before collecting anything for that period.

title: Keeping Domestic-Violence Information Private in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho's statutes put no confidentiality duty on a private landlord who learns that a tenant or applicant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. No statute says what you may do with a protection order or other paperwork a tenant shows you, and none sets a penalty for passing it on. Idaho's address confidentiality program does not bind you directly. A victim certified by the Secretary of State names the Secretary of State 'as agent for purposes of service of process and for the purpose of receipt of mail' (Idaho Code § 19-5703(1)(b)); the duty to accept that substitute address is placed on 'state and local agencies' (Idaho Code § 19-5705(1)); and the Secretary of State releases a participant's file only to law enforcement or on a court order (Idaho Code § 19-5706). A tenant in the program may ask you to send mail to the substitute address, and you may agree. Federal law does impose a duty if the home is assisted under a federal housing program covered by the Violence Against Women Act (for example public housing, Section 8 assistance or a low-income housing tax credit property). There, information a tenant gives you about being a victim 'shall be maintained in confidence' and 'may not be entered into any shared database or disclosed to any other entity or individual', unless the tenant asks or consents in writing, it is needed in an eviction under that section, or other law requires it (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(c)(4)). The cautious course for every Idaho rental: keep such paperwork in a separate, restricted file, share it only with staff who need it, never discuss it with the other person named in it, and leave it out of references and screening reports.

title: Deposit Timing When a Domestic-Violence Victim Leaves Early in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no domestic-violence lease-termination right, so it has no special deposit rule for one. The ordinary rule applies: the deposit is refunded, less amounts lawfully kept, 'within twenty-one (21) days if no time is fixed by agreement and, in any event, within thirty (30) days after surrender of the premises by the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-321(2)), and the refund duty arises 'Upon termination of a lease or rental agreement and surrender of the premises by the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)). No Idaho statute says whether that clock starts when one of several co-tenants moves out while the others stay. Where a victim leaves and co-tenants remain, the lease has not ended, so the cautious reading is that the deposit stays with the tenancy until the lease ends and all tenants have surrendered. If you agree to release a departing victim early, put in a written agreement signed by every tenant what happens to the deposit: whether you will refund the victim's share now or hold the whole deposit until the remaining tenants leave. In federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, removing the abuser from a shared lease (lease bifurcation) is allowed without penalizing the victim (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(b)(3)(B)); the statute says nothing about deposits, so follow the program's rules.

title: No Idaho Eviction Shield for Domestic-Violence Victims
bodyText: No Idaho statute bars you from evicting a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or because of violence done to the tenant by someone else. Idaho's eviction grounds turn on conduct and lease terms: holding over, unpaid rent, a breach of the lease, assigning or subletting or waste contrary to the lease, and drug activity on the premises (Idaho Code § 6-303). Two of those grounds can reach a victim for an abuser's acts, which is where care is needed: a lease covenant the abuser breaks (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)), and drug activity by 'any person' on the premises (Idaho Code § 6-303(5)). A protection order may exclude the abuser from the shared home (Idaho Code § 39-6306(1)(c)), but 'No order made under this chapter shall in any manner affect title to real property' (Idaho Code § 39-6306(3)); the order does not end or change the lease, and an abuser who signed it remains a tenant. Two other rules still apply. Federal and Idaho fair housing law bar sex discrimination in renting, and treating victims more harshly than other tenants can raise that claim (see edu-fair-housing-id). In housing assisted under a program covered by the Violence Against Women Act, a tenant may not be evicted 'on the basis that the applicant or tenant is or has been a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking' (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(b)(1)), an incident of that violence is not a serious or repeated lease violation or good cause against the victim (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(b)(2)), and the owner may instead bifurcate the lease to remove the abuser (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(b)(3)(B)). The cautious course everywhere: base any eviction on the tenant's own conduct or unpaid rent, not on violence done to the tenant.

title: Lock Changes for Domestic-Violence Victims in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute giving a domestic-violence, sexual-assault or stalking victim a right to have the locks changed, putting a lock-change duty on you, voiding a lease term about locks, or saying who pays. The only lock-change statute in the code is the sheriff's removal of squatters who were never tenants (Idaho Code § 6-310A(5)). What Idaho does have is the protection order. A court may order the abuser excluded 'from the dwelling which the parties share or from the residence of the petitioner' (Idaho Code § 39-6306(1)(c)), or on an emergency basis exclude 'any party from the dwelling shared' (Idaho Code § 39-6308(1)(b)), may order a peace officer to help place the victim 'in possession of the dwelling or residence' (Idaho Code § 39-6309), and makes it a crime for the abuser to violate 'a provision excluding the person from a residence' (Idaho Code § 39-6312(1)). Cautious course: if a tenant shows you an order excluding someone from the home and asks for new locks, change them promptly or allow the tenant to, keep a key, and give no key to the excluded person. Charge for re-keying only a reasonable amount the lease states, or one added by a written 30-day notice of the change (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(2)). Do not lock out a co-tenant or occupant without such an order or a court judgment: removing a person in possession without court process risks liability for forcible entry or detainer (see edu-self-help-eviction-id). In federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, an owner may comply with a court order about 'the rights of access to or control of property' (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(b)(3)(C)(i)).

title: Idaho's Protection-Order Citations Have Not Moved
bodyText: Idaho's domestic-violence protection order still sits where it was enacted in 1988: the Domestic Violence Crime Prevention Act, Idaho Code Title 39, Chapter 63, with the petition in Idaho Code § 39-6304, the full order in Idaho Code § 39-6306, the emergency (ex parte) order in Idaho Code § 39-6308 and enforcement of out-of-state orders in Idaho Code § 39-6306A. None of those sections has been renumbered or repealed. The other orders a tenant may show you are also where they started: the civil protection order for stalking, threatening telephone calls and malicious harassment (Idaho Code § 18-7907, added 2016), the criminal no contact order (Idaho Code § 18-920) and the address confidentiality program (Idaho Code Title 19, Chapter 57, added 2008). Four small points for anyone keeping forms. Two sections still call the police records system the 'Idaho law enforcement telecommunications system' (Idaho Code § 39-6306A(5)(a), Idaho Code § 39-6313), while the main section now calls it the 'Idaho public safety and security information system' (Idaho Code § 39-6311(2)(b)); that is a naming leftover with no effect on landlords. The written notice police must give a victim still says a suit for losses can go to small claims court 'if the total amount claimed is less than five thousand dollars ($5,000)' (Idaho Code § 39-6316(2)), while the small claims limit is now $15,000 (Idaho Code § 1-2301). From January 1, 2027 the address confidentiality application refers to guardians appointed under Idaho Code § 15-5-309 instead of Idaho Code § 15-5-304 (Idaho Code § 19-5703(1)). And the 2025 renumbering of Idaho Code Title 55, Chapter 3 moved the rent-increase and nonrenewal notice to Idaho Code § 55-304 and the fee rule to Idaho Code § 55-305; leases or guides printed before July 1, 2025 may cite the old section numbers, which now hold other rules. Because Idaho has no landlord-tenant domestic-violence statute, no lease citation to one is needed.

title: What Documents Prove Domestic Violence for Idaho Rentals
bodyText: Because Idaho gives victims no lease-termination, lock-change or eviction protection, Idaho law sets no list of documents a tenant must give a landlord to use one, and no time limit measured from a document's date. If you choose to release a victim from a lease or to act on a request, these Idaho definitions are useful guides. A 'protection order' includes an order under Idaho's domestic-violence act, a similar order from another jurisdiction, or a temporary or final order (not a support or custody order) in a criminal or civil case issued on a request for protection after notice and an opportunity to respond to the person restrained (Idaho Code § 39-6303(8)). Idaho enforces another state's or a tribe's order that names the parties, 'Is currently in effect' and was issued by a tribunal with jurisdiction after notice and an opportunity to be heard, which for an ex parte order may come after it issues (Idaho Code § 39-6306A(3)(d)). A full order lasts up to one year unless the court continues it or makes it permanent (Idaho Code § 39-6306(5)), and an emergency order lasts no more than 14 days unless reissued (Idaho Code § 39-6308(5)), so check the dates. The address confidentiality program accepts police, court or agency records, letters from a victim-services program or a professional the victim consulted, and a certified copy of a no contact order or civil protection order (Idaho Code § 19-5703(2)); that list governs only applications to the Secretary of State. In federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, federal law sets the list: you may ask in writing for documentation, and the tenant may choose an approved certification form, a statement signed by a victim-service provider, attorney, or medical or mental-health professional, or a law-enforcement, court or agency record; the tenant has 14 business days to provide it (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(c)(1)-(3)). Whatever you accept, ask only for what you need and keep it confidential (see edu-dv-confidentiality-id).

title: What Goes in an Idaho Notice to Vacate
bodyText: Idaho prescribes only a few contents for notices, and each comes from the statute that creates the notice. A three-day notice for unpaid rent must be in writing, require payment 'stating the amount which is due, or possession of the property', and tell the tenant that after a judgment a residential tenant has 72 hours to remove belongings (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)); to recover attorney fees it must also say fees will be awarded to the prevailing party (Idaho Code § 6-324). A three-day notice for another breach must require performance of the lease term or possession (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)); a notice for assigning, subletting or waste is a three-day notice to quit (Idaho Code § 6-303(4)). A notice ending a tenancy at will must be in writing and specify a period of not less than one month (Idaho Code § 55-208(1)); notice of a rent increase or of nonrenewal of a residential lease must be in writing at least 30 days ahead (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)). Idaho requires no statement of tenant rights, legal-aid information, reason, form or type size beyond these, and has no rule barring you from altering or renovating the unit while a notice is pending; work that makes the home unsafe while the tenant is still there can still support a tenant's damages claim after a three-day notice, except on agricultural tracts of five acres or more (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3), (d)-(e)). Extra terms in a notice usually bind no one, with one important exception: for a month-to-month tenancy, a written notice given at least 15 days before the end of the month changes the lease terms if the tenant stays on (Idaho Code § 55-304(1)), though a rent increase still needs 30 days' notice (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)) and a new or changed fee under a written lease needs 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)(b)(ii)). Keep termination notices to what the statute asks, and put any proposed new terms in a separate notice.

title: Idaho Termination Notices Need No Stated Reason
bodyText: Idaho has no good-cause rule for ordinary residential tenancies, and no statute requires a notice ending a tenancy to state a reason. A month-to-month or other tenancy at will ends on written notice of at least one month (Idaho Code § 55-208(1)), and a residential lease is not renewed on written notice at least 30 days ahead (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)); neither asks for a reason. Eviction notices are different because the ground is the point of the notice: a nonpayment notice must state the amount due (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)), and a notice for another breach must require 'the performance of such conditions or covenants' (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)), so name the lease term broken and what the tenant must do. Manufactured home parks and floating home marinas have their own statutes requiring reasons, and the library does not cover them. Federally assisted housing has program good-cause rules. Even without a reason requirement, a termination may not be discriminatory (see edu-fair-housing-id).

title: Tenancies at Will in Idaho
bodyText:
A tenancy at will is a tenancy with no fixed end, such as one that continues month to month after a lease ends or one agreed with no end date. Idaho's rules cover 'A tenancy or other estate at will, however created' (Idaho Code § 55-208), so an oral tenancy counts too; only a lease for longer than one year must be in writing (Idaho Code § 9-505(4)).

To end it, you give the tenant written notice, served as the code of civil procedure provides, to leave within a period of not less than one month stated in the notice (Idaho Code § 55-208(1)); the tenant ends it by written notice of a move-out date at least one month away (Idaho Code § 55-208(2)). No reason is needed (see edu-no-good-cause-notice-id). Only after the notice period has run may you 'reenter, or proceed according to law to recover possession' (Idaho Code § 55-209). Re-entry still may not involve force, threats or breaking in (Idaho Code § 6-301, Idaho Code § 6-302); in practice a tenant who stays is in unlawful detainer and you go to court (Idaho Code § 6-303(1)).

During a month-to-month tenancy you may change terms by written notice at least 15 days before the end of the month (Idaho Code § 55-304(1)), but a rent increase needs 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)) and a fee change under a written agreement needs 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)(b)(ii)).

Whether a month-to-month tenancy is a tenancy at will or a separate periodic tenancy in every respect is case law; the library applies the one-month notice to both (periodic-tenancy-notice-id).

Agricultural land has its own holdover rule: a tenant who stays more than 60 days after the term without a demand is treated as holding for another year (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)).

title: Idaho Has No Seasonal Tenancy Category
bodyText: Idaho has no seasonal tenancy: no seasonal exemption, shortened notice, seasonal lease form or seasonal disclosure. A stay offered for a fee for 30 days or less is a 'short-term rental' or 'vacation rental' (Idaho Code § 63-1803(4)), which the library does not cover; cities and counties may regulate those only within limits (Idaho Code § 67-6539). A building with more than ten rooms let to transient guests is a hotel (Idaho Code § 39-1801(2)). Anything longer, such as a summer cabin or a ski-season rental, is an ordinary residential tenancy with the usual rules: the deposit rules (Idaho Code § 6-321), the tenant's repair action (Idaho Code § 6-320), the fee rule (Idaho Code § 55-305) and the eviction process. A seasonal lease for a fixed term ends on its end date, but if you do not intend to renew it, give written notice at least 30 days before (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)). If the tenant stays on with your consent, it may become a tenancy at will ending on one month's notice (Idaho Code § 55-208). Seasonal agricultural tenancies have a holdover rule: a tenant who stays more than 60 days after the term without a demand is treated as holding for another year (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)).

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute letting you, or the tenant, end a lease because of wildfire smoke, flooding, contamination, a declared disaster or another environmental event, and no force-majeure rule for leases. One statute deals with a hazard in the home: once police notify you that a clandestine drug lab was found, 'The residential property shall remain vacant' until the state certifies the cleanup (Idaho Code § 6-2606(1)); it says nothing about the lease (see edu-meth-cleanup-id). The library's optional casualty clause covers the usual case: if the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty not caused by the tenant's side and becomes unfit or substantially impaired, either party may end the lease (casualty-termination-id). A broader opt-in right for you to end the lease after an environmental event that does not damage the home is lawful as far as Idaho's statutes go, but the library does not offer one: the casualty clause already reaches events that damage the home, and a right to end the lease for events that leave it usable would be vague and easy to dispute. If you want one, add your own clause after taking legal advice.

title: Repair Costs Do Not End an Idaho Lease
bodyText: No Idaho statute lets you end a lease, or refuse a repair, because the repair would cost too much, and none sets a cost threshold for either side. Your duties to provide waterproofing and weather protection, keep supplied electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling and sanitary facilities working, and not keep the premises hazardous are stated without any cost limit, and a tenant may sue for damages and specific performance after a three-day notice, except on agricultural tracts of five acres or more (Idaho Code § 6-320(a), (d)-(e)). Where the damage comes from fire or another casualty not caused by the tenant's side, the optional casualty clause lets either party end the lease (casualty-termination-id). Where the tenant caused it, the tenant pays (tenant-caused-damage-id), and waste contrary to the lease ends the lease on a three-day notice to quit (Idaho Code § 6-303(4)). A clause letting you end the lease whenever a repair is uneconomic is lawful as far as Idaho's statutes go, but the library does not offer one: the casualty clause covers the main case, and a general cost-based exit would sit uneasily with your repair duties under Idaho Code § 6-320(a) and the lease's maintenance clause. If you want one, add your own after taking legal advice.

title: Renting the Same Home Twice in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute on double-letting, that is, renting the same home or room to two tenants for the same period, and no statutory rent abatement for it. The consequences come from the lease, contract law and a few general statutes. The tenant who cannot get in has a claim against you for breach. The library's possession-delay clause does not help you here, because it applies only when you cannot deliver possession "through no fault of Landlord". Advertising or offering a rental 'with intent not to sell' it as advertised, or any misleading practice, can violate the Consumer Protection Act (Idaho Code § 48-603(9), (17)), and a tenant who loses money may treat the agreement as voidable or recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater (Idaho Code § 48-608(1)). You may not fix the problem by removing whichever tenant is in possession yourself: that risks forcible entry or detainer (Idaho Code § 6-301, Idaho Code § 6-302), and the fast forcible-detainer track may not be used against someone who had a landlord-tenant relationship with you, on pain of treble damages (Idaho Code § 6-310(5)). Cautious course: never sign a second lease for a unit until the first tenancy has ended and the unit is empty, and if it happens, tell the second tenant at once, refund everything they paid and offer to release them.

title: When an Idaho Tenant Can End a Lease Early by Law
bodyText: Idaho statutes give an ordinary residential tenant very few ways to end a fixed-term lease early. Know the ones that exist so you do not treat a lawful departure as an abandonment. First, a servicemember. Federal law lets a tenant who enters military service during the lease term, or who signs the lease while in service and then gets permanent-change-of-station or deployment orders of at least 90 days, end the lease by written notice with a copy of the orders. For a lease with monthly rent, the end is 30 days after the next rent due date following delivery of the notice. You may not charge an early termination fee, though unpaid rent up to that date (prorated) and other lease obligations, including reasonable excess-wear charges, remain due, and rent paid for later days must be refunded within 30 days (FEDERAL: 50 U.S.C. § 3955). Second, a deceptive or unconscionable practice. Idaho's Consumer Protection Act covers leasing real property (Idaho Code § 48-602(2), (6)). A tenant who loses money because of a practice the Act forbids, such as a misleading statement about the home (Idaho Code § 48-603(5), (17)) or an unconscionable practice (Idaho Code § 48-603C), 'may treat any agreement incident thereto as voidable' (Idaho Code § 48-608(1)), or sue for damages of at least $1,000. This is the nearest Idaho comes to a termination right for a landlord's misrepresentation; contract-law rescission for fraud is case law, not reviewed. Third, a month-to-month or other tenancy at will ends on the tenant's written notice at least one month ahead (Idaho Code § 55-208(2)); that is not an early termination, just the periodic notice. Idaho has no statutory early exit for domestic violence (edu-no-dv-termination-id), a tenant's death (edu-no-tenant-death-rule-id), illness or move to care (edu-no-infirmity-termination-id), fire or casualty (the optional casualty-termination-id clause fills that gap), or your failure to repair: the tenant's remedy there is a lawsuit for damages and specific performance after a three-day notice, not ending the lease, and the section does not cover agricultural tracts of five acres or more (Idaho Code § 6-320(a), (d)-(e)). No Idaho statute makes you forfeit rent already owed because the lease left out a required statement. The one similar rule is narrower: you recover attorney fees in a nonpayment eviction only if the three-day notice said fees would go to the prevailing party (Idaho Code § 6-324). The library's early-termination clause sets the terms on which a tenant may buy out a fixed term.

title: No Early Exit for Illness, Age or a Move to Care in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute letting a tenant end a lease early because of illness, disability, age, or a move into a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility, and no rule that a lease ends on a party's incapacity or death. Idaho also has no general rule on hirings like California's, under which a tenancy terminable at will ends on notice of a party's incapacity to contract. So a fixed-term lease keeps running. A month-to-month or other tenancy at will is different: the tenant, or someone with authority to act for the tenant, can end it by written notice at least one month ahead (Idaho Code § 55-208(2)). If the tenant can no longer manage their affairs, check who has authority before accepting a surrender. From January 1, 2027, a court-appointed conservator needs the court's specific authorization before the conservator may 'surrender a lease to the primary dwelling' of the person under conservatorship (Idaho Code § 15-5-414(1)(b)); the rules before that date were not reviewed. No Idaho statute requires you to re-let the home to reduce what a departing tenant owes; whether a court will expect it is case law not reviewed. A request to end the lease because of a disability may also be a request for a reasonable accommodation under fair housing law (see edu-fair-housing-id); get advice before refusing one. For a servicemember, federal law adds a narrow right to end the lease after a catastrophic injury or illness in service (FEDERAL: 50 U.S.C. § 3955(a)(4)).

title: Why the Idaho Lease Sets No Holdover Rate
bodyText: Idaho has no statute setting a holdover rent, a double-rent penalty, or a cap on a holdover charge written into a lease. A daily holdover rate in the lease is lawful as far as Idaho's statutes go. The library does not offer one for Idaho, because the statute already gives you a measure for every holdover, deliberate or not. A tenant who stays after the term without your permission is in unlawful detainer (Idaho Code § 6-303(1)); the court assesses 'the damages occasioned to the plaintiff' (Idaho Code § 6-316(1)) by the unlawful detainer, and 'judgment may be entered for three (3) times the amount at which the actual damages are assessed' (Idaho Code § 6-317). That actual-damages measure, normally the rental value for the time the tenant stays plus any loss the holdover causes, is what the Idaho lease's holdover clause claims (holdover-ca), and edu-holdover-damages-id explains it. A stated rate would sit inside a figure the court may already treble, and a rate set well above the rent risks being treated as a penalty, which is case law not reviewed. If you want a set holdover rate anyway, add your own clause after taking legal advice; set it near the daily rent, and remember that a fee must be reasonable and may not exceed the amount the lease states, and one the written lease does not include needs a written 30-day notice first (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(2)); stating it in the lease is the safe course. Agricultural land has its own rule: a tenant who holds over for more than 60 days without a demand for possession is treated as holding for another year (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)).

title: When a Tenant Files Bankruptcy in Idaho
bodyText: No Idaho statute deals with a tenant's bankruptcy; federal bankruptcy law controls. When a tenant files, an automatic stay stops starting or continuing an eviction or other case against the tenant, any act to get possession, and any act to collect rent owed from before the filing (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1), (3), (6)). Two exceptions matter. If you had a judgment for possession before the tenant filed, the stay does not stop the eviction (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(22)), unless the tenant certifies that state law would let the tenant cure the whole default after judgment, deposits the next 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy clerk, and then cures within 30 days (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(l)). For a home on five acres or less, Idaho's statutes give no right to cure after judgment (see edu-forfeiture-redemption-id); case law was not reviewed, and you may object to a tenant's certification, which gets a hearing within 10 days. Second, an eviction based on endangering the property or illegal drug use on it can go ahead 15 days after you file and serve a certification under penalty of perjury, unless the tenant objects and shows the court the problem did not exist or has been fixed (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(23), (m)). In a chapter 7 case the lease is deemed rejected if the trustee does not assume or reject it within 60 days after the order for relief, unless the court extends that time (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 365(d)(1)). Outside these exceptions you need the bankruptcy court's permission before filing or continuing an eviction. Talk to a lawyer before taking any step after a tenant files.

title: Rental Inspections in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes set up no rental inspection or rental licensing program for ordinary long-term rentals, and no statute lets a lease authorize a city or health inspector to enter a tenant's home. Cities and counties may adopt their own police, sanitary and other regulations that don't conflict with state law (Idaho Const. art. XII, § 2; Idaho Code § 50-302(1)), and a local government that enforces building codes does so under the Idaho Building Code Act (Idaho Code § 39-4116). Idaho's ban on local rent control (Idaho Code § 55-306) reaches only local rules that regulate the rent, fees or deposits charged for leasing private homes, or that force owners into an optional federal housing assistance program. It does not stop a city from inspecting long-term rentals.

Short-term rentals of 30 days or less are different. A city or county may not require inspections of a short-term rental that it would not require of the same home used otherwise, and may not require a license, permit or registration to operate one (Idaho Code § 67-6539(2)(a)(ix), (5); Idaho Code § 63-1803(4)).

The Idaho Constitution protects homes against unreasonable searches (Idaho Const. art. I, § 17). Whether a tenant's signature on a lease counts as consent for an inspector to enter is a question of case law. The cautious course, which the library follows, is a lease that asks the tenant to cooperate with an inspection and to tell you if the tenant refuses entry, without giving consent on the tenant's behalf (rental-inspection-cooperation-mn).

Check your city's code: ordinances in Boise, Meridian, Nampa, Idaho Falls, Pocatello and Coeur d'Alene were not reviewed.

title: Health District Rules and Rentals
bodyText: Idaho's public health districts are run by district boards of health, which enforce state and district health laws and may adopt their own rules (Idaho Code § 39-414(1); Idaho Code § 39-416). Idaho's statutes do not require a landlord to give tenants a copy of health-district rules, or to refer tenants to the health district, and they give health districts no rental-housing program of their own. A district's rules are adopted under the state rulemaking act (Idaho Code § 39-416(2)), but the current Idaho Administrative Code lists no health-district rules and no rules on rental housing, dwellings or sanitation in homes. Local district regulations were not reviewed, so ask your district whether it has any that reach rentals. Willfully breaking a lawful health-district rule or order is a misdemeanor (an infraction if the order applies to everyone in a county or district), and the violator can be made to pay the district's cost of removing a nuisance or health hazard (Idaho Code § 39-419(1), (2), (4)). Separately, a tenant may sue you for keeping the premises in a manner hazardous to the tenant's health or safety (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)), after giving you three days' written notice listing each problem (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)). That lawsuit does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). Idaho's ban on local rent control (Idaho Code § 55-306) covers rent, fees and deposits only and does not limit health rules.

title: Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not limit renting a home in a single-family zone, do not require an owner to live on a lot before renting it, and have no state lot-split or two-unit program with its own occupancy or rental-term rules. Two land-use statutes limit what cities can do instead. A city or county may not ban any type of short-term rental (30 days or less) or require the owner to live in it (Idaho Code § 67-6539(1), (2)(a)(i); Idaho Code § 63-1803(4)). And by February 1, 2027, every city of more than 10,000 people must allow one accessory dwelling unit on each lot zoned single-family (outside historic districts and historic properties) and must not require the owner to live in either the main home or the accessory unit (Idaho Code § 67-6541(2)(a), (e), (6)); see edu-accessory-dwelling-unit-id. Otherwise, cities and counties keep their zoning and police powers (Idaho Const. art. XII, § 2). Idaho's ban on local rent control (Idaho Code § 55-306) covers rent, fees, deposits and forced participation in optional federal housing programs, not zoning use rules, so no statute stops a city from limiting long-term rentals in a zone in other ways. Whether a particular limit is valid is a question of case law. Homeowner's associations are separate: an association may not add or enforce a new rental restriction unless the owner agreed to it in writing when it was adopted (Idaho Code § 55-3211; edu-hoa-rental-restrictions-id). Check your city's zoning code.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Idaho law protects accessory dwelling units but sets no rules for renting one. No city of more than 10,000 people may ban accessory dwelling units in a residential zone (Idaho Code § 67-6541(1), (6)). By February 1, 2027, every city of more than 10,000 people must allow one internal or one detached accessory unit on each lot zoned for single-family homes (outside historic districts), and approve qualifying projects as a matter of right (Idaho Code § 67-6541(2)(a), (3), (6)). They must not require the owner to live in either the main home or the accessory unit (Idaho Code § 67-6541(2)(e)). Those cities also may not, in most cases, demand off-street parking for the unit, charge it higher impact or connection fees than other single-family homes, or cap its size below 1,000 square feet or 75% of the main home (Idaho Code § 67-6541(2)(b)-(d)). Building, fire, utility and similar safety laws still apply (Idaho Code § 67-6541(7)). Idaho's statutes set no minimum rental term and no owner-occupancy rule for renting an accessory unit, so you may rent one under the same lease and law as any other home. An accessory unit offered for 30 days or less fits Idaho's definition of a short-term rental, so the limits on local short-term rental rules would then apply (Idaho Code § 63-1803(4); Idaho Code § 67-6539). Homeowner's associations may not add, amend or enforce a restriction that limits accessory units unless the owner agreed in writing, though they may adopt reasonable rules on design, size, parking and similar matters, and this protection does not cover short-term rentals (Idaho Code § 55-3212). A restrictive covenant entered into on or after July 1, 2023 that bans an internal accessory unit is void (Idaho Code § 55-618). A city or county may also let you divide off an accessory unit's land for financing only, without creating new building rights (Idaho Code § 50-1335). Check your city's code.

title: No Required Tenant Rights Guide
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to give a tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, before signing or at renewal, and no statute tells a state agency to publish one for that purpose. No signed acknowledgment of such a guide is required either. Federal law separately requires a lead hazard information pamphlet for older housing covered by the federal lead rules (see lead-based-paint). You may give tenants any accurate summary you like, but it is not part of the lease and should not be presented as a statement of Idaho law unless it is kept current. Idaho's ban on local rent control (Idaho Code § 55-306) does not stop a city from requiring a local notice, so check your city's code.

title: Code Orders and Receivership
bodyText: Idaho's statutes have no receivership program for substandard rental buildings and no state housing code that lets a city or a tenant ask a court to put a receiver in charge of a neglected rental. Idaho courts have a general power to appoint receivers in listed cases, such as mortgage foreclosure or to carry out a judgment, and 'in all other cases where receivers have heretofore been appointed by the usages of courts of equity' (Idaho Code § 8-601). Whether that reaches a code-enforcement case is a question of case law. What cities do have is nuisance power. A city may declare what is a nuisance and remove or abate it at the expense of those who created or keep it, and may charge the cost as a special assessment on the land, collected with city taxes (Idaho Code § 50-334; Idaho Code § 50-1008). A public nuisance may be abated by any public body or officer the law authorizes (Idaho Code § 52-205). A health district can also make a violator pay its cost of removing a nuisance or health hazard (Idaho Code § 39-419(2)), and a building used for lewd purposes can be ordered closed for a year (Idaho Code § 52-412; edu-lewd-use-lease-void-id). Cities and counties may adopt their own housing, building and nuisance rules (Idaho Const. art. XII, § 2; Idaho Code § 50-302(1)); Idaho's ban on local rent control (Idaho Code § 55-306) does not limit them. Separately, a tenant may sue you over the conditions listed in Idaho Code § 6-320(a) after three days' written notice (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)); that lawsuit does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho's statutes have no lead-safe or lead-free certificate for rentals, nothing requiring a lead certificate to be attached to a lease, and no state lead-paint inspection or abatement program for rental housing. The Idaho Code does not use the terms "lead-based paint" or "lead hazard" at all. Federal law still applies. Before a tenant is bound by a lease of older housing covered by the federal lead rules, you must give the tenant the federal lead hazard information pamphlet and disclose any known lead-based paint or hazards and any reports you have; the library's lead-based-paint clause covers this. Idaho's ban on local rent control (Idaho Code § 55-306) does not stop a city from adopting its own lead rule, so check your city's code.

title: Landlord Registration in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statewide landlord or rental registration. No statute requires you to register with the county assessor or any state agency before renting, to hire an Idaho broker or agent because you live out of state, or to be registered before you can win an eviction. Cities may license and charge a uniform license fee on any business within city limits and regulate it by ordinance (Idaho Code § 50-307), and cities and counties keep their general police powers (Idaho Const. art. XII, § 2), so a local rental registration or license ordinance is possible. Idaho's ban on local rent control (Idaho Code § 55-306) bars local rules that regulate the rent, fees or deposits charged for leasing, or that force owners into an optional federal housing assistance program; it does not on its face bar a local registration or license for long-term rentals. Whether a particular local fee counts as regulating fees charged for leasing is a question of case law. Short-term rentals (30 days or less) are protected: no city or county may require a license, fee, permit, certification or registration to operate one (Idaho Code § 67-6539(5); Idaho Code § 63-1803(4)). Check your city's code. Separate state registrations may apply to your business itself, such as an out-of-state entity's registration with the Secretary of State (see edu-nonresident-owner-agent-id).

title: Recording a Lease in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho does not require a residential lease to be recorded or registered, and recording a lease changes none of the rights between you and your tenant. An unrecorded lease is valid between the parties and anyone who knows of it (Idaho Code § 55-815). You may record a lease, or a signed and acknowledged summary of it, with the county recorder, because any instrument affecting the possession of real property may be recorded (Idaho Code § 55-801; Idaho Code § 55-818). Recording requires the signer's acknowledgment (Idaho Code § 55-805). Recording matters mainly to third parties. A lease for a term of more than one year that is not recorded is void against a later buyer or lender who acts in good faith, pays value and records first (Idaho Code § 55-812). A lease for one year or less is exempt from that rule. Whether a tenant's possession of the home gives a buyer or lender notice of an unrecorded lease is a question of case law. Idaho's recording statutes have no special rule for leases to a relative. A lease of more than one year must also be in writing to be enforceable (edu-lease-in-writing-id).

title: Out-of-State Owners in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho does not require an out-of-state landlord to name an Idaho agent in the lease, to hire an Idaho broker or manager, or to file anything before suing a tenant. Tenants are not required to withhold income tax from rent paid to an out-of-state owner. Owning rental property in Idaho does have consequences. Owning, using or possessing real property in Idaho subjects you to Idaho courts for claims arising from it (Idaho Code § 5-514(c)), and you can be served with a summons outside Idaho as if served in the state (Idaho Code § 5-515). If you own through an LLC, corporation or partnership formed in another state, the entity may not do business in Idaho until it registers with the Idaho Secretary of State. An unregistered entity doing business in Idaho may not bring a lawsuit here, including an eviction, until it registers (Idaho Code § 30-21-502(a), (b)). Its leases stay valid and it can still defend a suit (Idaho Code § 30-21-502(c)). Merely owning property is not doing business (Idaho Code § 30-21-505(a)(10)); whether renting homes is, is a question of case law, so the cautious course is to register before you need to file. If you rent under a name other than your own or your entity's true name, file a certificate of assumed business name first; until you do, you cannot maintain a lawsuit in Idaho courts (Idaho Code § 30-21-805; Idaho Code § 30-21-810(a)). If an entity that passes income through to its owners has owners living outside Idaho, it may have to withhold Idaho income tax on their share or file a composite return (Idaho Code § 63-3036B; Idaho Code § 63-3022L); ask a tax adviser. Give tenants a reliable Idaho-reachable address: a tenant's notice before suing over repairs or a deposit is served on you or your agent personally, on an employee at your usual place of business if you and your agent are absent, or by certified mail, return receipt requested (Idaho Code § 6-323; edu-no-owner-disclosure-id). If a third-party manager handles deposits, the deposits generally must be kept in a separate account (Idaho Code § 6-321(4)).

title: Police Cooperation and Reporting
bodyText: Idaho has no statute on crime-free lease addenda, none requiring tenants to cooperate with police, none requiring you to hand police information about tenants or open a unit to them without legal process, and none limiting a lease penalty for a tenant who calls the police or emergency help. Two specific duties can reach you as a landlord. When a court orders a wiretap, or a pen register or trap and trace device, you must on request give the officers the information, facilities and technical help needed to install it unobtrusively, and you are paid your reasonable expenses (Idaho Code § 18-6708(5); Idaho Code § 18-6723(1)-(3)). You cannot be sued for helping under the court order (Idaho Code § 18-6723(4)). One general reporting duty binds you and your staff as it binds anyone. A person who has reason to believe a child under 18 has been abused, abandoned or neglected must report it within 24 hours to law enforcement or the Department of Health and Welfare, and failing to report is a misdemeanor (Idaho Code § 16-1605(1), (4)). For a vulnerable adult, the reporting duty falls on listed professionals; anyone else may report (Idaho Code § 39-5303). For criminal activity at the property, Idaho gives you an eviction ground for drug activity on the premises (Idaho Code § 6-303(5); edu-expedited-drug-eviction-id), and other lease breaches follow the usual three-day notice (edu-cure-notice-id). A tenant's home is protected against unreasonable searches (Idaho Const. art. I, § 17); let police in to a tenant's home only with the tenant's consent, a warrant or an emergency, and take advice when in doubt.

title: Special District Disclosures
bodyText:
Idaho requires one special-district statement for leases. If your property is inside a business improvement district created by the city, you, as owner, must give the tenant a written disclosure before leasing that the property is in the district and that the tenant may be responsible for paying special assessments to the city (Idaho Code § 50-2623).
