The statute gives a form, and an alternative form is allowed if substantially similar (Idaho Code § 50-2624(2)); the library's special-district-representation clause follows it.

The statement must be the owner's own: a property manager or other agent may not make or verify it (Idaho Code § 50-2623). Within 30 days after the lease, you must also send the city a written copy of the notice of the lease and the tenant's identity (Idaho Code § 50-2624(1)).

These districts fund parking, public-space improvements, events and retail promotion, and their assessments fall on businesses and business property in the district (Idaho Code § 50-2601). If you want the tenant to pay any assessment, the lease must say so or you must give 30 days' written notice first (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)).

No other Idaho special district carries a lease statement. A community infrastructure district must record a notice and requires a disclosure signed by purchasers, not tenants (Idaho Code § 50-3115), and local improvement district and urban renewal laws set no tenant notice. Ask the city whether your property is in a business improvement district.

title: Tribal and Trust Land Leases
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require a government officer to approve a residential lease before it is valid, and they say nothing about leases of land held in trust for a tribe or a tribal member. Idaho has Indian reservations, and land there that is held in trust by the United States, or restricted against sale, is governed by federal and tribal law. Idaho's own law expressly does not authorize the encumbrance of that property, and does not give Idaho courts power to decide who owns or has the right to possess it (Idaho Code § 67-5103). Idaho took on only limited jurisdiction in Indian country, for listed matters such as child welfare and domestic relations, not landlord-tenant cases (Idaho Code § 67-5101), unless a tribe consents to more (Idaho Code § 67-5102). So if you plan to lease trust or restricted land, or rent a home on a reservation, federal approval rules, tribal law and the proper court for an eviction must be checked first. Federal and tribal law were not reviewed, and the library's lease is not drafted for trust or restricted land. Leases of ordinary fee land inside a reservation boundary raise the same court question; take advice before relying on an Idaho eviction there.

title: Leases by a Life Tenant
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Idaho law does not use; the word does not appear in the Idaho Code. The closest Idaho interest is a life estate, for example a surviving spouse who holds a home for life while the children own the remainder. Idaho's statutes do not say what happens to a residential lease signed by a life tenant when the life estate ends. They do say that a grant by the owner of an estate for life that purports to transfer more than the owner could lawfully transfer passes only what the owner could transfer (Idaho Code § 55-607). So a tenant who rents from a life tenant generally gets no more than the life tenant held; how that applies to a lease running past the life tenant's death is a question of case law. A life tenant must keep the buildings and fences in repair against ordinary waste and pay the taxes and annual charges (Idaho Code § 55-314), and a tenant for life or for years who commits waste can be sued for treble damages (Idaho Code § 6-201). If you lease property you hold only for life, or under a trust or estate, tell the tenant in the lease and take advice on what happens when your interest ends. The library offers no clause for this; an owner in that position can add one after taking advice.

title: Eminent Domain and Leases
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes do not say what happens to a lease or the rent when leased property is taken by eminent domain. No statute ends the lease, reduces the rent, or lets the condemnation court cancel the lease, so the lease decides.

In the condemnation case, the court or jury values the property and each separate estate or interest in it, which includes a tenant's leasehold (Idaho Code § 7-711(1)), and anyone occupying or claiming an interest in the property may appear and defend even if not named (Idaho Code § 7-709). A lease clause that ends the lease on a total taking, adjusts rent on a partial taking and gives the award to you, while leaving the tenant any separate relocation payment, is lawful as far as Idaho's statutes go; the library offers one (eminent-domain-vi).

Tenants displaced by a state or local public project may receive relocation help, including rent supplement payments, from the acquiring agency (Idaho Code § 40-2001; Idaho Code § 40-2005(2)); the clause leaves those payments to the tenant. Idaho also limits condemnation for private or economic-development purposes (Idaho Code § 7-701A). How courts split an award between landlord and tenant without a lease clause is a question of case law.

title: No Variance Notice to Tenants
bodyText: Idaho has no state sanitary or housing code for rentals, and its statutes do not require you to give tenants, or attach to a lease, a copy of any variance, exception or waiver an agency has granted for your property. Building codes are adopted and enforced locally under the Idaho Building Code Act, and a local government may amend them only within the limits that act sets (Idaho Code § 39-4116). Zoning variances change lot, setback, height and similar requirements and need notice only to adjoining owners (and a local airport manager where an aviation hazard could result), not tenants (Idaho Code § 67-6516). If a city or health district grants you a variance that affects how tenants use the home, telling the tenant in writing is good practice, but no Idaho statute requires it.

title: Child Care in a Rental
bodyText: Idaho has no statute requiring a landlord to let a tenant run a child care business in a rental, and none limiting a lease term that forbids it. The library's residential-use-only clause bars commercial use, which includes paid child care. Homeowner's associations are treated differently: an association may not add, amend or enforce a covenant after July 1, 2024 that prohibits a family daycare home (six or fewer children), though it may require licensing and apply its general rules on parking, noise and similar matters (Idaho Code § 55-3213; Idaho Code § 39-1102(8)). That rule binds associations, not landlords. If you choose to allow child care, know the state rules your tenant must follow. A home caring for seven or more unrelated children needs a basic daycare license (Idaho Code § 39-1102(5); Idaho Code § 39-1103). A family daycare home caring for four to six children need not be licensed but must pass a criminal history check, may face fire inspections and may choose to be licensed (Idaho Code § 39-1114). Smoking is banned in a licensed child care facility in a private home while a child in its care is present (Idaho Code § 39-5502(12)(k)). Idaho law sets no insurance or liability terms for this; if you permit child care, put your conditions, such as licensing and liability insurance, in a written addendum after taking advice. The library offers no child care clause.

title: Home Businesses in Rentals
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not make a home-based business a permitted use of a home, and nothing in them stops a lease from limiting or forbidding business use. The library's residential-use-only clause bars commercial use of the property. Whether a business may operate from a home is otherwise a matter of local zoning and licensing: cities may license and regulate any business within city limits (Idaho Code § 50-307), and zoning ordinances set what uses a residential zone allows (Idaho Const. art. XII, § 2). The one statewide protection close to this topic binds homeowner's associations, not landlords: an association may not ban a family daycare home under a covenant adopted after July 1, 2024 (Idaho Code § 55-3213; edu-family-child-care-id). If you are willing to allow a quiet home office or similar use, say so in writing and set conditions such as no customer traffic, signs or employees on site.

title: Portfolio Size Thresholds
bodyText: Idaho's landlord-tenant duties do not change with the number of units you own. The deposit, notice, repair-lawsuit, fee and eviction rules apply the same way to a one-home landlord and a large company, and there is no small-landlord exemption from them. A few Idaho rules turn on other facts, and each should be read with all of its parts. The state ban on discrimination in real estate transactions (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)) does not apply to renting a unit in a building with housing for no more than two families when you or a family member lives in the other unit (Idaho Code § 67-5910(7)(a)). Both parts of that exemption must be true. It also does not apply to renting rooms in a home where you or a family member lives (Idaho Code § 67-5910(7)(b)). Federal fair housing law has its own rules (edu-fair-housing-id). The separate-account rule for deposits binds only a third-party manager, and does not apply to the owner, a manager with common members or principals of the owner entity, a real estate licensee or a nonprofit organization (Idaho Code § 6-321(4)); any one of those is enough. Some rules turn on land size, not portfolio size: the tenant's repair lawsuit does not apply to farm tracts of five acres or more (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)), and the fast-track eviction applies to tracts of five acres or less (Idaho Code § 6-310(1)).

title: No Student Housing Rule
bodyText: Idaho has no special landlord-tenant rule for student housing: no exemption for dormitories or student buildings, and no extra duty for landlords who rent to students. Privately owned student apartments, including buildings leased to or managed for a school, follow the same Idaho rules as any other rental. The state's statutes on student housing concern how public colleges and junior college dormitory housing commissions build, finance, lease and run dormitories and set their rents (Idaho Code § 33-3701; Idaho Code § 33-2122); they do not change tenants' or landlords' rights. Idaho also has no rent cap or just-cause eviction rule for an exemption to matter (edu-rent-control-preemption-id; edu-no-just-cause-id). Whether a school's room-and-board agreement for a dormitory creates a tenancy is a question of case law. When renting to several students, the library's joint-liability clause applies as for any other co-tenants.

title: Housing Your Employees
bodyText: Idaho has no statute on housing you provide to your own employees, such as a resident manager, caretaker or farm hand. No law requires a written disclosure of when the employee must leave, an offer of a rental agreement when the job ends, or a filing with the government. Idaho's eviction statute is written for 'a tenant of real property' (Idaho Code § 6-303), and it does not say whether an employee who lives in housing as part of the job is a tenant. That is a question of case law. If the arrangement is a tenancy at will, it ends on at least one month's written notice (Idaho Code § 55-208). The sheriff's quick removal process for unauthorized occupants cannot be used against current or former tenants under a written or oral rental agreement (Idaho Code § 6-310A(2)(f)), so do not rely on it to remove a former employee. The cautious course is a separate written housing agreement. It should state the rent or that the housing is part of pay, what happens to the housing when the job ends, and how much notice the employee gets to leave. If the employee does not leave, use the court process. Farm labor contractors must give each worker at hiring a written statement of the terms of any housing provided and its cost (Idaho Code § 44-1607(7)(e)).

title: No Senior Housing Work Cards
bodyText: Idaho has no work card, permit or background-check requirement for people who work at housing for older persons (such as 55-and-over communities), and no special landlord-tenant rule for age-restricted rentals. Licensed care facilities are regulated separately and are outside this library. If you run age-restricted housing, federal fair housing law sets the conditions for it; that law was not reviewed here (edu-fair-housing-id).

title: No Veteran Landlord Incentive
bodyText: Idaho has no statute giving landlords a tax credit, payment, deposit guarantee or other incentive for renting to veterans, and no state program that pays a veteran tenant's back rent to stop an eviction. Idaho's veteran property tax relief and similar benefits go to the veteran's own home, not to rental owners. Veteran status is not a protected class under Idaho's Human Rights Act housing rules (edu-fair-housing-id), and Idaho has no source-of-income rule (edu-source-of-income-id).

title: Hunting Rights on Rented Land
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not say whether a tenant of rented farmland or rural property gets hunting, fishing or trapping rights, so the lease decides. Under Idaho's trespass law, hunting on private land requires permission, defined as written authorization from the owner or his agent that is signed and names the person, the dates and the property, or another form of permission or invitation recognized by law (Idaho Code § 18-7008(1)(f); Idaho Code § 36-1603(a)). A tenant under a valid lease is not a trespasser on the leased land (Idaho Code § 18-7008(6)(a)(iii), (7)), but the statute does not say whether a tenant may give others permission to hunt. Whether a lessee counts as an owner for that purpose is a question of case law. The cautious course for a rural lease is to say whether the tenant may hunt, fish or trap on the property and, if you want the tenant to be able to let guests hunt, to appoint the tenant in writing as your agent for giving permission. You may revoke a bare permission at any time, but not a right the lease itself grants (Idaho Code § 18-7008(5), (6)(a)(iii)). The Department of Fish and Game may issue a permit to a bona fide owner or lessee whose property is being damaged by furbearing animals to trap or kill them on the owned or leased premises (Idaho Code § 36-1107(a)(4)). The library offers no hunting clause; its lease is written for homes, not farm tracts.

title: Habitability Rules Idaho Lacks
bodyText: Idaho has no residential landlord-tenant act and no habitability code. Its repair standard is the list of failures a tenant may sue over: weather protection, working electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling and sanitary facilities you supply, premises not hazardous to health or safety, deposit return, lease terms affecting health and safety, and smoke detectors (Idaho Code § 6-320(a); edu-landlord-duties-id). These habitability rules found in other states are confirmed absent from Idaho's statutes. (1) No "fit and habitable" standard or statutory warranty of habitability. (2) No rule against waiving the repair duties in an ordinary lease; the only bans on waivers in rental agreements cover manufactured-home lot rentals and floating-home moorage rentals (Idaho Code § 55-2007(2)(a); Idaho Code § 55-2706(5)). Whether a waiver would be enforced is case law, and the library includes none. (3) No rent withholding, rent escrow or general repair-and-deduct remedy. The one self-help right is for smoke detectors: after written notice by certified mail and 72 hours, the tenant may install them and deduct the cost from the next month's rent (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6)). (4) No repair deadline; the tenant must give three days' written notice listing each problem before suing (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)). (5) No minimum heat or hot-water temperature. (6) No carbon monoxide alarm rule for long-term rentals; the only statute on carbon monoxide detectors in rentals lets cities and counties require them in short-term rentals (Idaho Code § 67-6539(3)(b)). (7) No state rental inspection, code-enforcement receivership, variance notice or lead-safe certificate (edu-rental-inspection-id, edu-substandard-property-receivership-id, edu-no-code-variance-notice-id, edu-no-lead-safe-certification-id), and no mold, bed bug or radon rule (edu-no-mold-disclosure-id, edu-no-bed-bug-rule-id, edu-no-radon-disclosure-id). The tenant's lawsuit does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

title: More Rules Idaho Lacks
bodyText: These rules found in other states are confirmed absent from Idaho's statutes, so in each case your lease, not a statute, decides. (1) Double letting: no statute deals with leasing the same home to two tenants or gives the shut-out tenant a remedy. Separately, renting or leasing a home to someone knowing you have no ownership or leasehold interest in it is a felony (Idaho Code § 18-3622). (2) False rental applications: no statute gives you a termination ground for a lie on an application. The library's rental-application-accuracy clause makes a material falsehood a lease breach, which you enforce with the three-day notice to perform or quit (Idaho Code § 6-303(3); edu-cure-notice-id). (3) Payment-method fees: no statute bans or caps a convenience or card fee for paying rent. Any such fee must be stated in the lease or noticed 30 days ahead and must be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1), (2)). (4) Occupancy limits: no statute sets how many people may live in a long-term rental; the only state occupancy cap concerns short-term rentals (Idaho Code § 67-6539(3)(d)). Fair housing law limits how you set your own cap (edu-fair-housing-id). (5) Subletting: no statute requires you to consent to a sublet or assignment, or to be reasonable in refusing. A tenant who assigns or sublets contrary to the lease ends the lease, and you may recover possession on a three-day notice to quit (Idaho Code § 6-303(4)). (6) Also absent, each in its own row: a state rights guide (edu-no-rights-guide-id), home-business and child-care rules (edu-no-home-business-rule-id, edu-family-child-care-id), student-housing rules (edu-no-student-housing-rule-id), duties tiered by portfolio size (edu-portfolio-thresholds-id) and veteran incentives (edu-no-veterans-incentive-id).

title: Squatters, Receipts, Registration
bodyText: Three things landlords look for outside the landlord-tenant chapters were checked across the whole Idaho Code. First, Idaho does have a fast squatter remedy. An owner may ask the county sheriff to remove people unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling who were never tenants under a rental agreement the owner authorized, using a verified complaint in the statutory form (Idaho Code § 6-310A). A court track for forcible detainer by someone who never had a lease with the owner sets trial within 72 hours (Idaho Code § 6-310(3), (4)). Neither may be used against a current or former tenant, and misuse brings damages (Idaho Code § 6-310A(6); Idaho Code § 6-310(5)); see edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-id. Second, Idaho has no duty to give a receipt for rent paid in cash, or any rent receipt. Give one anyway; in a nonpayment case the proof is yours to produce. Third, Idaho has no landlord registration or license that must be in place before a court will enter a possession judgment (edu-landlord-registration-id). Two business statutes can still stop you from suing. An out-of-state LLC or corporation doing business in Idaho may not bring a lawsuit until it registers with the Secretary of State (Idaho Code § 30-21-502(b)). A person doing business under an assumed name may not maintain a lawsuit until the assumed business name certificate is filed (Idaho Code § 30-21-810(a)); see edu-nonresident-owner-agent-id.

title: Who Can Represent an LLC or Corporation Landlord in Idaho Court
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not say whether an LLC or corporation that owns rentals must hire a lawyer to bring an eviction. Practicing law without admission is contempt and a misdemeanor (Idaho Code § 3-104; Idaho Code § 3-420), with a narrow exception for an unpaid, disinterested representative on claims of $300 or less in the magistrate division (Idaho Code § 3-104). In the small claims department, which hears money claims up to $15,000 but not evictions, a business organization is represented only by an owner of a substantial interest or a nonattorney employee, and lawyers may not appear (Idaho Code § 1-2301; Idaho Code § 1-2307(1), (2)). An out-of-state entity doing business in Idaho must register before it can sue (Idaho Code § 30-21-502(b)), and a business using an unfiled assumed name cannot maintain a lawsuit until it files (Idaho Code § 30-21-810(a)); see edu-nonresident-owner-agent-id. The Idaho Rules of Civil Procedure (court rules) do not say either. Whether an entity may bring an eviction through a manager or employee who is not a lawyer is decided by case law. The cautious course is to have an Idaho lawyer file and appear for an entity landlord in any eviction, and to use an owner or employee only in small claims.

title: Disclosing a Foreclosure
bodyText: No Idaho statute requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that your loan is in default or that the property is in foreclosure, before or after the lease is signed. Idaho's searched statutes put the tenant notices on the trustee who sells under a deed of trust. The trustee must mail the notice of sale at least 120 days before the sale to any lessee whose interest appears of record before the notice of default was recorded, or of whom the trustee or lender has actual notice (Idaho Code § 45-1506(2)(b)). The trustee must also make at least three good-faith attempts, on different days over at least seven days and each at least 30 days before the sale, to serve the notice of sale on an adult occupant, and post it on the property (Idaho Code § 45-1506(5)). The buyer at the sale is entitled to possession on the tenth day after it, and anyone then holding under an interest that came after the deed of trust becomes a tenant at sufferance (Idaho Code § 45-1506(11)); what that means for your tenant is in edu-foreclosure-tenants-id. Your lease and your duties under it go on until the sale: keep the unit in repair, keep collecting rent, and keep the deposits ready for whoever owns the property when the tenancy ends (Idaho Code § 6-321(3)). If an applicant asks, do not misstate the property's status: leasing is covered by the Consumer Protection Act, which bars misleading statements (Idaho Code § 48-603(17)).

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to notify tenants when you sell the property or change managers, and none releases you from the lease once you give notice. A buyer takes over your remedies against the tenant: the right to collect rent and to enforce the lease, including for waste or forfeiture (Idaho Code § 55-301). The tenant keeps the same remedies against the buyer for breach of the lease that the tenant had against you, except on covenants against encumbrances or relating to title or possession of the premises (Idaho Code § 55-303). A sale of the property or of the rents takes effect without the tenant's attornment (consent), but a tenant who paid rent to you before learning of the sale must not suffer for it (Idaho Code § 55-610). So tell tenants in writing, as soon as the sale closes, who the new owner or manager is, where to send notices and where to pay rent. The new owner becomes liable to refund the deposits (Idaho Code § 6-321(3)), so transfer them or credit them to the buyer at closing (edu-deposit-successor-id). Whether you stay liable to the tenant after the sale is a question of case law. A lease for more than one year that is not recorded is void against a buyer or lender who takes in good faith and for value and records first (Idaho Code § 55-812); whether a tenant's possession puts a buyer on notice is case law, not reviewed, so a tenant on a long lease, or you, may want the lease or a memorandum of it recorded. If a court appoints a receiver, the receiver may take possession and collect the rents (Idaho Code § 8-605). Idaho has no statute on entry for showings; the lease controls (edu-no-entry-statute-id). Foreclosure is covered in edu-foreclosure-tenants-id.

title: Lawsuits and Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to tell tenants or applicants that the property faces a lawsuit, foreclosure, tax deed, condemnation or code case, and do not require a tenant to tell you when the tenant is served with papers about the property. Tenants may hear from others instead. In a trustee's sale the trustee mails the notice of sale to a lessee of record or a lessee the trustee or lender knows of, and must make up to three good-faith attempts on different days to serve it on an adult occupant, posting it at the property each time, at least 30 days before the sale (stopping once an occupant is served) (Idaho Code § 45-1506(2)(b), (5); see edu-no-foreclosure-disclosure-id). Before a county takes a tax deed, the tax collector mails notice to the record owner and the parties in interest of record, and any party in interest may file a written request for the notice (Idaho Code § 63-1005(2), (5)); a tenant whose lease is not of record is not on that list. Because nothing requires your tenant to pass on papers delivered to the property, the library's clause requires the tenant to tell you promptly of any proceeding to recover the property and to hand over the notice (tenant-forward-proceedings-ca).

title: Association Documents and Your Tenant
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes do not require you to disclose an association's obligations to a tenant, give the tenant the declaration, bylaws or rules, put any association statement in the lease, or send the lease to the association's board. The Homeowner's Association Act's disclosure duties run from the association to its members: account statements, the yearly fee disclosure and financial disclosures (Idaho Code § 55-3205).

In a condominium, though, Idaho binds your tenant directly: condominium owners, their tenants and anyone else using the property are subject to the Condominium Property Act and to the project's declaration and bylaws (Idaho Code § 55-1516). Your tenant can be bound by documents the tenant has never seen, and you are the one who holds them.

The cautious course is to give the tenant a copy of the declaration, bylaws and rules before signing and say so in the lease; the library's optional clause does this (association-documents-delivery-ks), and hoa-compliance-id makes the tenant follow the association's rules. An association may not add or enforce a rental restriction against you unless you agreed in writing when it was adopted (edu-hoa-rental-restrictions-id).

Any association fine you want to pass on to the tenant is a charge under Idaho Code § 55-305: it must be reasonable, no more than the lease states, and, if a written lease does not include it, charged only after a written 30-day notice of the change (Idaho Code § 55-305(1), (2); edu-fees-in-lease-id).

title: State Lead Notices
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes add nothing to the federal lead disclosure. They require no state lead notice, certificate, inspection, registration or information packet with a lease, and no lead-safe certification for rental housing.

For federal 'target housing' the federal rule still applies: before the tenant is bound by the lease, you must give the federal lead pamphlet, disclose any lead-based paint or lead hazards you know of, and hand over any lead report you have (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 4852d(a)(1)). The library's lead-based-paint disclosure carries this. The search covered the Idaho Code only.

title: Asbestos in Rental Housing
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to test for asbestos, to tell a tenant about asbestos in the building, or to put an asbestos notice in the lease. The only places the Idaho Code mentions asbestos are a law limiting the asbestos-injury liability of successor corporations, the solid-waste rules that treat asbestos waste as a special waste rather than demolition waste, and a mineral-rights definition. None of these reaches a landlord's dealings with a tenant. Disturbing asbestos during repairs or demolition may be covered by federal and state air-quality rules; check before you renovate. If you know of damaged asbestos material in the unit, keeping the premises in a way hazardous to the tenant's health or safety can support a tenant's lawsuit after a three-day written notice, except on tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3), (d), (e); edu-landlord-duties-id).

title: Environmental Contamination
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to tell a tenant about a release of hazardous substances or other contamination on the property, and do not require a lease to include any environmental restriction. One rule can reach your tenant. Where a cleanup has left an environmental covenant on the property, a copy of the covenant must be given to each person in possession of the property, among others, by the persons and in the manner the environmental agency requires; a failure to give it does not make the covenant invalid (Idaho Code § 55-3007). The covenant runs with the land (Idaho Code § 55-3005(1)), and its use limits bind the property whether or not your lease mentions them. If your property carries one, read it, follow what the agency requires, give your tenant a copy, and add its use limits to the lease. Covenants are recorded in the county land records (Idaho Code § 55-3008) and listed in a public registry kept by the Idaho Department of Environmental Quality (Idaho Code § 55-3012(1)). Clandestine drug labs have their own cleanup and vacancy rules (edu-meth-cleanup-id).

title: Private Wells Serving a Rental
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to test a private well that serves a rental, to give the tenant well test results, or to put a water-quality notice in the lease. If your water system is large enough, though, it is a public drinking water system: one with at least 15 service connections, or that regularly serves an average of at least 25 people daily at least 60 days a year (Idaho Code § 39-103(12)). Such a system is regulated by the Idaho Department of Environmental Quality's drinking water rules, so check them before relying on a shared well for a larger property. Whatever the size, plumbing and water facilities you supply must be kept in good working order, and keeping the premises in a way hazardous to the tenant's health or safety can support a tenant's lawsuit after a three-day written notice, except on tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2), (a)(3), (d), (e); edu-landlord-duties-id).

title: What Idaho Requires in a Lease
bodyText: Idaho has no list of required disclosures for an ordinary residential lease and no state form (a rental agreement for a lot in a manufactured-home community has its own required contents, Idaho Code § 55-2007(1)). These are the requirements found. (1) Lead paint, federal: for housing built before 1978, give the federal pamphlet and disclose known lead paint and hazards before the tenant is bound (lead-based-paint). (2) Disability modifications: if you make your permission for a tenant's disability modification depend on the tenant restoring the unit, Idaho requires that restoration provision to be included in the lease (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(h); disability-modification-restoration-id). Rentals in an owner-occupied building of two or fewer families and rooms in your own home are exempt (Idaho Code § 67-5910(7)). (3) Fees: you may not charge a fee, fine, assessment, interest or other cost in an amount greater than the lease states, or one the written lease does not include unless you first give 30 days' written notice of the change (Idaho Code § 55-305(2); edu-fees-in-lease-id). (4) Signing: leasing is covered by the Consumer Protection Act, which bars getting a signature on a contract with blanks to be filled in later and failing to give a legible copy at signing (Idaho Code § 48-603(12), (13); edu-consumer-protection-act-id). (5) Lease with an option to buy: for a building of one to four dwelling units, a lease with an option to purchase is a transfer under the Property Condition Disclosure Act, so you must give the tenant the state property disclosure form within 10 days after you accept the tenant's offer (Idaho Code § 55-2504, Idaho Code § 55-2509). There are exemptions, including a buyer who has lived in the property as a home for at least the year immediately before the transfer (Idaho Code § 55-2505(13)). If you deliver the form after the agreement is signed, the tenant may rescind it within three business days by written objection (Idaho Code § 55-2515). Idaho does not require a lease to name the owner or manager, or to disclose radon, mold, bed bugs, flood risk, a foreclosure, association rules, military zones or a past drug lab (see the no- rows on those topics).

title: Military Installations and Air Zones
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require a lease disclosure for property near a military installation or in an aircraft noise or accident-potential zone, and give the tenant no right to end the lease on that ground. The one Idaho statute tying military bases to rentals is the foreign adversary rule: a foreign principal from a foreign adversary country may not buy, hold, rent or otherwise control property within a defined area of southwestern Idaho (Idaho Code § 55-115(1)). You are not required to determine or ask whether an applicant is subject to that rule and bear no liability under it (Idaho Code § 55-115(11)); see edu-foreign-adversary-rental-id.

title: Sex Offender Registry Information
bodyText: You do not have to tell a tenant or applicant whether a registered sex offender lives in or near the property, and you do not have to check. Idaho's registry law says no person, other than those it charges with collecting the information, has a duty to inquire, investigate or disclose information about registered sexual offenders, and no such person can be held liable for failing to disclose it (Idaho Code § 18-8325(1), (2)). Separately, the psychologically impacted property law covers the fact that a registered or suspected sex offender occupied or lives near the property (Idaho Code § 55-2801(3)); see edu-psychologically-impacted-id. The registry is public on the internet (Idaho Code § 18-8323(1)), so point a tenant who asks to it. Registry information may be used only for the protection of the public, and anyone who passes it on must include the registry's cautionary statements (Idaho Code § 18-8323(6), (7)). Using it to commit a crime or to cause harm to a person or property is a misdemeanor (Idaho Code § 18-8326). Do not misstate what you know if asked.

title: Registered Offenders Living Together
bodyText: Idaho limits how many registered sex offenders may live in one dwelling. A person required to register may not reside in a residential dwelling unit with more than one other person who is also required to register, so, apart from arrangements in place when the law took effect and court-ordered exceptions, no unit may house more than two registrants (Idaho Code § 18-8331(1), (3)). The rule covers houses, apartments, duplexes, mobile homes, condominiums and townhouses in residential zones; licensed health care facilities are not covered (Idaho Code § 18-8331(2)(b)). No person or entity may operate a residence house for registered offenders beyond that limit, except under a city or county ordinance that sets standards for such houses, or for an existing treatment-program house grandfathered within set capacity limits, and a knowing and intentional violation is a misdemeanor (Idaho Code § 18-8331(3)-(5), (7)); a city or county may also get an injunction against such a house (Idaho Code § 18-8331(8)). Separately, an adult registrant generally may not live within 500 feet of a school or a licensed or city- or county-approved daycare, with exceptions for residences established before set dates (Idaho Code § 18-8329(1)(d)). These rules bind the registrant and anyone operating a group residence; Idaho's statutes do not make an ordinary landlord check whether an applicant is registered, and say no person outside the registry agencies has a duty to inquire (Idaho Code § 18-8325(1)). A lease term making it a breach for an occupant to live there in violation of these rules is not barred by any Idaho statute read, but the library does not offer one: Idaho gives a landlord no safe harbor for such a statement, and the duty already falls on the registrant. A landlord who wants such a term can add their own after taking advice, including on federal fair housing limits on screening by criminal record.

title: Certificate of Occupancy
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to give a tenant a certificate of occupancy, disclose whether one was issued, or put one in the lease, and no statute bars renting a unit for lack of one. The Idaho Code mentions certificates of occupancy only in unrelated settings (continuing-care escrow, school construction funding, driving-school licensing and a tax exemption). Whether a certificate of occupancy is needed before a building is used is a building-code question: Idaho's building code rules (IDAPA) and city or county codes were not reviewed, so check with the local building department before renting a new, converted or remodeled unit.

title: Defective Drywall
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to disclose defective or imported drywall to a tenant, and have no rule on corrosive drywall at all. The only Idaho statute that mentions gypsum board sets a lining requirement for furnace and water-heater compartments when a mobile home is rehabilitated. If you know of drywall that gives off fumes or corrodes wiring and plumbing, keeping the premises in a way hazardous to the tenant's health or safety can support a tenant's lawsuit after a three-day written notice, except on tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3), (d), (e); edu-landlord-duties-id).

title: Billing Tenants for Utilities
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require a disclosure when you bill tenants for electricity, gas or water through a submeter or by splitting a master-metered bill. Reselling utilities can raise a regulatory question. Idaho's public utility law treats as an electrical corporation every person operating an electric plant for compensation, except where the electricity is generated on or distributed by the producer through private property alone, solely for the producer's own use or the use of the producer's tenants and not for sale to others (Idaho Code § 61-119(1)); gas has the same exception (Idaho Code § 61-117), and the water definition has none (Idaho Code § 61-125). Whether billing tenants for metered utilities makes a landlord a utility under the Public Utilities Commission is decided by Commission orders and case law. The cautious course is to charge tenants no more than the utility's actual charges, and to state any utility charge in the lease as an amount or an objective method, since a cost the written lease does not include cannot be charged without 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(2); edu-fees-in-lease-id). If a utility regulated by the Public Utilities Commission plans to shut off service to a master-metered building, the Commission's rules require it, except for a dangerous condition or a termination order, to give the residents written notice at least two calendar days before, excluding weekends and holidays (IDAPA 31.21.01.312).

title: Inspection and Condemnation Orders
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to tell a tenant or applicant about an outstanding building-code violation, a failed inspection, an order to vacate or a condemnation order, and Idaho has no statewide rental housing code or rental inspection program. Local codes may: cities and counties may adopt their own police and health regulations (Idaho Const. art. XII, § 2), and those were not reviewed. Statewide, keeping the premises in a way hazardous to the tenant's health or safety can support a tenant's lawsuit after a three-day written notice, except on tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3), (d), (e); edu-landlord-duties-id), and a drug-lab property must stay vacant until cleanup is certified (edu-meth-cleanup-id). Condemnation by a government for public use is covered in edu-adverse-proceeding-notice-id. If you receive an order affecting the unit, tell your tenant promptly and do not misstate the property's status to an applicant (Idaho Code § 48-603(17)).

title: Pesticide Use Notices
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to notify tenants before pesticides are applied in or around a rental, to post notices, or to put a pest-control disclosure in the lease. The Idaho Code's pesticide chapter deals with applicator and dealer licensing, damage claims and restricted uses; none gives tenants a notice right. Cities and counties cannot add one: no city, county or other political subdivision may adopt or keep any ordinance or rule on pesticide sale, use or application, including notification of use (Idaho Code § 22-3426). The Department of Agriculture's pesticide rules (IDAPA) may set label or applicator requirements. Giving tenants advance notice of any treatment, with access under the lease's entry clause, is good practice.

title: Property Tax Share of Rent
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to tell tenants what share of their rent goes to property taxes, on a schedule or on request. Idaho's property tax reduction program is for homeowners: a claimant must own the homestead it claims on (Idaho Code § 63-701(1)), and the claimant's household does not include tenants (Idaho Code § 63-701(3)). The program gives renters no credit for property tax paid through rent, so there is no statement for you to supply. Idaho's income tax and agency rules were not reviewed for any renter's credit beyond this search.

title: Lease Formatting and Occupancy Notices
bodyText: Idaho's statutes set no type size, bold print or first-page placement for any residential lease disclosure, and do not require a single-family home lease to carry an occupancy notice. The searched type-size and conspicuousness rules all sit outside ordinary rentals: self-storage rental agreements, floating-home marinas, rent-to-own agreements for goods, online automatic subscription renewals, and some consumer and insurance laws. Idaho also has no rule presuming that a person in a home without a written lease has no right to be there; an owner may ask the sheriff to remove unauthorized occupants who were never tenants under an agreement the owner authorized, if the other conditions of the statute are met (Idaho Code § 6-310A(2); edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-id). Make each required term easy to find anyway: the Consumer Protection Act bars getting a signature on a contract with blanks to be filled in later and requires a legible copy at signing (Idaho Code § 48-603(12), (13)).

title: Fire Sprinkler Disclosure
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to tell a tenant whether the building has fire sprinklers, and offer no state grant, loan or tax credit for retrofitting them. The only statute linking sprinklers and rentals limits local government: a city or county may not require additional fire protection or fire sprinklers for a short-term rental beyond what it requires of other homes (Idaho Code § 67-6539(2)(a)(v)). Single-family homes and dwellings of up to two units are exempt from the code provisions that would require automatic sprinklers (Idaho Code § 39-4116(3)). You must still install approved smoke detectors in each unit and confirm they work when the tenancy starts (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6); smoke-detectors-id).

title: Tenant Energy Usage Data
bodyText: Idaho's statutes have no rule on energy benchmarking or on releasing a tenant's utility usage data to a landlord: nothing requires a utility to give you the data, nothing requires you to benchmark a building, and nothing lets or forbids a lease to authorize the release. The Public Utilities Commission's customer relations rules, have no rule on releasing a customer's usage data either. Where the account is in the tenant's name, the utility will follow its own release policy, so a lease term can only commit the tenant to sign the utility's release form. The library's optional clause does that (energy-data-release-wy).

title: Recycling Notice
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to tell tenants where or how to recycle, to provide recycling at a rental, or to put recycling information in the lease. Recycling service is set by cities, counties and haulers, whose rules were not reviewed. If your property has recycling, say in the lease or the property rules where the bins are and what goes in them.

title: Statement of Tenant Rights
bodyText: Idaho does not require you to give tenants a government statement or summary of their rights, to attach one to the lease, or to get a signed acknowledgment, and no lawsuit by a landlord depends on having given one. The rights statements in Idaho's statutes are for other settings, such as residential care facility residents and children in state care. Idaho's manufactured-home and floating-home acts set their own disclosures, but they do not reach an ordinary house or apartment rental.

title: Truth in Renting
bodyText: Idaho has no truth-in-renting law. Its statutes do not require you to give tenants a government statement of rights, to print a warning that some lease clauses may be unenforceable, or penalize you generally for offering a lease that contains a forbidden term. The one exception is narrow: a provision in a written instrument relating to real property that forbids or restricts its lease or occupancy because of race, color, ethnicity or national origin is void, and it is unlawful to insert one (Idaho Code § 55-616(1), (2)). Idaho also has no general list of banned residential lease terms (edu-prohibited-lease-terms-id). What does reach lease terms: a clause that stops a party from enforcing the contract in Idaho courts, or shortens the time to sue, is void, though an agreement to arbitrate inside Idaho is not affected (Idaho Code § 29-110(1)); fees must be reasonable, no more than the lease states, and, if a written lease does not include them, charged only after a written 30-day notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(1), (2)); no deposit may be kept for normal wear and tear (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)); and the Consumer Protection Act, which covers leasing, makes unconscionable practices unlawful (Idaho Code § 48-603C(1)).

title: Lease Language and Translation
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require a lease to be in any language other than English, do not require you to translate a lease negotiated in another language, and set no type size or verbatim text for any residential lease term. One state law points the same way as a translation duty: in deciding whether a practice is unconscionable under the Consumer Protection Act, a court considers whether the person took advantage of a consumer reasonably unable to protect his interest because of, among other things, inability to understand the language of the agreement (Idaho Code § 48-603C(2)(a)). If you negotiate in another language, give the tenant a translation or make sure the tenant understands the terms before signing. Idaho's only Spanish-language notice rule is for trust-deed foreclosures, not leases.

title: Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require a utility disclosure attached to the lease: no form explaining how a shared bill is split, no average-bill statement and no submeter disclosure. What Idaho does require is that any fee or other cost you charge the tenant be no more than the amount the written lease states, and that a cost the lease does not include be charged only after 30 days' written notice of the change (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)). So if the tenant pays you for any utility, state in the lease which utilities each party pays, and for any utility you bill, the amount or the objective method you will use to figure it (edu-fees-in-lease-id, utilities-responsibility). Billing tenants for metered utilities is covered in edu-electric-submetering-id.

title: Tenant Right to Buy
bodyText: Idaho's statutes give a tenant of an ordinary house or apartment no right of first refusal or opportunity to buy when you sell, and require no notice to tenants of a sale or of any purchase right, so no such notice belongs in your lease. The one Idaho purchase-notice rule is for manufactured-home communities where residents rent lots: a resident association formed to buy the community may give the landlord written notice of its interest and ask, in writing, to be told 15 days before the owner signs a purchase agreement, and the landlord must then notify its three designated members, except for listed transfers such as a foreclosure sale, a taking or a gift (Idaho Code § 55-2013A(2)-(5)). That act does not apply where the landlord rents both the lot and the home (Idaho Code § 55-2004). Selling a rented property is covered in edu-sale-or-management-change-id.

title: Exemption Notices
bodyText: Some states require a lease statement telling tenants that a unit is exempt from a rent cap, a just-cause eviction rule or a tenant's right to buy. Idaho has none of those laws, so there is nothing to be exempt from and no exemption notice to give. Idaho has no statewide rent control, and local governments may not enact, keep or enforce any ordinance that would regulate the rent, fees or deposits charged for leasing private residential property, though they may manage housing in which they hold an interest (Idaho Code § 55-306; edu-rent-control-preemption-id). Idaho requires no cause to end a periodic tenancy (edu-no-just-cause-id), and ordinary tenants have no right to buy (edu-no-tpa-notice-id).

title: Sunset Dates in Tenant Law
bodyText: None of Idaho's core landlord-tenant statutes is on a repeal or expiration clock. The unlawful detainer and tenant-remedy chapter (Idaho Code Title 6, Chapter 3) and the tenancy and owner chapters (Title 55, Chapters 2 and 3) carry no sunset date in the compiled code. Watch instead for new session laws: Idaho amends these chapters often, and in 2025 it renumbered several of them, for example the fee rule, now Idaho Code § 55-305.

title: Chemical Exposure Warnings
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warnings do not apply in Idaho, and Idaho's statutes have no counterpart: nothing requires a landlord to warn tenants about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, or to post such warnings at a rental. The Idaho Code mentions such chemicals only in hazardous-waste, injection-well, pharmacy and public-health definitions. Federal rules still apply, such as the lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978 (lead-based-paint). Contamination and drug-lab rules are covered in edu-hazardous-contamination-disclosure-id and edu-meth-cleanup-id.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared Meters
bodyText: Idaho's statutes require none of these three pre-signing disclosures. Nothing requires you to tell a tenant about a former military ordnance site nearby, about a planned demolition of the building, or that the tenant's utility meter also serves other units or common areas. If you plan to demolish or convert the building, the lease and Idaho's notice rules govern how the tenancy ends: a fixed term runs to its end unless the lease says otherwise, and you must give written notice at least 30 days before nonrenewal of a residential lease (Idaho Code § 55-304(2); edu-nonrenewal-notice-id). If a tenant's meter also serves areas the tenant does not use, say so in the lease and bill the tenant no more than the lease states; a charge the written lease does not include needs a written 30-day notice first (Idaho Code § 55-305(2); edu-utility-disclosure-attachment-id).

title: Shoreline and Public Access
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require a lease to disclose that a property is on or near a lake or river shoreline, that the public may use the shore, or that a public right of way crosses the land. Two rules can matter for waterfront rentals. No encroachment, such as a dock or pier, may be placed on, in or above the beds or waters of a navigable lake without approval under Idaho's navigational encroachment law (Idaho Code § 58-1301), so check before letting a tenant build one. And an owner, a term that includes a tenant or lessee, who lets the public use land or water for recreation without charge owes those users no duty to keep it safe or to warn of dangers (Idaho Code § 36-1604(b)(4), (c)); that protection does not apply to anyone who permits the use for compensation (Idaho Code § 36-1604(h)(3)) and does not change your duties to your own tenant under the lease. Neither creates a lease disclosure.

title: Pets and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to give a tenant a state fact sheet or any other notice about pets and eviction, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat, and no statute deals with pets left behind after an eviction. Property left after an eviction is handled under the post-eviction property rules (edu-post-eviction-property-id), and animal control falls to local officers. Say in the lease and in any eviction notice that the tenant must take all pets when leaving.

title: No Idaho Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to set a water heater to any temperature, at move-in or at any other time, and set no maximum or minimum hot-water temperature for rentals. The only water-heater temperature rule in the code is for licensed foster homes: 'The home shall have proper water heater temperature' (Idaho Code § 39-1211B(6)). That is a licensing condition for the foster parent, not a landlord duty, though a tenant who is a foster parent may ask you for help meeting it. Water heaters are part of the plumbing system (Idaho Code § 54-2604(1)(i)), and their installation is governed by the Idaho state plumbing code, the Uniform Plumbing Code as amended by the Idaho plumbing board (Idaho Code § 54-2601(1)). If you supply the water heater, keeping it in good working order is part of your duty for plumbing facilities you supply, enforceable by the tenant's action except on tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2), (e)), and a scalding-hot setting could make the premises 'hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)). The cautious course is to check the setting at each turnover and keep it at a safe level; manufacturers commonly recommend about 120 degrees Fahrenheit, though no Idaho statute sets that figure.

title: No Idaho Rental Pool Safety Rule
bodyText: Idaho's statutes put no pool, hot-tub or spa safety duty on a residential landlord: no barrier or fence rule, no gate or drain rule, no lifeguard rule and no lease notice. The Department of Health and Welfare's chapter defines a 'public swimming pool' and expressly leaves out a pool 'operated solely for and in conjunction with' an 'apartment, condominium or any other residential facility containing multiple dwellings' (Idaho Code § 56-1001(10)). The pool-barrier rules in the code are licensing conditions for licensed daycare facilities (Idaho Code § 39-1109(1)(f)) and foster homes (Idaho Code § 39-1211B(9)), not landlord duties; a tenant who runs a home daycare or is a foster parent must meet them and may ask you for help. One rule binds anyone running a pool: 'No person shall prohibit the use of a life jacket or other flotation device in a swimming pool' by a person whose physician's signed statement shows a disability needs it (Idaho Code § 18-5801), so pool rules banning flotation devices need that exception. Pool construction and barriers are building-code matters. The Idaho residential code and International Building Code, adopted under the Idaho Building Code Act, govern new and altered pools and their surroundings where a city or county enforces them (Idaho Code § 39-4116). A pool kept unsafe could leave the premises in 'a manner hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)), and injuries around a pool raise negligence questions that turn on case law. Cautious course: keep pools fenced with self-closing, self-latching gates, post rules (hours, supervision of children, no glass), and have tenants follow them through the lease's rules section (common-area-use).

title: No Idaho Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require periodic inspection of balconies, decks, exterior stairways or other elevated elements of rental buildings, and set no reporting or repair deadline for them. The only statute that mentions balconies keeps certified interior designers from designing changes to them (Idaho Code § 54-306(8)(a)(ii)). Balconies and decks are governed when they are built or altered: the Idaho residential code and the International Building Code, adopted under the Idaho Building Code Act, apply where a city or county enforces them, and work on them usually needs a permit (Idaho Code § 39-4111(2), Idaho Code § 39-4116). Without an inspection statute, your duty comes from the tenant's action: a rotted or loose balcony or railing may leave the premises in 'a manner hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)), which a tenant may sue over after three days' written notice, except on tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(d), (e)). Injury claims turn on negligence case law. The cautious course is to have a qualified person look at balconies, decks, railings and exterior stairs on a regular schedule, fix problems promptly, and keep records. The lease's rules section can limit weight and storage on balconies (common-area-use).

title: No Idaho Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Idaho's statutes have no rule on steam radiators or radiator covers: you need not install covers on request, and no lease rider is required. If your building has steam or hot-water radiators, they are part of the heating facilities you supply and must be kept in good working order (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2)); an exposed radiator hot enough to burn a child could also leave the premises in 'a manner hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)). A tenant may sue over either after three days' written notice, except on tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(d), (e)). The cautious course is to cover or guard very hot radiators, especially where a tenant tells you young children live in the unit. Heating generally: edu-heating-id.

title: No Idaho Common Area Lighting Rule
bodyText: Idaho's statutes set no lighting standard for the hallways, stairways, entrances, walkways or parking areas of an ordinary rental property, and no rule on who pays for common-area lights. The only lighting duties are in the residency acts for rented manufactured-home lots and floating-home moorages, which this library does not cover: there 'The landlord shall maintain street lights, entry lights and common area lighting, if any, in good working condition' (Idaho Code § 55-2007(3)(d)), with a like duty for floating-home marinas (Idaho Code § 55-2708(11)). For an ordinary rental, keep common-area lighting working anyway. A dark stairway or entrance may leave the premises in 'a manner hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant', which a tenant may sue over after three days' written notice (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3), (d)); a lease promise to maintain common areas can also be enforced that way where it materially affects health and safety (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5)). The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). Building codes adopted under the Idaho Building Code Act govern lighting in new and altered buildings (Idaho Code § 39-4109, Idaho Code § 39-4116). If common-area lights are wired to a tenant's meter, say so in the lease and have the tenant agree to pay for that service: Idaho does not let you charge a tenant under a written lease a cost the lease does not include unless you first give 30 days' written notice of the change (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)). Whether you are liable for an injury in a poorly lit common area is negligence case law.

title: No Idaho Security Device Rule
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require any lock, deadbolt, door viewer, window latch or other security device in a rental, do not require you to rekey or change locks between tenants, and set no rule on who pays for security devices. Your statutory duties are the ones a tenant can enforce by suing after three days' written notice, and none of them names locks (Idaho Code § 6-320(a), (d)). A lease promise about locks or security can become enforceable that way if it materially affects the tenant's health and safety (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5)), and a door that cannot be secured may leave the premises in 'a manner hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)). The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). Whether you owe a tenant a duty of reasonable security, and are liable in negligence if a crime follows a lock failure, is case law. Cautious course: give each unit working locks on exterior doors and latches on accessible windows, rekey or change the locks between tenants, keep a record of keys issued (the lease's keys section), and fix a broken lock promptly. Charge a tenant for keys or rekeying only as the lease states, or after 30 days' written notice of a new charge (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)). Building codes adopted under the Idaho Building Code Act govern door and window hardware in new and altered buildings (Idaho Code § 39-4116).

title: No Idaho Key Control Mandate
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes require no key-control policy, no locked storage of master keys, no log of who holds keys, and no background check for employees or contractors who have keys to tenants' homes, at any size of property. They also have no rule on when a tenant may change the locks.

The one statute that mentions changing locks is outside ordinary tenancies: after a sheriff serves a notice to vacate on people who were never tenants, the owner may ask the sheriff to stand by while the owner 'changes the locks' (Idaho Code § 6-310A(5)). Whether you are liable if someone misuses a key you control is a question of negligence case law.

The cautious course: keep master and spare keys locked up, record who has which key, rekey between tenants, limit keys to staff who need them, and consider screening employees and vendors who get unsupervised access. If you screen applicants for jobs, federal and Idaho employment and consumer-report rules may apply.

The optional lock-change clause (lock-change-ak) has the tenant get your written agreement before changing a lock and give you a key, with an emergency exception. If a tenant shows you a protection order excluding someone from the home, act promptly on a request for new locks (see the domestic-violence rows). Idaho has no statute on entry notice (edu-no-entry-statute-id), so the lease's entry clause governs how you use your key.

title: No Idaho Smart Access Rule
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not regulate smart locks, keypad or app-based entry systems, key cards or fobs, or other connected devices in rentals. They don't require you to offer a physical key, set rules for entry codes or access logs, or let a domestic-violence survivor have a device account cut off. Because Idaho also has no statute on when you may enter a tenant's home (edu-no-entry-statute-id), your lease's entry clause governs entry by smart lock just as it governs entry by key; an access log does not change that. Cautious course if you use a smart access system: say in the lease that the unit uses one, how the tenant gets and changes codes or app access, whether a physical key or keypad backup exists, what happens when the battery, power or internet fails, and what entry data you collect and keep. Don't use remote access to enter outside what the lease's entry clause allows. Change codes and remove app access between tenants. Charge for replacement cards or fobs only as the lease states, or after 30 days' written notice of a new charge (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)). A system that locks a tenant out could also raise the self-help eviction issues in edu-self-help-eviction-id.

title: No Idaho Stove or Refrigerator Rule
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require you to supply a stove, oven, refrigerator or any other kitchen appliance in a rental. The only kitchen rule is for licensed foster homes, whose living space must have 'A properly operating kitchen with a sink, refrigerator, stove, and oven' (Idaho Code § 39-1211B(2)(b)); that is a licensing condition for the foster parent, not a landlord duty. If you do supply appliances, list them in the lease (appliances-included) and keep the ones that are electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling or sanitary facilities in good working order: a tenant may sue for damages and specific performance over 'Failure to maintain in good working order electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling, or sanitary facilities supplied by the landlord' after three days' written notice (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2), (d)). Whether a stove or refrigerator is such a facility is not settled by the statute, and a lease promise to maintain listed appliances can be enforced the same way where a failure materially affects health and safety (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5)), so the cautious course is to treat supplied kitchen appliances as yours to repair unless the tenant's side caused the damage (landlord-maintenance). The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). Items you leave behind but won't maintain: appliances-excluded-la.

title: Excluding Appliances in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho has no statute on appliances or equipment left at a rental that you don't intend to maintain, and no presumption that whatever is in the unit is supplied by you.

What matters is the tenant's action: your repair duty reaches 'electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling, or sanitary facilities supplied by the landlord' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2)). Saying clearly in the lease what you supply (appliances-included) and what you don't (the optional clause appliances-excluded-la) helps fix what is 'supplied'. Whether a court would treat an item you left in the unit as supplied despite an exclusion is case law.

So the exclusion clause is written cautiously: never list an item whose failure could make the premises hazardous to health or safety, such as a furnace, water heater, gas appliance or the only source of heat or cooking, because you remain answerable for 'Maintaining the premises in a manner hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)), and the clause does not reach defects you knew of and the tenant didn't. The tenant initials the clause so the exclusion is brought to their attention. The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

title: Furnished Rentals in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes have no rule on renting a home furnished: no required inventory, no furniture deposit rule and no special duty for furnishings.

Two general rules apply. Any money a tenant deposits with you 'for any purpose other than the payment of rent' is a security deposit, so a furniture deposit is part of the deposit and must be refunded under the usual rules, and you may not keep any of it to cover normal wear and tear (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)). And a charge for damaged furnishings must be one the lease includes or one you gave 30 days' written notice of (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)).

Use the optional furnished-rental clause (furnishings-included-la) with a signed inventory of each item and its condition, and record condition at move-in (existing-condition). If you supply furnished appliances that are electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling or sanitary facilities, your repair duty under Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2) reaches them (appliances-included).

title: No Idaho Cooling Device Rule
bodyText: Idaho's statutes give a tenant no right to install a portable, window or other cooling device, don't require you to supply air conditioning, and don't require a lease that restricts window units to say anything in particular. So the lease decides: you may allow window or portable units, allow them with conditions (a secure installation that doesn't damage the window or block a required escape window, no extension cords, removal at move-out), or ban them under the lease's alterations section (no-alterations). A ban or condition must still allow reasonable modifications a tenant with a disability needs under fair-housing law (edu-fair-housing-id). If you do supply cooling, it is one of the facilities you must keep in good working order: a tenant may sue over 'Failure to maintain in good working order electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling, or sanitary facilities supplied by the landlord' after three days' written notice (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2), (d)). List supplied cooling equipment in the lease (appliances-included). The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

title: Promises to Repair in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute requiring your promise to clean, repair or improve a rental to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. Whether an oral or pre-lease promise binds you is contract law; a written lease with an entire-agreement clause (entire-agreement) may make a promise left out of it hard for either side to rely on. Three Idaho rules make writing the promise into the lease the safer course. First, once a repair promise is a term of the lease, a tenant can enforce it through the statutory action if breaking it materially affects health or safety: the action covers 'Breach of any term or provision of the lease or rental agreement materially affecting the health and safety of the tenant, whether explicitly or implicitly a part thereof' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5)), after three days' written notice (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)), with possible treble damages (Idaho Code § 6-317). Second, the Consumer Protection Act reaches leasing (Idaho Code § 48-602(2)) and makes unlawful any act 'that is otherwise misleading, false, or deceptive to the consumer' (Idaho Code § 48-603(17)), so a promise made to win a tenant that you don't intend to keep is a risk (edu-consumer-protection-act-id). Third, a lease longer than one year must be in writing and signed (edu-lease-in-writing-id). What to do: list every promised repair, cleaning or improvement, with a completion date, in the lease or a signed addendum, and don't make promises you won't keep. The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

title: Shifting Maintenance in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute that lets, or forbids, a lease to shift a maintenance duty to the tenant, and none that sets conditions such as a separate writing, a rent reduction or a list of permitted tasks. Idaho also has no general rule voiding lease waivers. What Idaho has is a short list of things a tenant can sue you over: failing to provide 'reasonable waterproofing and weather protection', failing to keep in good working order the electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling or sanitary facilities you supply, and keeping the premises in a way hazardous to the tenant's health or safety (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(1)-(3)). Whether a lease can shift those duties to the tenant is case law, so the cautious course, which the library follows, is to keep them with you. Routine upkeep is different, and the library already shifts it by lease: keeping the home clean and disposing of garbage (tenant-maintenance), yard care (landscaping-irrigation), snow removal (snow-removal) and smoke detector upkeep, which Idaho's statute itself puts on the tenant (smoke-detectors-id). For other specific tasks in exchange for something from you, use the optional tenant repair agreement (tenant-repair-agreement-id). Keep in mind that a lease promise you make about maintenance becomes enforceable through the tenant's action where its breach materially affects health and safety (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5)), and that the plumbing, HVAC and electrical licensing exemptions for unlicensed work cover owners, not tenants (edu-tenant-repair-agreement-id). The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

title: Tenant Repair Agreements in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho has no statute on agreements for a tenant to do repairs or maintenance in exchange for a rent reduction or other benefit: no separate-writing rule, no consideration rule, no good-faith recital and no limit by type of dwelling. Such an agreement is an ordinary contract term, lawful as far as Idaho's statutes go, and the library offers it as an optional clause (tenant-repair-agreement-id).

Four Idaho points shape it. First, keep your statutory duties: waterproofing and weather protection, the electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling and sanitary facilities you supply, and premises free of health or safety hazards (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(1)-(3)). Whether a lease can shift them is case law, so the clause keeps them with you.

Second, licensing: Idaho's plumbing and HVAC licensing laws let an unlicensed person work on a single-family home or duplex only 'provided that such person owns or is a contract purchaser of the premises' (Idaho Code § 54-2602(1)(a), Idaho Code § 54-5002(1)(a)), and the electrical exemption covers a property owner working in 'the owner's primary or secondary residence' (Idaho Code § 54-1016(2)(a)). A tenant is neither, so don't have a tenant do plumbing, HVAC or electrical work that the licensing laws reserve for licensed trades.

Third, liens: anyone who does construction, alteration or repair work on a building may have a lien on it (Idaho Code § 45-501); whether a tenant hired under a lease counts as your agent, so that the lien reaches your interest, is case law, so the clause has the tenant do the listed tasks personally and hire no one without your written consent.

Fourth, any lease promise you make, including the benefit you give in return, may be enforced through the tenant's action where it materially affects health and safety (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5)). Any parts or materials the tenant installs under the agreement become yours.

title: Repair Requests and Repairers in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho has no statute that lets a tenant hire a repairer at your cost, requires you to name a repair contact or approved repairer, or sets how fast you must respond to a repair request. A tenant's remedy for your failure to repair is a lawsuit for damages and specific performance after three days' written notice, not repair-and-deduct or rent withholding (Idaho Code § 6-320(a), (d); edu-tenant-remedies-id).

The one exception is smoke detectors: if you fail to install working ones, the tenant may, after certified-mail notice and 72 hours, install them 'and deduct the cost from the tenant's next month's rent' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6)).

So no Idaho statute bars a lease term naming your repair contact and requiring your written approval before any repair at your cost, and the optional clause designated-repairer-id does that, keeping the smoke-detector right. It also has the tenant hire no one to work on the property without your consent, because anyone who repairs a building may claim a lien on it (Idaho Code § 45-501), and lets the tenant take reasonable steps in an emergency to prevent further damage, such as shutting off water.

Use licensed plumbing, electrical and HVAC contractors for work Idaho's licensing laws cover; an owner's own-work exemptions are limited (Idaho Code § 54-2602(1)(a), Idaho Code § 54-5002(1)(a), Idaho Code § 54-1016(2)(a)). Give tenants a working repair contact and answer requests promptly: a slow response can still leave the premises hazardous, which a tenant may sue over (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)). The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

title: Repair Notices in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has one notice rule for repairs, and it is about lawsuits, not repair requests. Before a tenant may sue you over a repair failure, the tenant 'must give his landlord three (3) days written notice, listing each failure or breach upon which his action will be premised and written demand requiring performance or cure' (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)), served by personal delivery to you or your agent, if you and your agent are absent from your usual place of business, by leaving it with an employee there, or by certified mail, return receipt requested (Idaho Code § 6-323). For smoke detectors the tenant's notice goes by certified mail, return receipt requested (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6)). Idaho has no statute on how routine repair requests must be made, and no tenant remedy or defense that turns on what you knew rather than on written notice (no rent withholding or repair-and-deduct beyond smoke detectors). So the lease may set how repair requests are made, and the library's maintenance clause asks for prompt written notice (landlord-maintenance). Letting tenants also report by phone, text or a portal is fine and doesn't waive the statutory notice: the lease's notices clause says nothing in the lease designates another method for a notice the law governs (notices). Don't rely on a written-request term to put off a repair you know about: a condition hazardous to health or safety remains your responsibility however you learn of it (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)), and negligence claims may turn on what you knew. What to do: name the repair contact and accepted methods, log every report however it arrives, and answer in writing. The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

title: No Idaho Rent Escrow Exemption
bodyText: Some states let a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' rent-escrow or repair remedies by giving a notice. Idaho has nothing to opt out of: it has no rent-escrow, rent-withholding or general repair-and-deduct remedy, so there is no exemption and no exemption notice. A tenant's remedy is a lawsuit for damages and specific performance after three days' written notice (Idaho Code § 6-320(a), (d)), with possible treble damages (Idaho Code § 6-317), plus the smoke-detector install-and-deduct right (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6)). That action has no small-landlord exemption; its only exception is for 'tracts of land of five (5) acres or more used for agricultural purposes' (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)), which turns on the land, not on a notice. Don't add an exemption or waiver notice to the lease. See edu-tenant-remedies-id.

title: Heating in Idaho Rentals
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes set no heating standard for rentals: no minimum indoor temperature, no heating season, and no rule that you must supply heat or that heat may be shifted to the tenant only in certain ways.

What Idaho has is the tenant's action.
