If you supply the heating, you must keep it in good working order, and a tenant may sue you for damages and specific performance for 'Failure to maintain in good working order electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling, or sanitary facilities supplied by the landlord' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2)). A home left without heat in an Idaho winter may also be a premises kept 'in a manner hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)).

The tenant must first give you three days' written notice listing each failure and demanding cure (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)), and a court may award three times the actual damages (Idaho Code § 6-317). The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

Because the duty reaches heating 'supplied by the landlord', say in the lease what heating equipment you supply (appliances-included). A lease may make the tenant pay the gas, electric or fuel bill for heat (utilities-responsibility). Whether a lease can also make the tenant repair heating equipment you supply is not settled by statute: Idaho has no general rule voiding lease waivers, and how a court would treat such a shift is case law. The cautious course, which the library follows, is to keep heating repair yours (landlord-maintenance) and use the optional freeze-protection clause (heat-freeze-protection-id) for the tenant's part.

Building codes: the Idaho residential code and the International Building Code, adopted under the Idaho Building Code Act, govern construction, alteration and repair, and cities and counties that adopt them enforce them through building permits (Idaho Code § 39-4109, Idaho Code § 39-4111, Idaho Code § 39-4116).

Winter utility shutoffs: if the tenant is the customer of a gas or electric utility regulated by the Public Utilities Commission, the Commission's rules bar a shutoff from December through March, except on the grounds in its Rule 303 such as a dangerous condition, for a residential customer who says they cannot pay in full and whose household includes children, elderly or infirm persons (IDAPA 31.21.01.306).

Check your city's housing code: ordinances in Boise, Meridian, Nampa, Idaho Falls, Pocatello and Coeur d'Alene were not reviewed.

title: Smoke Drift Waivers in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute on smoke drifting between units, and none that lets a lease make a tenant accept drifting smoke or give up claims over it. Idaho's Clean Indoor Air Act bans smoking in a public place, defined as enclosed indoor places of business, commerce or service 'to which persons not employed at the public place have general and regular access or which the public uses' (Idaho Code § 39-5502(12)). A private apartment is not on its list. The Act names the common areas of hotels, motels and 'other similar lodging facilities' (Idaho Code § 39-5502(12)(j)) but not apartment buildings, so whether an apartment building's enclosed hallways and lobbies are public places is unsettled. Your leasing office, if the public uses it, is likely covered, and smoking is banned in 'any elevator generally accessible to the public' (Idaho Code § 39-5505). Cities and counties may adopt stricter smoking rules (Idaho Code § 39-5511). A drift waiver is not offered in this library. Idaho has no statute voiding lease waivers, but drifting smoke can be a nuisance, meaning anything 'injurious to health' or 'offensive to the senses' that interferes 'with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property', which a person whose enjoyment is lessened may sue over (Idaho Code § 52-111), and a tenant may sue, after three days' written notice, over premises kept in 'a manner hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)), except on tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(d), (e)). Whether a court would enforce a tenant's advance waiver of those claims is case law. The cautious course, which the library follows, is to prevent drift rather than ask tenants to accept it: ban smoking on the property in the lease (smoking-policy-id). If you allow smoking in some units, tell applicants before they sign, and deal with complaints promptly.

title: No Idaho Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: Idaho has no statute that delays rent, bars late fees, or limits eviction for federal or state government workers who miss pay during a government shutdown or furlough. The lease's ordinary rent and late-fee terms apply, and so does the ordinary eviction process: a three-day written notice demanding the rent or possession before an eviction for nonpayment (Idaho Code § 6-303(2); edu-nonpayment-notice-id). Any late fee must be one the lease states (or one added on 30 days' written notice) and reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1), (2)). If a tenant tells you a shutdown has interrupted their pay, consider agreeing in writing to a short payment plan or waiving the late fee for the period; a written agreement avoids later disputes over whether the default was excused. Servicemembers on active duty have separate federal protections (edu-no-servicemember-statute-id).

title: Disasters and Idaho Leases
bodyText: Idaho has no statute that ends a tenancy, suspends or abates rent, or bars evictions after a declared disaster or emergency, or that sets what rent is owed while a home can't be reached. The Governor may declare a disaster emergency, and the order has the force of law, but 'During any state of disaster emergency, the governor may not alter, adjust, or create any provision of the Idaho Code' (Idaho Code § 46-1008(1), (8)); so an order can't rewrite Idaho's eviction or rent statutes, though it can control the occupancy of premises in a disaster area and order evacuations (Idaho Code § 46-1008(5)(e), (g)). Idaho's price-gouging rule during a declared emergency covers only 'fuel or food, pharmaceuticals, or water for human consumption' (Idaho Code § 48-603(19)(a)), not rent; rent increases still need the usual written notice (edu-rent-increase-notice-id). What happens to the lease after disaster damage is set by the lease: the optional casualty clause lets either side end the lease, with rent prorated, if a casualty the tenant's side didn't cause makes the home unfit, and reduces rent for a part that can't be used (casualty-termination-id). Without such a clause, the answer turns on contract case law. Your repair duties still apply to what remains (Idaho Code § 6-320(a); edu-landlord-duties-id). Cautious course: don't charge rent for a period the home can't lawfully or safely be lived in, document damage, keep tenants informed in writing, and return the deposit within the usual deadline if the lease ends (Idaho Code § 6-321(2)). One narrow rule: a nonprofit owner claiming Idaho's low-income housing tax exemption may not evict tenants for 'inability to pay for a period of three (3) months if such inability is due to a catastrophic event' (Idaho Code § 63-602GG(3)(b)), meaning a sudden serious medical condition or injury, not a natural disaster.

title: No Idaho Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Idaho has no statute that lets a tenant shelter people displaced by a disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, bars you from enforcing those limits after a disaster, or places evacuees in private rentals through the lease. The lease's guest and occupancy terms still apply (guest-policy, guest-policy-day-limit, permitted-occupants). Two state powers are worth knowing. During a declared disaster emergency the Governor may 'commandeer or utilize any private property, real or personal, if he finds this necessary to cope with the disaster emergency' (Idaho Code § 46-1008(5)(d)) and may 'Make provision for the availability and use of temporary emergency housing' (Idaho Code § 46-1008(5)(i)); compensation for property taken or used is limited and must be claimed (Idaho Code § 46-1012). And the interstate Emergency Management Assistance Compact deals with evacuees between governments, not through private leases (Idaho Code § 46-1018A). Cautious course after a disaster: be flexible, agree in writing to any temporary extra occupants (who they are and for how long), and apply fair-housing rules to occupancy decisions (edu-fair-housing-id). If a tenant asks to shelter displaced family or friends, answer in writing with a time limit and any conditions.

title: No Idaho Alternate Housing Duty
bodyText: Idaho has no statute that makes a private landlord provide or pay for alternate housing when a rental becomes unfit to live in, during repairs, or after a fire or disaster, whether or not the tenant asks. The relocation help that exists is governmental: tenants displaced by a state or local government program or project may get relocation payments and advice from the agency, including 'rent supplement or purchase assistance payments to tenants' (Idaho Code § 40-2001), and during a declared disaster the Governor may 'Make provision for the availability and use of temporary emergency housing' (Idaho Code § 46-1008(5)(i)). If a fire official orders a building remedied or removed as especially liable to fire, the owner or occupant must comply unless they appeal (Idaho Code § 41-259), and no statute requires you to house the tenant elsewhere meanwhile. What happens to the lease and rent while the home is unfit is set by the lease: the optional casualty clause ends the lease or reduces rent after a casualty the tenant's side didn't cause (casualty-termination-id). If the home is unfit because you failed to keep up waterproofing, supplied facilities or safe premises, the tenant may sue for damages and specific performance after three days' written notice, with possible treble damages (Idaho Code § 6-320(a), (d); Idaho Code § 6-317), and the cost of temporary lodging could be claimed as damages. Cautious course: say in the lease what happens to rent while the home can't be lived in, stop charging rent for any period it is ordered vacated, and refund prepaid rent and the deposit balance promptly if the lease ends. The action does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)).

title: Pest Cooperation in Idaho
bodyText:
Idaho has no statute on bed bugs or other pests in rentals: nothing requires a tenant to report or cooperate with treatment, prepare the unit, or pay for it, and nothing sets your treatment duty or deadline.

So the lease fills the gap, through the optional pest cooperation clause (pest-cooperation-id): the tenant reports suspected pests promptly, lets you and your pest control operator in under the lease's entry section, and follows written preparation instructions.

An infestation you don't treat can leave the premises in 'a manner hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant', which a tenant may sue over after three days' written notice, except on tracts of five acres or more used for farming (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3), (d), (e)). Idaho has no entry-notice statute, so entry for inspection and treatment goes through the lease (landlords-access; edu-no-entry-statute-id).

Charging the tenant for treatment needs care: Idaho bars charging a tenant any cost greater than the lease states, and under a written lease bars a cost the lease does not include unless you give 30 days' written notice of the new charge (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)). Whether a "reasonable cost" formula is an amount 'agreed upon' is unsettled, so the Idaho clause charges only the pest control operator's or contractor's actual bill, with no markup, and only where the tenant's side caused the infestation.

Disclosure: edu-no-bed-bug-rule-id.

title: Other Facilities in Idaho Rentals
bodyText: Idaho's statutes don't list facilities a landlord must supply inside a rental beyond smoke detectors (smoke-detectors-id), and put no duty on you for garage door openers, screens, mailboxes, laundry machines or garbage containers. If you supply electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling or sanitary facilities, you must keep them in good working order (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2)); list what you supply in the lease (appliances-included) and what you don't (appliances-excluded-la). Elevators are the one building facility with its own owner duties. Under the Idaho Elevator Safety Code Act, the owner of an elevator, escalator, platform lift or dumbwaiter 'shall be responsible for the safe operation and proper maintenance of the conveyance' and for having the required periodic tests done by a qualified elevator inspector (Idaho Code § 39-8609(2)); no conveyance may operate without a state certificate to operate, renewed each year on a satisfactory inspection (Idaho Code § 39-8611, Idaho Code § 39-8617); and the state may order an unsafe conveyance shut down (Idaho Code § 39-8613). The Act does not apply to 'Conveyances located in private residences' (Idaho Code § 39-8606(a)(1)), meaning a separate dwelling or apartment occupied by one family (Idaho Code § 39-8603(17)), so it reaches elevators and lifts in an apartment building's common areas but not a stair lift inside a single unit. Willful violations are misdemeanors, and the state may impose civil penalties of up to $500 per violation, each day counting as a separate violation (Idaho Code § 39-8619, Idaho Code § 39-8620).

title: No Idaho Window Guard Rule
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not require window guards or window-opening limits for children in rentals, do not regulate security or burglar bars on windows, and require no lease notice about either. Window design is a building-code matter. The Idaho residential code and the International Building Code, adopted under the Idaho Building Code Act and enforced by cities and counties through building permits, govern construction, alteration and repair (Idaho Code § 39-4109, Idaho Code § 39-4116). The only statute that names escape openings is the single-stairway apartment rule: a city may allow a single stairway in some apartment buildings only if 'Emergency escape and rescue openings shall comply with the requirements of the International Building Code on all floors served by the single exit' (Idaho Code § 39-4109C(1)(p)). For short-term rentals, a city or county may require 'That removable escape ladders be available in all sleeping areas with a window that are located above the ground floor' (Idaho Code § 67-6539(3)(c)). Cautious course: don't add bars, grilles or fixed guards to a bedroom window unless they can be opened from inside without a key or special knowledge, since a window that can't be opened may block an escape route the building code requires and could leave the premises 'hazardous to the health or safety of the tenant' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(3)); get a building permit where your city requires one (Idaho Code § 39-4111(2)). If a tenant with young children asks for window stops or guards, consider providing ones that release from inside.

title: Idaho Building Code Editions
bodyText: Idaho's construction codes mostly are not frozen at one edition: the statutes name a starting edition and let a state board adopt later editions by rule, so the edition in force can change during a lease. Building: the 2006 International Building Code applies 'until such time as a subsequent version is adopted by the Idaho building code board' (Idaho Code § 39-4109(1)(a)); the Idaho residential code is whatever version of the International Residential Code the Board adopts, and the Board may not make it more restrictive than the published code (Idaho Code § 39-4109(1)(b), (3)); the International Existing Building Code works the same way (Idaho Code § 39-4109(1)(d)). A new edition takes effect 'on January 1 of the year following its adoption' (Idaho Code § 39-4109(4)), and cities and counties that enforce building codes must adopt the Board's editions by ordinance (Idaho Code § 39-4116(2)). Fire: the International Fire Code, 2000 edition, 'and such later editions as may be so published and adopted by the state fire marshal' (Idaho Code § 41-253(1)). Plumbing and mechanical: the Uniform Plumbing Code and the 2006 International Mechanical and Fuel Gas Codes, with later editions the plumbing and HVAC boards adopt (Idaho Code § 54-2601(1), Idaho Code § 54-5001). Two are fixed in statute: the electrical code is the 2023 National Electrical Code with board amendments (Idaho Code § 54-1001), and the energy code is the 2018 International Energy Conservation Code as amended by the Board and approved by the legislature (Idaho Code § 39-9701(1)). Which editions are in force today is set in the boards' and the State Fire Marshal's rules (IDAPA 24.39.30 for building, IDAPA 18.08.01 for fire). What it means for you: new work must meet the code in force when you apply for the permit, since 'Permits shall be governed by the laws in effect at the time the permit application is received' (Idaho Code § 39-4116(6)), and a permit for an alteration generally can't make you upgrade unaffected parts of a building that met the code when built, unless the work creates a specific substantial safety hazard (Idaho Code § 39-4111(3)). Ask your city or county building department which editions it enforces before you renovate.

title: Idaho Fire and Building Codes for Rentals
bodyText: Idaho's fire code is the International Fire Code. The statute adopts its 2000 edition 'and such later editions as may be so published and adopted by the state fire marshal' (Idaho Code § 41-253(1)), and the State Fire Marshal's rule adopts the code with Idaho amendments (IDAPA 18.08.01, agency rule). The rule text does not name the edition in force, so ask the State Fire Marshal's office or your local fire department which edition applies. New construction and alterations follow the codes the Building Code Board adopts: the 2018 International Building Code, the 2018 International Residential Code (Parts I, II, III and IX) for one- and two-family dwellings, and the 2018 International Existing Building Code, each with Idaho amendments (IDAPA 24.39.30.600, agency rule). A city or county that issues building permits must adopt them by ordinance (Idaho Code § 39-4116(2)). For a building you already rent out, the key Idaho change is that the fire code's construction requirements for existing buildings apply 'only, if in the opinion of the fire code official, they constitute a distinct hazard to life or property' (IDAPA 18.08.01.030, agency rule). Local fire chiefs, or the sheriff where there is no fire department, enforce the code as assistants to the State Fire Marshal (Idaho Code § 41-256(1)). They may inspect buildings 'except the interior of private dwellings' (Idaho Code § 41-259). A building found especially liable to fire is ordered remedied or removed, and the owner or occupant must comply unless they appeal (Idaho Code § 41-259).

title: Fire Sprinklers in Idaho Rentals
bodyText: No Idaho statute or rule requires you to add fire sprinklers to a building you already rent out. Single-family homes and buildings of up to two dwelling units are exempt from any code requirement to have automatic sprinklers (Idaho Code § 39-4116(3)). Idaho's residential code deletes the sprinkler requirement for one- and two-family dwellings, and does not require them in townhouses separated by the specified fire-rated walls, or when an existing townhouse without sprinklers is altered or added to (IDAPA 24.39.30.600.03, agency rule). Apartment buildings follow the building code when built. A new apartment building served by a single stairway must be sprinklered throughout (Idaho Code § 39-4109C(1)(d)). Any retrofit duty would sit in the fire code's requirements for existing buildings, and Idaho applies those only where the fire code official finds a distinct hazard to life or property (IDAPA 18.08.01.030, agency rule). So a retrofit is required only if the fire code official orders it. A city or county may not require a short-term rental to add fire protection or sprinklers beyond what applies to the same type of housing (Idaho Code § 67-6539(2)(a)(v)). If your building has sprinklers, keep them working.

title: Voucher Payments Withheld for Repairs in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no rule on this; the federal Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) rules control. You must keep a voucher unit up to the federal housing quality standards. A life-threatening deficiency must be fixed within 24 hours of notice, and others within 30 days or an extension the housing agency approves (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(a)(3)). If you don't fix deficiencies found after the initial inspection, the agency may withhold its payment once it notifies you in writing (where the agency lets a unit with only non-life-threatening deficiencies be leased after the initial inspection, it must withhold payments if you miss a 30-day cure period, FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.405(j)(4); the alternative-inspection rules, FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.406, were not reviewed). If you then make the repairs within the cure period, the withheld payments are made up; if you don't, the agency must abate the payments, and abated payments are never made up (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(d)(1), (2), (4)). The family is not responsible for the agency's share (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.451(b)(4)(iii)), so you may not charge the family the withheld or abated amount, and you may not end the tenancy because of the withholding or abatement (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(d)(3)). While payments are abated the family may end the tenancy by notice to you and the agency. If the repairs are not made within 60 days of the abatement notice, or a longer period the agency sets, the agency terminates the contract (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(d)(5)). A deficiency the family caused, beyond ordinary use, is the family's responsibility; the agency may then waive your duty to fix it, and its payment is not withheld or abated (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(a)(4), (b)). These rules apply to contracts signed on or after, or renewed after, June 6, 2024; older contracts follow the earlier version, which was not reviewed (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(f)).

title: Voucher Unit Inspections in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no rule on this; the federal Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) rules control. The family 'must allow the PHA to inspect the unit at reasonable times and after reasonable notice' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.551(d)). The housing agency inspects before the lease starts, at least every two years (every three for a small rural agency), and within 24 hours or 15 days after a deficiency is reported, depending on how serious it is (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.405(a), (b), (d)). The agency may not charge the family for an inspection or reinspection (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.405(g)). It may charge you a reasonable fee for a reinspection that finds a deficiency you were responsible for still uncorrected, but you 'may not pass this fee along to the family' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.405(h)). If the family refuses an inspection, report it to the agency: the duty runs to the agency, which decides what to do about the family's assistance under rules not reviewed here. Whether a refusal is also a breach of your lease depends on your lease's entry clause; Idaho has no entry statute (see edu-no-entry-statute-id).

title: Tenant's Unpaid City or District Utility Bills
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not say whether a tenant's unpaid water, sewer or trash bill can be charged against your property, and they give owners no general exemption or affidavit procedure for tenant accounts. What happens depends on who provides the service. Water and sewer districts: the district fixes its rates; charges unpaid 30 days after they are due become delinquent, and the district must certify them to the county tax collector, who puts them on the tax roll and collects them like other district taxes, with the lien dating from the day the charge became delinquent. The district must also shut off service for delinquencies (Idaho Code § 42-3212(l)). The statute makes no exception for a tenant's account, so a tenant's unpaid district bill can end up on your property tax bill. Counties: a county may set a solid waste fee and have it certified and collected the same way as property taxes (Idaho Code § 31-870(2)). Irrigation districts: a district may stop delivering irrigation or domestic water to land whose charges, against the land or its owner, lessee or occupant, are more than 90 days delinquent, or sooner in a district with a federal domestic-water contract (Idaho Code § 43-327). Cities: a city that runs water, sewer or other works sets its own rates and its own methods of collection and penalties, including denial of service for nonpayment (Idaho Code § 50-1030(f)); whether a city puts unpaid bills on the property is in its ordinances. The cautious course: ask the city or district serving the property how it collects a tenant's unpaid bill, and whether it will bill or notify you. If the account is in the tenant's name, use the lease to make the tenant responsible and to require proof of payment on request (utilities-responsibility, utility-payment-evidence). If an unpaid bill could fall on the property, consider keeping that service in your name and charging the tenant a stated amount or an objective method written in the lease (Idaho Code § 55-305(2); edu-fees-in-lease-id). A security deposit can cover unpaid utility charges only if the deposit terms in the lease list them (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)).

title: Conservation Charges That Follow the Meter
bodyText: Idaho law lets the Public Utilities Commission approve an electric or gas utility's schedule of charges for energy-conservation measures, services or payments provided to a property owner or customer. The schedule can spread the cost over time and can apply the payment obligation to later owners or customers at the premises where the measures were installed. The utility must record a notice of the payment obligation with the county recorder, and the Commission may set other ways of telling owners and customers about it (Idaho Code § 61-336). No Idaho statute requires you to tell a tenant about such a charge, and the Commission's customer rules (IDAPA 31.21.01, agency rule) contain no notice rule for it. Because the charge can follow the meter, a tenant who opens service in the tenant's own name may be billed for it. The cautious course: if you agreed to a conservation program for the property, tell each applicant in writing before the lease is signed what the charge is, how long it runs and who pays it. Leasing is covered by the Consumer Protection Act, which bars acts that are misleading, false or deceptive to the consumer (Idaho Code § 48-603(17)). If you will pay the charge and collect it from the tenant, state the amount or the objective method in the lease, since a cost the written lease does not include can't be charged without 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(2); edu-fees-in-lease-id). Idaho's statutes also have no rules for submetered water: no rate limit, no ban on a meter surcharge and no required statement of meter readings (edu-electric-submetering-id). City-owned utilities and cooperatives are outside the Commission's rules and set their own programs.

title: Billing Tenants for Shared or Submetered Utilities
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes do not stop you from making a tenant pay for a utility that is not separately metered to the unit, whether you split a master-metered bill by a formula or read a submeter you installed. There is no required disclosure form, no cap and no ban on any billing method (edu-electric-submetering-id).

Two rules shape how you do it. First, you can't charge more for a utility than the lease states, and under a written lease a utility cost the lease leaves out needs 30 days' written notice before you can charge it (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)). So state in the lease each utility you will bill and the method: a submeter reading at the provider's rate, or a formula such as equal shares or square footage.

Second, Idaho's public utility law excepts electricity and gas supplied by an owner to the owner's tenants 'not for sale to others' (Idaho Code § 61-119(1); Idaho Code § 61-117); whether billing tenants turns you into a utility the Public Utilities Commission regulates is decided by Commission orders. The cautious course is to bill no more than the provider actually charges you. The optional clause utility-billing-id does this.

A billing method you add after the lease is signed counts as a change in a cost, which needs 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)(b)(ii)).

title: Interruptions of Submetered or Master-Metered Service
bodyText: Idaho has no statute on interrupting electricity that a landlord submeters or resells to tenants, and no statute giving tenants special protection when the landlord is the utility's customer for a master meter. The protections come from two places. First, the Public Utilities Commission's customer rules: except for a dangerous condition or an order to shut off service, a gas, electric or water company regulated by the Public Utilities Commission may not shut off a master-metered building, or a home where the billed customer does not live, without written notice to the residents at least two calendar days before, not counting weekends and holidays, delivered to the premises or posted in common areas; the notice must tell residents how to get service in their own names (IDAPA 31.21.01.312). City-owned and cooperative utilities are not under those rules (Idaho Code § 61-104). Second, your own duties: if you supply the electrical, heating or plumbing facilities, a tenant may sue you, after a three-day written notice, for failing to keep them in good working order (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2), (d)), and for breaching a lease term that materially affects the tenant's health and safety (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5)); damages can be trebled in some cases (Idaho Code § 6-317). That suit is not available for tracts of land of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). Do not cut off a submetered tenant's power to collect a bill or force a move-out: Idaho's statutes do not address landlord shutoffs, and the courts may treat one as unlawful self-help (edu-self-help-eviction-id). Pay the master-meter bill on time, and collect a tenant's unpaid share through the lease. Billing tenants is covered in edu-electric-submetering-id.

title: Utility Accounts in the Landlord's Name
bodyText: When a utility account for the rental is in your name, you are the utility's customer and you owe the bill. Idaho has no statute that lets tenants pay your unpaid utility bill and deduct it from rent, that appoints a receiver when an owner does not pay the utilities, or that makes you notify the utility that a building is master-metered. The protections tenants have come from the Public Utilities Commission's rules for gas, electric and water companies it regulates (IDAPA 31.21.01). Except for a dangerous condition or an order to shut off service, before shutting off service to a master-metered building, or to a home where the billed customer does not live, the utility must give the residents written notice at least two calendar days before, not counting weekends and holidays, posted or delivered at the premises and telling them how to get service in their own names (IDAPA 31.21.01.312). A utility may not shut off one customer's service for another customer's bill unless that customer is legally obligated to pay it (IDAPA 31.21.01.310), and it may not hold a customer responsible for the unpaid bill of someone living at the customer's premises whose name is not on the bill unless the customer agreed in writing or otherwise expressly accepted it, or is legally obligated (IDAPA 31.21.01.206). City-owned and cooperative utilities are outside these rules (Idaho Code § 61-104). If the lease makes you responsible for a utility and service stops because you did not pay, the tenant may sue for breach of a lease term materially affecting health and safety, or for failure to keep facilities you supply in working order, after a three-day written notice (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(2), (a)(5), (d)); that suit is not available for tracts of land of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). Pay the accounts in your name on time, and keep the lease's list of utilities you provide accurate (utilities-paid-by-landlord, services-utilities-provided-ks-oh).

title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText: Idaho has no statute limiting when a utility may shut off a residential customer, in winter or otherwise. The limits are in the Public Utilities Commission's customer rules for the gas, electric and water companies it regulates (IDAPA 31.21.01); city-owned and cooperative utilities are not covered (Idaho Code § 61-104) and set their own policies. Under those rules: before a shutoff for an unpaid bill, the utility mails a written notice at least seven calendar days ahead and a final notice at least three calendar days ahead, not counting weekends and holidays for the final notice (IDAPA 31.21.01.304). From December through March, a gas or electric utility may not shut off a residential customer who declares an inability to pay in full and whose household includes children, people 62 or older, or people whose health or safety would be seriously impaired by the shutoff; such a customer may also join a Winter Payment Plan, which, if set up before November 1, protects against shutoff from November through March (later plans protect from the day they are set up); both protections yield to the Rule 303 exceptions such as a dangerous condition (IDAPA 31.21.01.306). This is a protection that depends on the customer's declaration, not a blanket winter ban. A physician's or public health official's certificate of serious illness or medical emergency postpones a shutoff for 30 days (IDAPA 31.21.01.308). Shutoffs for nonpayment are not allowed on Fridays, weekends, holidays or the day before a holiday (IDAPA 31.21.01.311). For you, this matters in two ways. A tenant with service in the tenant's own name has these protections against the utility, and the utility cannot hold you responsible for, or cut off your service over, a tenant's unpaid bill unless you agreed to pay it or have a legal obligation to (IDAPA 31.21.01.206; IDAPA 31.21.01.310). And a utility can shut off an account in your name if you don't pay it, after notice to the residents (IDAPA 31.21.01.312; edu-utility-landlord-account-id).

title: Submetering Disclosures
bodyText: Outside floating home marinas, where a landlord billing master-metered utilities must state the cost separately each period with the opening and closing meter readings and post the utility's rates (Idaho Code § 55-2708(9)), Idaho's statutes require no lease disclosure for submetered or landlord-billed utilities: no prescribed form, type-size rule, billing cap or late-fee limit for utility charges, and no utility-regulator disclosure rule; the Public Utilities Commission's customer rules (IDAPA 31.21.01) govern utilities, not landlords. What you must do, and the utility-status question for landlords who bill electricity or gas, is in edu-electric-submetering-id; how to set out the billing method in the lease is in edu-utility-apportionment-id and the optional clause utility-billing-id. In short, any utility charge may be no more than the amount or method the written lease states, and a charge the lease does not include needs 30 days' written notice before you can charge it (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)).

title: Moving Utility Accounts to the Tenant
bodyText:
Idaho has no statute that sets a deadline for a tenant to put utilities in the tenant's own name, or that lets or forbids you to cut off a utility the tenant failed to transfer. The lease decides who holds each account (utilities-responsibility), and the optional clause utility-transfer-id adds a transfer date and a reimbursement duty.

If an account stays in your name, you are the utility's customer and owe the bill, and the utility will end service at your request. For gas, electric and water companies regulated by the Public Utilities Commission, a utility that keeps serving the occupants after you ask to end service may not shut it off without written notice to them at least two calendar days before, not counting weekends and holidays, telling them how to get service in their own names (IDAPA 31.21.01.312). City-owned and cooperative utilities are outside those rules (Idaho Code § 61-104). Closing your own account after written notice is the course the optional clause takes.

Don't use it, or any other interruption, to make a tenant move out: Idaho's statutes do not address landlord shutoffs, and a court may treat one as unlawful self-help (edu-self-help-eviction-id). Give the tenant time to open an account before you close yours, especially in cold weather.

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText:
Under Idaho's mechanics' lien law, anyone who does work on or supplies materials for a building has a lien for it, whether the work was ordered by the owner or the owner's agent (Idaho Code § 45-501). When a tenant orders the work, the lien reaches the land only if it belonged to the person who ordered the work or that person was acting as the owner's agent; if that person owns less than the full ownership, only that person's interest is subject to the lien (Idaho Code § 45-505). So a tenant's own improvements should reach only the tenant's leasehold, unless the tenant is treated as your agent.

Idaho's statutes have no notice of nonresponsibility that an owner can post or record, and nothing says whether your consent to an alteration makes the tenant your agent or exposes your interest; those are questions for the courts. The statute also says every contractor in charge of the work is held to be the agent of the owner for the purposes of the lien law (Idaho Code § 45-501), and how that applies to a tenant's contractor is unsettled.

The cautious course: require your written consent before any alteration (no-alterations), make clear in the lease that the tenant is not your agent and must pay for and clear any lien from work the tenant orders (no-liens-id), and do not pay a tenant's contractor or direct the work yourself.

title: Satellite Dishes, Antennas and Cable
bodyText:
No Idaho statute gives a tenant a right to install a satellite dish, antenna or cable, gives a cable, satellite or internet provider a right to enter or wire a rental building, or bars charging cable subscribers different rent. Idaho's video service law forbids a provider from denying service to an area because of residents' income, and says a provider's inability to serve someone because it is prohibited from placing its own facilities in a building or property is not a violation (Idaho Code § 50-3008(1), (2)); it does not make you admit a provider.

So under Idaho's statutes, installations by a tenant are alterations that need your written consent (no-alterations), and the optional clause telecom-access-mn sets the ground rules: consent before installing, the tenant arranges and attends the installer, and the tenant removes the installation and repairs damage at the end.

Federal law does protect some devices. The FCC's rule overrides any lease provision that impairs installing, maintaining or using a satellite dish or certain wireless antenna one meter or less across, or a television broadcast antenna, on property 'within the exclusive use or control of the antenna user' where the user has a leasehold interest, such as a tenant's own balcony or patio (FEDERAL: 47 C.F.R. § 1.4000(a)(1)). A restriction impairs a device if it unreasonably delays or prevents installation, unreasonably increases its cost, or blocks an acceptable signal (FEDERAL: 47 C.F.R. § 1.4000(a)(3)); a safety or historic-preservation restriction that meets the rule's conditions is allowed (FEDERAL: 47 C.F.R. § 1.4000(b)).

The rule does not reach roofs, exterior walls or other areas the tenant does not control alone. Both no-alterations and telecom-access-mn yield to this right, so for a dish on the tenant's own balcony you may set reasonable safety rules but may not ban it or use a consent requirement that unreasonably delays it or raises its cost.

A tenant with a disability may also ask for a reasonable modification at the tenant's expense (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(h)).

title: Tenant Solar Devices
bodyText: No Idaho statute gives a tenant a right to install solar panels or a plug-in or balcony solar device, or limits your refusal. Idaho's solar rule binds homeowner's associations, not landlords: an association may not prohibit solar panels or collectors on a rooftop within its jurisdiction, though it may choose their location on the roof (so long as a south-facing placement, within 45 degrees of due south, is allowed) and adopt reasonable installation rules, and its rule-making power under that law covers only rooftops owned, controlled and maintained by the homeowner (Idaho Code § 55-3208). That protects you as the owner if you want to add rooftop solar to a rental in an association; it gives your tenant nothing. Idaho's residential solar disclosure act governs solar sellers and lessors dealing with consumers and does not apply to renting a home where the solar system is only incidental to the rental (Idaho Code § 48-1803(2)(a)). So a tenant who wants to attach any solar device needs your written consent under no-alterations. The library does not offer a separate solar clause; if you allow a device, give consent in writing that covers location, mounting, safety and removal. A tenant with a disability may ask for a reasonable modification at the tenant's expense (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(h)).

title: Tenant EV Charging
bodyText: No Idaho statute gives a tenant a right to install or use an electric vehicle charger, or limits your refusal. The state and local governments may not require charging stations, EV parking spaces or charging conduit in building plans (Idaho Code § 39-4109B), so there is no statewide EV-ready mandate either. A tenant who wants a charger, or who wants to run a cord from the unit or a shared outlet, needs your written consent under no-alterations. If you agree, the optional clause ev-charger-installation-hi sets the terms (edu-ev-charging-requirements-id). A tenant with a disability may ask for a reasonable modification at the tenant's expense (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(h)).

title: Rules for Chargers You Allow
bodyText:
If you let a tenant install a charger, or install one yourself and charge tenants for it, Idaho's statutes set few rules. Idaho's public utility law excepts from regulation electricity bought from a public utility to charge the batteries of an electric vehicle, as provided by order or rule of the Public Utilities Commission (Idaho Code § 61-119(2)).

Idaho's weights-and-measures law leaves out electricity meters only when they are operated in a public utility system (Idaho Code § 71-108(2)), so whether a charger you meter for tenants falls under the Department of Agriculture's device rules is a question for those rules. Idaho exempts from sales tax electricity delivered to consumers at the place of use by wires (Idaho Code § 63-3622F); whether that reaches charging you sell to tenants is for the State Tax Commission's rules, also not reviewed.

The simplest course is to have the tenant reimburse your actual electricity cost, measured by a separate meter or a method stated in the lease, rather than selling charging by the kilowatt-hour at a profit, and to state that method in the lease (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)).

The optional clause ev-charger-installation-hi requires your written consent to the system and location, a licensed installer, permits, association compliance, optional liability insurance, reimbursement of electricity by a stated method, and a choice at the end of the lease between removal and leaving the system. Any money you hold to secure those duties is a security deposit (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)). Building and electrical code permits, city ordinances and association rules were not reviewed.

title: Chargers in Shared Parking
bodyText: Idaho's statutes say nothing about a tenant installing a charger in a shared parking area: no right to a reserved space, no fee rule and no rule on who pays for damage. It is your choice under the lease. If you allow a charger in a shared lot, put the space and its terms in writing (ev-charger-installation-hi). You may charge for reserving that space, but only an amount stated in the lease; a fee the written lease does not include can't be charged without 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)), and any fee must be reasonable (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)). The library does not offer the shared clause ev-charging-shared-area-co for Idaho because it lets you charge an unstated "reasonable fee". No statute bars a stated, reasonable reservation fee; if you want one, add your own clause naming the amount after taking advice. If the parking area is a condominium or association common area, the association's documents control what you may allow (edu-hoa-rental-restrictions-id); Idaho's statutes have no EV-charging rule for associations.

title: EV Chargers When the Lease Ends
bodyText: Idaho has no statute on who owns, removes or pays for a tenant's EV charger when the lease ends. The general fixtures rule applies: a tenant may remove, during the lease term, anything the tenant attached for domestic use if removal causes no injury to the premises, unless the way it was attached made it an integral part of the premises (Idaho Code § 55-307). A hard-wired charger may or may not be integral; that is a question for the courts, whose decisions were not reviewed. Avoid the question by deciding it in writing before installation. The optional clause ev-charger-installation-hi has you choose at the start: the tenant removes the system and repairs any damage, or leaves it and it becomes yours. The shared clause ev-charging-end-of-tenancy-co is not offered for Idaho because it makes the system the tenant's property in every case and lets the tenant remove it after the lease ends, which takes away that choice. Surrender and damage are covered by surrender-end-of-term-ks-ne and tenant-caused-damage-id.

title: Agreed Ways to Give Notice
bodyText: Idaho's statutes do not use an "actual notice" standard for landlord-tenant notices, and do not say whether a lease may add a method such as text message. They do fix the method for the notices that matter most. Three-day eviction notices go to the tenant in person; if the tenant is absent from both home and usual place of business, by leaving a copy with a suitable person at either place and mailing a copy; and only if those places cannot be found or no suitable person is there, by posting on the property, delivering a copy to a resident if one can be found, and mailing (Idaho Code § 6-304). A landlord's notice ending a month-to-month or other tenancy at will is served in the manner the civil procedure rules prescribe (Idaho Code § 55-208(1)); the tenant's notice need only be in writing (Idaho Code § 55-208(2)). A tenant's three-day notice before suing over repairs or a deposit goes to you or your agent in person, to an employee at your usual place of business if you are absent from it, or by certified mail, return receipt requested (Idaho Code § 6-323). A lease can't replace those methods with e-mail or text. Idaho's electronic transactions law lets parties who have agreed to deal electronically meet a writing requirement with an electronic record the recipient can keep, but a law that specifies a delivery method still controls; a certified-mail requirement can be met electronically only with the recipient's express consent, and either party may refuse to keep dealing electronically (Idaho Code § 28-50-105, Idaho Code § 28-50-107, Idaho Code § 28-50-108). For other notices, such as a rent increase or term change (Idaho Code § 55-304), the statutes require writing but name no method; e-mail or text may work if the tenant agreed to receive notices that way, but deliver statutory notices by a method you can prove, and send an electronic copy only as an extra (notices, edu-notice-service-id).

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Idaho's statutes require written notice for each of the main landlord-tenant notices:
- a three-day notice to pay rent or leave, to perform a lease term or leave (Idaho Code § 6-303(2), (3)), or to quit (Idaho Code § 6-303(4), served by delivering a copy under Idaho Code § 6-304)
- a notice ending a month-to-month or other tenancy at will, by either side, with at least one month's notice (Idaho Code § 55-208)
- a notice changing the terms of a month-to-month lease, at least 15 days before the end of the month (Idaho Code § 55-304(1))
- a notice of a rent increase or of nonrenewal of a residential lease, at least 30 days before (Idaho Code § 55-304(2))
- a notice adding or changing a fee under a written lease, 30 days before (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)(b)(ii))
- the tenant's three-day notice before suing over repairs, a deposit or smoke detectors (Idaho Code § 6-320(d), (a)(6)).

An oral notice does not meet any of these. How each is delivered is in edu-notice-service-id and edu-actual-notice-method-id. Idaho's statutes do not require other lease notices to be in writing; the library's notices clause asks for writing anyway (notices).

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText:
Idaho's landlord-tenant statutes have no rule for a lease that renews automatically: no reminder notice, no limit on how early a tenant must decide, and no ban.

Two statutes still shape such a clause. First, you must give written notice at least 30 days before you decline to renew a residential lease or raise the rent (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)); a renewal clause does not replace that notice.

Second, the Consumer Protection Act's subscription-renewal section covers an agreement entered into over the internet to provide goods or services for a set time and price that renews automatically unless the consumer cancels. Leasing is covered by the Act, and "goods" include real property, so a lease signed online that renews automatically may fall within it; whether it does is unsettled, and case law and Attorney General rules were not reviewed.

If it applies, you must clearly and conspicuously disclose the renewal terms and how to cancel, offer an easy online way to cancel at no extra fee, and, for a renewal term of 12 months or more, remind the tenant 30 to 60 days before the renewal (Idaho Code § 48-603G). The section is enforced under the Act, gives no private right to sue under it, and bars civil penalties against a seller who tries in good faith to comply.

The cautious course is to follow it for any automatically renewing lease: set the renewal terms apart in bold, say how to cancel, and send the reminder. The optional clause automatic-renewal-id does this.

A lease that rolls into month-to-month after the term is a tenancy at will that either side ends on one month's written notice (Idaho Code § 55-208; periodic-tenancy-notice-id).

title: What a Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Idaho has no statute listing what a residential lease must contain: no rule that the start and end dates appear on the first page, no required list of terms and no required lease form. A few statutes make content matter. If you want a tenant with a disability to restore the premises after a modification, the restoration term must be in the lease (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(h); disability-modification-restoration-id). Under a written lease, a fee, fine, interest or other charge you want to collect must be stated in the lease, or added later on 30 days' written notice, and may not exceed the amount the lease states (Idaho Code § 55-305(2); edu-fees-in-lease-id). What you may keep from a security deposit is limited to the contingencies the deposit terms specify (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)). A lease for longer than one year must be in writing and signed by the party to be held to it (Idaho Code § 9-505(4); edu-lease-in-writing-id). Federal law adds a lead-based paint disclosure for older housing (lead-based-paint). The rules in the code that do list required contents cover manufactured-home lots, self-storage units and rent-to-own goods, not ordinary residential leases.

title: Initialing Lease Clauses
bodyText: No Idaho statute requires a tenant to initial any lease clause, page or disclosure, or makes a clause unenforceable because it was not initialed. The only statutory initialing requirement found that touches rentals is in the sheriff's complaint form for removing people who were never tenants, where the owner initials each statement (Idaho Code § 6-310A(3)). Initials can still help you prove the tenant saw a term, such as an automatic renewal, a fee or the restoration term for a disability modification, and the library's signature blocks are enough without them. Have both parties initial any change made to the lease after it is printed, and fill in or strike every blank before signing (edu-lease-completeness-id).

title: Lease Length and Signing Formalities
bodyText: Idaho sets no maximum term for a private residential lease. It does set formalities for longer leases. A lease for more than one year must be in writing, signed by the party to be held to it, and an agent who signs for that party needs written authority (Idaho Code § 9-503; Idaho Code § 9-505(4); edu-lease-in-writing-id). An unrecorded lease for more than one year is void against a later good-faith buyer or lender for value who records first (Idaho Code § 55-812), so a long-term tenant may want it recorded. If you are married, two rules may require your spouse to sign. Neither spouse may sell, convey or encumber community real estate unless the other joins in the instrument or has given an express power of attorney (Idaho Code § 32-912), and a married person's homestead may not be conveyed or encumbered without the other spouse's consent, shown by both spouses signing and acknowledging the instrument (or by a power of attorney or an interspousal deed) (Idaho Code § 55-1007). The statutes do not say whether a lease is a conveyance or an encumbrance for these rules. The cautious course: if the property is community property or your homestead, have both spouses sign the lease, and have both sign before a notary for any lease longer than one year. Leases of state, county and other public land have their own limits that don't apply to private rentals.

title: Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Pricing
bodyText: No Idaho statute requires a month-to-month tenant's terms to match a fixed-term tenant's, bars more burdensome terms for either, or limits how much more rent you may charge for a shorter term. Idaho also has no local rent control, and cities may not regulate the rent, fees or deposits charged for private rentals (Idaho Code § 55-306; edu-rent-control-preemption-id). Pricing by lease type is your choice, within fair housing law (edu-fair-housing-id). The rules that do differ by type are notice rules: you may change a month-to-month lease's terms on written notice at least 15 days before the end of a month (Idaho Code § 55-304(1)), either side may end a tenancy at will on one month's written notice (Idaho Code § 55-208), and any residential rent increase needs 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)).

title: Type Size in Leases
bodyText: Idaho has no minimum type size for a residential lease and no evidence rule penalizing small print. The plain-language and type-size rules found in the code cover other documents, such as continuing-care contracts, self-storage notices and some consumer forms (edu-no-plain-language-rule-id). One related duty: if the Consumer Protection Act's subscription-renewal section reaches an automatically renewing lease signed online, the renewal terms and the way to cancel must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously (Idaho Code § 48-603G(2); edu-automatic-renewal-id). Use a readable size throughout; the library's Idaho lease does so as a drafting choice.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Apart from the business improvement district disclosure (Idaho Code § 50-2624(2)), Idaho supplies no statutory lease form and no verbatim text for a residential lease, a move-in condition report, a rental application or a landlord's eviction notice. The statutes set what some notices must say, not their wording: a three-day notice for unpaid rent must demand payment or possession, state the amount due, and tell the tenant that after a judgment a residential tenant has 72 hours to remove belongings before the landlord may remove and dispose of them (Idaho Code § 6-303(2); edu-nonpayment-notice-id). One form applies to some leases: a lessor of property inside a city business improvement district must use the statutory disclosure form, or one substantially similar (Idaho Code § 50-2624(2); special-district-representation-id). Another form Idaho prescribes near this field is the sworn complaint an owner gives the sheriff to remove people who are not and never were tenants, which must be in substantially the statutory form (Idaho Code § 6-310A(3); edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-id). Sellers of homes, and landlords who lease with an option to purchase one to four units, use the property condition disclosure form set under Idaho Code § 55-2508 (Idaho Code § 55-2504; edu-optional-lease-terms-id). Court forms and federal forms, such as the lead-based paint disclosure, were not reviewed here.

title: Converting Rentals to Condominiums
bodyText: Idaho has no statute requiring notice to tenants, a right of first refusal or relocation help when rental housing is converted to condominiums or other ownership units, or converted to short-term or transient use. The Condominium Property Act binds condominium owners and their tenants to the declaration and bylaws once a project is created (Idaho Code § 55-1516) but has no conversion rule. Cities may not adopt rules that regulate rent, fees or deposits for private rentals (Idaho Code § 55-306), but whether a city may regulate conversions in other ways was not reviewed. Your duties to existing tenants in a conversion are the ordinary ones: honor each lease to its end, give written notice of nonrenewal at least 30 days before (Idaho Code § 55-304(2)), end a month-to-month tenancy only on one month's written notice (Idaho Code § 55-208), and refund deposits when tenancies end (Idaho Code § 6-321(2)); a buyer of a unit during a tenancy becomes liable for refunding the deposit (Idaho Code § 6-321(3)). Short-term rental rules are in edu-rental-inspection-id.

title: Penalty for Entering Without Notice
bodyText: Idaho has no statute requiring notice before you enter or inspect a rental, so there is no statutory penalty for entering without notice (edu-no-entry-statute-id). Your notice duty comes from the lease: the library's Idaho lease promises at least 24 hours' notice except in an emergency (landlords-access, inspection-rights). Breaking that promise is a breach of the lease, and if it materially affects the tenant's health and safety the tenant may sue for damages and specific performance after a three-day written notice (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5), (d)); that suit is not available for tracts of land of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). Entering by force or threats is a forcible entry, with possible treble damages (Idaho Code § 6-301; Idaho Code § 6-317). Trespass and privacy claims are case law.

title: Optional Clauses in the Idaho Lease
bodyText: Idaho's library offers these optional clauses. Use each only if it fits your rental; no Idaho statute forbids any of them and, where a charge is involved, the lease states the amount or method, as Idaho's fee law requires (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)). Casualty termination (casualty-termination-id): no Idaho statute governs destruction of leased premises, so the lease may let either side end it. Tenant-caused damage (tenant-caused-damage-id): rent keeps running while you repair damage the tenant caused; Idaho also allows treble damages for waste by a tenant for years (Idaho Code § 6-201). Notice-service fee (notice-service-fee-id), a stated reasonable fee (Idaho Code § 55-305(1), (2)). Collection fee (collection-fee-id): a licensed collection agency may collect fees the agreement creating the debt expressly authorizes, except as otherwise prohibited by law (Idaho Code § 26-2229A(4)(c)). Interest on unpaid amounts (unpaid-amounts-interest-id), at a written rate; without a written rate the statutory legal rate is 12% a year (Idaho Code § 28-22-104(1)), but under a written lease an owner may not charge interest the lease does not include without 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)(b)). Shared optional clauses that apply in Idaho as written: utility allowance (utility-allowance-cap-co), utility shutoff notices to you (utility-shutoff-notice-authorization-co), television and internet installations (telecom-access-mn), EV charger installation (ev-charger-installation-hi) and a guaranty (guaranty-as). Idaho clauses added for utilities, liens and renewal: utilities you bill (utility-billing-id), utility transfer (utility-transfer-id), no liens for tenant work (no-liens-id) and automatic renewal (automatic-renewal-id). Other Idaho optional clauses, each stating your dollar maximum or method where it charges anything: government fees (government-fee-reimbursement-id), government fines the tenant causes (governmental-fines-id), carpet cleaning at move-out (carpet-cleaning-id), scheduled rent changes (rent-escalation-id), property tax increases (tax-escalation-id), tenant minor repairs (tenant-repair-agreement-id), approved repairers (designated-repairer-id), heat and freeze protection (heat-freeze-protection-id), pest reporting and treatment (pest-cooperation-id), property rules (rules-id), notice of extended absence (extended-absence-notice-id) and your right to remedy a tenant's breach (landlord-self-cure-id). More shared optional clauses that apply in Idaho as written: showings (showing-notice-la), receipt of the lease copy (lease-copy-receipt-hi), move-in condition report (move-in-condition-report-as), rent concessions (rent-concession-wi), owner occupancy (owner-occupancy-termination-ar), government inspections (rental-inspection-cooperation-mn), condemnation (eminent-domain-vi), association documents (association-documents-delivery-ks), furnishings and items not included (furnishings-included-la, appliances-excluded-la), marijuana (cannabis-restrictions-ak), firearm discharge and storage (firearm-rules-ks), waterbeds (waterbed-mn), animal care in the tenant's absence (animal-care-access-vi), scheduled services entry (scheduled-services-entry-la) and an emergency contact (emergency-contact-co). Binding arbitration of money claims (arbitration-agreement) is also offered; see edu-binding-arbitration-id. If the property is inside a city business improvement district, the statutory disclosure (special-district-representation-id) is required, not optional (Idaho Code § 50-2624). One option has its own statute: a lease with an option to purchase a property of one to four dwelling units is a transfer under Idaho's Property Condition Disclosure Act, so you must give the buyer-tenant a signed disclosure form within 10 days after accepting the offer, and a tenant who gets the form after signing may rescind within three business days for a specific objection, with listed exemptions (Idaho Code § 55-2504; Idaho Code § 55-2509; Idaho Code § 55-2515; Idaho Code § 55-2505). Idaho has no separate statute for rent-to-own or lease-option homes, and the library offers no option clause; get advice before granting one.

title: Flags and Signs at an Idaho Rental
bodyText: Idaho has no statute giving a tenant a right to display a flag, a political sign or anything else at a rental, and none that limits what your lease or rules may forbid. Idaho's flag and sign statutes bind homeowner's associations, not landlords. An association may not add, amend or enforce a covenant 'in such a way that prohibits or has the effect of prohibiting the display of a political sign' (Idaho Code § 55-3209(1)), or of the United States flag, the Idaho flag, the POW/MIA flag or an armed forces flag (Idaho Code § 55-3210(1)), though it may adopt reasonable rules on the 'time, size, place, number, and manner of display of political signs' (Idaho Code § 55-3209(2)) and on flagpoles and flag size (Idaho Code § 55-3210(2)). A political sign there is 'any fixed, ground-mounted display in support of or in opposition to a candidate for office or a ballot measure' (Idaho Code § 55-3209(5)). The protection is written for a 'member', meaning 'any person or entity owning or possessing an interest in residential real property' in the association (Idaho Code § 55-3203(8)); whether a tenant counts is not settled, so assume your association may apply the same rules to your tenant's signs and flags as to yours. Idaho's Constitution says 'Every person may freely speak, write and publish on all subjects' (Idaho Const. art. I, § 9); whether that limits a private landlord is a question only case law could answer, and the library treats it as a limit on government. So your lease decides. The library's use-of-property clause (common-area-use) bars signs visible from outside without your consent and keeps any display the law entitles the tenant to make. Cautious course: keep any display rule content-neutral (size, placement, safety, damage), apply it to every tenant, and don't single out religious or national-origin displays, which risks a fair-housing claim (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(b)).

title: Candidates and Canvassers at an Idaho Rental
bodyText: No Idaho statute requires you to let political candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration workers into an apartment building or onto the common areas of your rental to reach tenants' doors, or to set aside space for campaign literature. The one Idaho access right is in the Manufactured Home Residency Act, which this library does not cover: a resident association in a manufactured home community may use its facilities, 'Subject to reasonable notice and community facility rules', for 'forums for or speeches by public officials or candidates for public office' (Idaho Code § 55-2013A(1)). Idaho's ban on electioneering within 250 feet of a polling place on voting days does not apply 'to conduct occurring on private property located adjacent to a building designated as a polling place' (Idaho Code § 18-2318(2)(b)), but it does apply inside a building that is itself a polling place (Idaho Code § 18-2318(2)(a)), so if a room in your property is used as one, keep campaigning out of that building on voting days. Idaho's Constitution protects speech (Idaho Const. art. I, § 9) and the right 'to assemble in a peaceable manner' (Idaho Const. art. I, § 10); whether those clauses reach a private landlord is a question only case law could answer. So outsiders' access to common areas is your decision as owner. Your tenants may still invite a candidate or canvasser into their own unit as a guest (see edu-no-guest-rights-statute-id). Cautious course: if you limit soliciting or canvassing, post one rule and apply it the same way to every campaign, cause and faith, since uneven enforcement against a religious group risks a fair-housing claim (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(b)).

title: Religious and Cultural Displays in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute giving a tenant a right to display religious or cultural items (for example a doorpost item, a wreath or a prayer flag) at a rental, and none that limits a landlord's display rules. Two rules shape any limit you set. First, Idaho's Human Rights Act makes it unlawful to discriminate 'in the terms, conditions or privileges of a real estate transaction' because of religion or national origin (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(b)), and a rental is a real estate transaction (Idaho Code § 67-5902(12)); the federal Fair Housing Act says the same for the 'terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling' (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b)). A rule that allows some displays but not those of a particular faith or culture, or is enforced that way, is risky. Idaho's housing rules do not apply to a room in your own home or to a two-family building where you or your family live in one unit (Idaho Code § 67-5910(7)); federal law has its own exemptions. Second, Idaho's religious-freedom statute binds only 'government' (Idaho Code § 73-401(3)), and whether the Constitution's guarantee of 'The exercise and enjoyment of religious faith and worship' (Idaho Const. art. I, § 4) reaches a private landlord is a question only case law could answer. What to do: keep any display rule content-neutral (size, placement, fire safety, damage to doors and walls), apply it to every tenant, and consider allowing small doorpost or door-frame items that cause no damage. The library's use-of-property clause (common-area-use) already keeps any display the law entitles the tenant to make.

title: Tenant Organizing in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute giving tenants of ordinary rentals a right to form or join a tenant association, or barring a landlord from interfering with one. Idaho's two organizing statutes cover only parks this library does not cover: residents of a manufactured home community 'have the right to organize a resident or homeowner's association' and 'the right to peacefully assemble and freely associate' (Idaho Code § 55-2013A(1)), and a community landlord may not retaliate against a resident who has 'Organized, become a member of or served as an official in a community resident association' (Idaho Code § 55-2015(3)); floating home marina tenants have a similar right (Idaho Code § 55-2716(1)). The Constitution's right 'to assemble in a peaceable manner' (Idaho Const. art. I, § 10) is generally read as a limit on government; whether it reaches a private landlord was not researched in case law. Two rules still point toward caution. Idaho's Human Rights Act makes it unlawful to discriminate against anyone who 'has opposed any practice made unlawful by this chapter' (Idaho Code § 67-5911), and the federal Fair Housing Act bars interfering with anyone 'on account of his having aided or encouraged any other person' (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3617) in exercising fair housing rights, so a tenants' group raising discrimination complaints is protected. Idaho has no general anti-retaliation statute for ordinary rentals (see edu-no-retaliation-statute-id). What to do: don't end tenancies, raise rent or cut services because tenants meet, organize or complain together; you may set neutral rules for using common rooms that apply to everyone.

title: No Idaho Guest-Rights Statute
bodyText:
Idaho has no statute giving tenants a right to receive guests, visitors or suppliers, barring a fee for guests, or making any guest right non-waivable, in any size of building. Guest rules are lease terms: the library's guest clauses (guest-policy and guest-policy-day-limit) carry Idaho.

Three Idaho rules touch guests. Any charge you make for guests is a fee, which 'shall be reasonable' (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)) and, under a written lease entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, must be in the lease or added on 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)-(3)). Damage a guest causes is not normal wear and tear, which excludes misuse 'by the tenant or members of his household, or their invitees or guests' (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)), so you may charge it against the deposit if the deposit terms cover damage. And fair housing law requires reasonable accommodations in rules for a tenant with a disability (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B)), which can include a caregiver's visits or a live-in aide.

Cautious course: courts generally treat ordinary visitors as part of a tenant's use of the home, so don't bar ordinary visits; set even-handed limits on overnight stays instead.

title: Marijuana Rules for Idaho Rentals
bodyText:
Marijuana is illegal in Idaho for every purpose. 'It is unlawful for any person to possess a controlled substance' without a valid prescription or other authority under the controlled substances chapter (Idaho Code § 37-2732(c)); possessing more than three ounces of marijuana is a felony and smaller amounts a misdemeanor with a fine of at least $300 for adults (Idaho Code § 37-2732(e)). Idaho has no medical or adult-use marijuana law, its Constitution says nothing about cannabis, and no Idaho statute protects a marijuana user in housing or limits a landlord's marijuana rule. A tenant's medical card from another state gives no protection here.

So you may ban smoking, vaping, growing, possessing and using marijuana anywhere on the property. The library's smoking clause (smoking-policy-id) already bans smoking marijuana; the optional marijuana clause (cannabis-restrictions-ak) lets you also ban growing and any possession or use.

Drug use on the premises is also an eviction ground on its own: a tenant is in unlawful detainer if anyone 'is, or has been, engaged in the unlawful delivery, production or use of a controlled substance on the premises of the leased property' during the term (Idaho Code § 6-303(5); see edu-expedited-drug-eviction-id). Recover possession only through the court.

Two things are not marijuana and should not be swept into your rule by accident: an FDA-approved cannabidiol or nabiximols drug, because 'Marijuana' does not include 'drug product in finished dosage formulation that has been approved by the United States food and drug administration' (Idaho Code § 37-2701(u)), and licensed industrial hemp with no more than 0.3% THC (Idaho Code § 37-2701(u)(1)). Store-bought hemp or CBD products sit in a grey zone, because THC-containing material possessed without a hemp license is presumed to be marijuana (Idaho Code § 37-2701(u)); the library's clause names marijuana only.

If a tenant asks to use marijuana as a disability accommodation, answer in writing and take advice; no Idaho statute allows it, and federal fair housing law was not reviewed on this point.

title: Firearm Rules in Idaho Leases
bodyText:
No Idaho statute limits a private landlord's lease rules on firearms, and none protects keeping a firearm in a locked vehicle in a rental parking lot. Idaho's Constitution says 'The people have the right to keep and bear arms, which right shall not be abridged' (Idaho Const. art. I, § 11); it is written as a limit on lawmaking, and whether it reaches a private lease term is a question only case law could answer.

The concealed-weapons statute expressly leaves private rights alone: 'Nothing in subsection (3) or (4) of this section shall be construed to limit the existing rights of a private property owner, private tenant, private employer, or private business entity' (Idaho Code § 18-3302(25)). The same statute lets a person carry a concealed weapon without a license 'On property in which the person has any ownership or leasehold interest' (Idaho Code § 18-3302(3)(b)), so your tenant needs no license to carry at home, and a lease rule on firearms is a contract term you enforce as a breach of the lease, not a crime.

Except where a state statute expressly allows it, cities and counties may not regulate the possession, carrying or storage of firearms (Idaho Code § 18-3302J(2)), though they may regulate discharge (Idaho Code § 18-3302J(3)-(4)); if you are a public body such as a housing authority, that ban may reach your own firearm policy, so take advice.

The library offers an optional firearm clause (firearm-rules-ks) that bars discharge except in lawful defense, requires safe storage and makes the tenant answer for firearm damage. A lease ban on keeping firearms in the home is not barred by any Idaho statute, but the library does not offer one because the constitutional question is unsettled; if you want one, add your own clause after taking legal advice.

title: Quiet Possession in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute that writes a covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession into a residential lease or says what breaches one. Whether every Idaho lease carries one by implication is a question for case law; assume it does. Idaho's statutes protect a tenant's possession in other ways. A landlord who, 'after entering peaceably upon real property, turns out, by force, threats or menacing conduct, the party in possession' commits a forcible entry (Idaho Code § 6-301), and damages for a forcible or unlawful entry 'may be entered for three (3) times the amount at which the actual damages are assessed' (Idaho Code § 6-317); recover possession only through the court (see edu-self-help-eviction-id). A tenant may also sue for 'Breach of any term or provision of the lease or rental agreement materially affecting the health and safety of the tenant, whether explicitly or implicitly a part thereof' (Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5)), after giving you three days' written notice listing each breach (Idaho Code § 6-320(d)); this does not apply 'to tracts of land of five (5) acres or more used for agricultural purposes' (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)), and damages in such a suit may be trebled too (Idaho Code § 6-317). What to do: enter only as the lease's entry clause allows (landlords-access), don't change locks or cut services to pressure a tenant, and act promptly on complaints about other tenants who disturb the peace (no-disturbance).

title: Illegal Use and the Idaho Lease
bodyText: Two Idaho statutes end a lease because of how the premises are used. First, if a tenant or occupant uses the place 'for the purposes of lewdness, assignation, or prostitution, such use makes void the lease or other title under which he holds, at the option of the owner' (Idaho Code § 52-414) (see edu-lewd-use-lease-void-id). A lessor who acts in good faith to void the lease this way also avoids a court order closing the building while a moral-nuisance case is pending (Idaho Code § 52-406(2)). The statute lets the owner re-enter 'without process of law', but go to court if the facts are disputed. Second, a tenant is in unlawful detainer if anyone is or has been engaged in the unlawful delivery, production or use of a controlled substance on the premises during the term (Idaho Code § 6-303(5)), and a judgment on that ground declares the lease forfeited (Idaho Code § 6-316(1)) (see edu-expedited-drug-eviction-id). No Idaho statute voids or ends a lease for any other illegal use, such as gambling or stolen goods. For those, your remedy comes from the lease: the library's residential-use clause (residential-use-only) bars illegal and non-residential use, and a breach lets you serve a three-day notice to perform or quit (Idaho Code § 6-303(3)). Recover possession through the court.

title: Children in Idaho Rentals
bodyText: No Idaho statute requires a lease to say anything about children who will live in the unit, and none limits renting to, or bars discrimination against, households with children. Idaho's Human Rights Act protects race, color, religion, sex, national origin and disability in housing, but not familial status (Idaho Code § 67-5909). Federal law does: the Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful 'to refuse to negotiate for the sale or rental of, or otherwise make unavailable or deny, a dwelling to any person because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin' (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a)), to set different terms or services on that basis (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b)), or to publish any notice, statement or advertisement indicating a preference based on familial status (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c)).
