The federal definition of familial status and the federal exemptions, including housing for older persons, were not reviewed for this row. No Idaho statute sets an occupancy limit for private rentals; any limit you set should be reasonable and applied to everyone. What to do: list every occupant, adults and children, in the occupants clause (permitted-occupants); don't charge more, steer families to certain units or set different rules (for pools, yards or quiet hours) because children live there; and don't advertise "adults only" or "no kids".

title: Parking Rules for Idaho Rentals
bodyText:
No Idaho statute requires you to give a tenant written parking rules before signing, to state in the lease whether parking comes with the unit, or to limit mid-lease parking changes or the vehicle details you may ask for.

Four Idaho rules still shape a parking policy. Towing: you may have an unauthorized vehicle towed or booted if a sign 'in a clearly conspicuous location, in large print' says unauthorized vehicles will be removed or booted at the owner's expense and names the towing firm (Idaho Code § 49-1806(1)), and 'No vehicle shall be considered unauthorized and subject to removal or booting' (Idaho Code § 49-1806(3)) just because its registration is expired or improper (see edu-towing-id).

Fees: a parking fee, permit charge or parking fine is a fee that 'shall be reasonable' (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)) and, under a written lease entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, must be in the lease or added on 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)-(3)).

Changes: in a month-to-month tenancy you may change parking terms by written notice at least 15 days before the end of a month (Idaho Code § 55-304(1)); during a fixed term, change them only by agreement.

Your own rules: the library's vehicle clause (parking-vehicle-rules-id) already sets them for Idaho.

What to do: put your parking rules and any fee in the lease or an addendum signed with it, post a compliant towing sign before relying on towing, and give written notice of any change.

title: Charging Separately for Parking in Idaho
bodyText: No Idaho statute requires you to price parking separately from rent ("unbundled" parking), and none bars it. If you charge for parking separately, Idaho's fee rules apply: the charge 'shall be reasonable' (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)), and you may not charge a fee 'In an amount greater than that agreed upon in the rental agreement' (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)(a)), or one 'That is not included in the rental agreement' (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)(b)) unless the lease is oral or you give 30 days' written notice of the change (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)(b)(i)-(ii)), for leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023 (Idaho Code § 55-305(3)). If you instead build parking into the rent, the fee rules do not limit the amount, because the fee statute does not 'limit the amount that can be charged for rent' (Idaho Code § 55-305(4)). Cities set off-street parking standards through zoning (Idaho Code § 67-6518), and larger cities must stop requiring off-street parking for most accessory dwelling units by February 1, 2027 (Idaho Code § 67-6541(2)(b), (6)). A city may not adopt an ordinance that would 'regulate rent, fees, or deposits charged for leasing private residential property' (Idaho Code § 55-306), so a local rule forcing separate parking prices may be open to challenge (not tested in case law reviewed here). What to do: state any parking charge, and whether a space comes with the unit, in the lease (see parking-ks-oh-ca and assigned-parking-space).

title: Barring Non-Tenants in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho's criminal trespass statute lets you, as owner, bar a person who is not your tenant from property you control, such as the common areas and parking lots of a multi-unit building. A person has reason to know he is not permitted when, 'except under a landlord-tenant relationship, he fails to depart immediately from the real property of another after being notified by the owner or his agent to do so, or he returns without permission or invitation within one (1) year, unless a longer period of time is designated by the owner or his agent' (Idaho Code § 18-7008(2)(a)). You may revoke permission to be on your property 'at any time, for any reason, orally, in writing, or by any other form of notice reasonably apparent to the permitted person' (Idaho Code § 18-7008(5)); the civil trespass statute says the same (Idaho Code § 6-202(6)). The limits: the statute does not reach your tenant, who is 'a tenant pursuant to a valid lease' (Idaho Code § 18-7008(7)); to remove a tenant you must evict through the court. It also excuses a person present on 'An invitation, whether express or implied' (Idaho Code § 18-7008(6)(a)(i)), and whether your tenant's invitation lets a barred person into the tenant's own unit, or across common areas to reach it, is not settled by the statute. Police, paramedics and other emergency workers acting within their lawful duties are excused (Idaho Code § 18-7008(6)(b)). What to do: give any no-trespass notice in writing, naming the person, the reason and the period, keep a copy, and apply the practice evenly to avoid a fair-housing claim. Ask your tenants in writing not to invite a barred person; no Idaho statute bars a lease covenant to that effect, but the library does not offer one (the shared barred-person clause carries terms built on another state's law), so add your own after taking advice.

title: Tenant Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText: No Idaho statute gives a tenant a right to install a security camera or video doorbell, or limits a landlord's rule on them. Your lease decides: the library's use-of-property clause (common-area-use) already bars fastening anything to the property's surfaces without your consent, and the alterations clause (no-alterations) covers wiring and installation. Idaho's criminal laws set outer limits on how anyone, tenant or landlord, may use cameras. Recording sound: it is a felony to willfully intercept an oral communication (Idaho Code § 18-6702(1)), but 'It is lawful under this chapter for a person to intercept a wire, electronic or oral communication when one (1) of the parties to the communication has given prior consent' (Idaho Code § 18-6702(2)(d)), so a doorbell that records conversations the user is not part of carries risk. Recording images: video voyeurism covers an imaging device placed with a sexual or degrading purpose at 'a place where a person would have a reasonable expectation of privacy, without the knowledge or consent of the person using such place' (Idaho Code § 18-6605(2)), and it is a misdemeanor to peer into the window of an inhabited building on another's property 'without visible or lawful purpose' (Idaho Code § 18-7006). What to do: decide whether you allow tenant cameras, require written consent for anything attached to the building, ask that cameras not point into other units' windows or doors, and suggest turning off audio recording in shared spaces. If you install cameras yourself, keep them out of the inside of units and other private spaces.

title: Questions You May Not Ask Applicants
bodyText: Idaho's Human Rights Act has its own inquiry and record rule, separate from the ban on refusing to rent. It is unlawful for an owner or anyone else engaging in a rental 'to use a form of application for a real estate transaction, or to make a record or inquiry in connection with a prospective real estate transaction, which indicates, directly or indirectly, an intent to make a limitation, specification, or discrimination' (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(f)) because of race, color, religion, sex or national origin, and the housing provisions also cover disability (Idaho Code § 67-5909). A rental is a real estate transaction (Idaho Code § 67-5902(12)). The same subsection covers ads, statements and signs. The rule does not reach a room in your own home or a two-family building where you or your family live in the other unit (Idaho Code § 67-5910(7)). The federal Fair Housing Act separately bars any notice or statement 'with respect to the sale or rental of a dwelling that indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination' based on its protected classes, which add familial status (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c)). What to do: take religion, race, national origin, sex, disability and pregnancy questions off your application and out of interviews; ask every applicant the same questions; ask about disability only to verify a requested accommodation; and don't keep notes that record an applicant's protected traits.

title: Immigration Status and Idaho Rentals
bodyText: No Idaho statute bars you from asking about an applicant's immigration or citizenship status, and none requires you to ask or makes it unlawful to rent to someone who is not lawfully present. Idaho's Immigration Cooperation and Enforcement Act creates crimes of illegal entry and reentry and of knowingly transporting 'into this state a dangerous illegal alien' (Idaho Code § 18-9006(1)), but it says nothing about renting or housing. National origin is protected: refusing to rent, setting different terms, or using an application or inquiry that indicates an intent to discriminate because of national origin is unlawful (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)), and federal law also bars discrimination because of national origin in renting (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a)). Because immigration questions can look like national-origin screening, the cautious course is not to ask about immigration status at all; if you need to verify identity or income, ask every applicant for the same kinds of documents and accept a range of them (for example, a foreign passport or other government ID).

title: Screening Applicants in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute that regulates tenant screening as such. Nothing limits your use of criminal history, credit reports, eviction history or income tests, sets look-back periods, requires a conditional offer before a criminal check, or shields you from negligence claims for renting to someone with a record. Your criteria are your own, within these Idaho rules. Fair housing: you may not refuse to rent or set different terms because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin or disability (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)), and your application and questions must not indicate an intent to discriminate (Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(f)); federal law adds familial status (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604). Apply the same written criteria to every applicant. Source of income is not protected in Idaho (see edu-source-of-income-id). Credit freezes: a tenant's credit freeze does not stop a screening company from reporting to you, because a freeze does not prohibit disclosure where 'The third party is using the information solely for criminal record information, tenant screening, employment screening' (Idaho Code § 28-52-105(2)(f)). Eviction records: dismissed eviction cases filed on or after January 1, 2025 can be shielded from public court records, so a court search may not show them (see edu-eviction-record-shielding-id). Registered sex offenders: except as the section otherwise provides (including a court order under Idaho Code § 18-8331(3)), a person required to register 'may not reside in any residential dwelling unit with more than one (1) other person who is also required to register' (Idaho Code § 18-8331(1)), and no one may operate a residence for registrants in violation of that limit (Idaho Code § 18-8331(5)); if two registrants already live in a unit, don't add a third. Application fees: Idaho does not limit them (see edu-no-application-fee-rule-id). Federal consumer-report rules on how you obtain and use screening reports also apply and were not reviewed here.

title: No Idaho Rule on Screening Rental Staff
bodyText: No Idaho statute requires you to run background checks on maintenance workers, leasing agents or other employees who have keys or access to tenants' homes, and none limits such checks for rental staff. Idaho's Human Rights Act still governs how you hire: it bars employment discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age (40 and over) and disability (Idaho Code § 67-5909(1)). Cautious course: because you hold keys to tenants' homes and the library's entry clause (landlords-access) lets your agents and contractors enter, screen anyone you give key access to, using the same written criteria for every candidate; keep a key log; and require your contractors to vouch for their workers. Federal consumer-report rules apply if you use a screening company for employees and were not reviewed here.

title: Keeping Tenants' Information Private
bodyText: No Idaho statute bars a landlord from sharing a tenant's or applicant's information, sets a consent rule for doing so, or requires a privacy notice. A few general rules apply. 'a person shall not intentionally communicate an individual's social security number to the general public' (Idaho Code § 28-52-108(1)). If you keep computerized data with a tenant's name plus a Social Security number, driver's license or Idaho ID number, or a financial account or card number with its access code, with the name or those numbers unencrypted (Idaho Code § 28-51-104(5)), and that data is illegally acquired, you must investigate and, if misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely, notify the tenant 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay' (Idaho Code § 28-51-105(1)); an intentional failure to give notice can bring a fine of up to $25,000 per breach (Idaho Code § 28-51-107). See edu-tenant-records-id. Cautious course: share tenant information only with the tenant's written consent, with your own agents and contractors who need it, or as the law requires (for example a subpoena); when another landlord asks for a reference, stick to facts you can document; and keep Social Security numbers and bank details out of anything posted or emailed broadly. Federal consumer-report rules on sharing screening reports were not reviewed here, nor were privacy torts in case law.

title: Rent Records and Data Security in Idaho
bodyText: Idaho has no statute requiring a landlord to keep a rent ledger, give receipts, give a tenant a payment history on request, attach a ledger to a nonpayment notice or answer a records request. The records duties Idaho does impose are these. Deposits: if you refund less than the full deposit, you must send 'a signed statement itemizing the amounts lawfully retained by the landlord, the purpose for the amounts retained, and a detailed list of expenditures made from the deposit' (Idaho Code § 6-321(2)), so keep receipts for deposit deductions; a third-party manager must also hold deposits in a separate account (Idaho Code § 6-321(4)). Nonpayment notices must state 'the amount which is due' (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)), which needs accurate records. Data security: Idaho has no statute requiring a written information-security program, but an individual or business that owns or licenses computerized personal information about an Idaho resident (a name with a Social Security number, driver's license or Idaho ID number, or a financial account or card number with its access code) must investigate a breach and notify affected residents if misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely (Idaho Code § 28-51-105(1)); keeping your own notice procedures that meet the statute's timing counts as compliance (Idaho Code § 28-51-106(1)). Applicant files with Social Security numbers and bank details are covered. What to do: keep a ledger for each tenancy and give the tenant a copy when you serve a nonpayment notice or on request; keep deposit receipts; encrypt or lock up applicant and tenant financial data and shred it when no longer needed; and have a written breach-notice plan.

title: Online Portals for Idaho Tenants
bodyText:
No Idaho statute regulates tenant portals or bars you from requiring rent to be paid online; the library's payment clause (acceptable-payment-methods) lets you list the methods you accept.

Three Idaho rules shape a portal. First, Idaho's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act applies 'only to transactions between parties each of which has agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means' (Idaho Code § 28-50-105(b)), and a party who agrees 'may refuse to conduct other transactions by electronic means', a right that 'may not be waived by agreement' (Idaho Code § 28-50-105(c)). What counts as an "other transaction" under a lease is not settled, so a lease term forcing every future signature or notice through the portal may not hold if the tenant later refuses.

Second, an electronic record you send is 'not enforceable against the recipient' if you stop the tenant from storing or printing it (Idaho Code § 28-50-108(c)), so let tenants download everything.

Third, notices whose method a statute sets, such as three-day eviction notices, must still be served the statutory way (Idaho Code § 6-304; see edu-notice-service-id), so a portal message is not enough.

Any portal or convenience fee is a fee that must be reasonable and, under a written lease entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, must be in the lease or added on 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)-(3)). No Idaho statute bars a lease term requiring the portal for payments.

The library offers no mandatory-portal clause for notices and signatures because of the non-waivable right to refuse; if you want one, add your own after taking advice.

title: Rent-Pricing Software and Idaho Antitrust Law
bodyText: No Idaho statute mentions setting rents with an algorithm or pricing software, and Idaho's ban on local rent regulation (Idaho Code § 55-306) means no city may limit how you set rent. But Idaho's Competition Act applies to landlords like any other business: 'A contract, combination, or conspiracy between two (2) or more persons in unreasonable restraint of Idaho commerce is unlawful' (Idaho Code § 48-104), and the Act is read 'in harmony with federal judicial interpretations of comparable federal antitrust statutes' (Idaho Code § 48-102(3)). A person injured by a violation may sue for damages, costs and attorney's fees, and a court must raise the award up to three times the damages for a per se violation of the restraint-of-trade rule (Idaho Code § 48-113); the Attorney General can also sue (Idaho Code § 48-108). No Idaho case reviewed here says whether shared pricing software is such a combination, and federal antitrust law was not reviewed. Cautious course: set your own rents and lease terms; don't agree with other landlords on rents, concessions or terms; don't share your nonpublic rent, occupancy or lease data with competitors; and avoid a pricing service that pools competitors' nonpublic data to recommend rents. Using public listings and your own data is the safer path.

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance in Idaho
bodyText:
No Idaho statute requires renter's insurance, bars a lease from requiring it, caps the coverage you may require, lets the tenant choose the insurer, regulates insurance you buy for the tenant and bill back, or requires you to tell the tenant in writing that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings.

The lease decides: the library's renter's insurance clause (tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca) carries Idaho; it requires the tenant to carry renter's insurance with liability coverage of at least the amount you set, and says your insurance does not cover the tenant's property.

If you buy a policy for a tenant who fails to carry one and charge the tenant for it, or charge any fee tied to insurance, that charge is a fee that 'shall be reasonable' (Idaho Code § 55-305(1)) and, under a written lease entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, must be stated in the lease or added on 30 days' written notice (Idaho Code § 55-305(2)-(3)).

What to do: state the minimum liability amount in the lease, let the tenant choose any licensed insurer, ask for proof at signing and each year, and decide in advance (and write into the lease) what happens if coverage lapses.

title: Insurance Claims Between Landlord and Tenant
bodyText: No Idaho statute governs how a tenant's or landlord's insurance claims are handled between you: nothing requires you to cooperate with a tenant's claim, bars your insurer from pursuing the tenant for damage the tenant caused (subrogation), or makes a lease waiver of subrogation required or void. These are matters for the lease, your policies and case law. The library's clauses already set the main terms for Idaho: the tenant carries renter's insurance and your insurance does not cover the tenant's property (tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca), the tenant answers for damage the tenant's household or guests cause (tenant-caused-damage-id), and casualty without tenant fault is handled by casualty-termination-id. Damage beyond normal wear and tear caused by the tenant, household 'or their invitees or guests' may be charged against the deposit if the deposit terms cover damage (Idaho Code § 6-321(1)). What to do: read your landlord policy for subrogation terms before agreeing to any lease waiver of subrogation, ask tenants to name you as an interested party on their renter's policy, and report losses to your insurer promptly.

title: No Idaho Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: No Idaho statute requires a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to register a policy with any government office, or to tell tenants whether you are insured, and Idaho has no state rental registration program. A city or county may not adopt an ordinance that would 'regulate rent, fees, or deposits charged for leasing private residential property' (Idaho Code § 55-306); whether that would reach a local insurance or registration rule is not settled. Your lender, homeowner's association or condominium association may still require coverage. What to do: carry landlord liability and property coverage anyway, check any loan or association insurance conditions, and keep the lease's statement that your policy does not cover the tenant's belongings (tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca).

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Idaho follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Idaho Code § 28-3-310). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Idaho Code § 28-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Idaho's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Idaho's eviction and lease statutes searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Idaho's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
